profiles.name: Ashwagandha
profiles.summary: Ashwagandha probably lowers cortisol a little and may modestly help stress and sleep, especially in people with insomnia, but results are inconsistent, trials are small and short, and claims about muscle gains are not established.
profiles.description: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) is an evergreen shrub whose root has long been used in Ayurvedic medicine. Most supplements are root extracts; some use root and leaf. Many trials test branded extracts such as KSM-66, Shoden or Sensoril.
profiles.biological_function: Ashwagandha extracts contain withanolides, described by NIH ODS as key constituents. In trials it lowered cortisol, a stress hormone, and shifted some other hormones, including testosterone in men and thyroid hormone T4. How these changes link to how people feel is not well understood.

formulations.name: Root extract
formulations.notes: Most common commercial form (NIH ODS). Used in most trials.

formulations.name: Root-and-leaf extract
formulations.notes: Root and leaf have different chemical compositions (NIH ODS), so results from one may not apply to the other.

formulations.name: Branded standardised extracts
formulations.notes: Products such as KSM-66, Shoden and Sensoril differ in withanolide content and dose; a 2026 meta-analysis suggested hormone effects may vary with withanolide content.

claims.claim: Ashwagandha lowers cortisol
claims.popular_framing: Ashwagandha crushes your cortisol.
claims.question: Does ashwagandha lower cortisol?
claims.outcome: Blood (serum) and morning cortisol levels
claims.population: Mostly stressed but otherwise healthy adults, many trials in India.
claims.bottom_line: Probably, a little. Several meta-analyses find cortisol drops modestly compared with placebo, but the trials are small and it is unclear how much that lab change matters for how people feel.
claims.what_research_found: A 2025 meta-analysis (7 cortisol trials) found cortisol fell by 1.16 µg/dL versus placebo. A 2024 meta-analysis (9 trials, 558 people) found a 2.58 µg/dL fall, and a 2026 hormone meta-analysis (23 trials, 1,706 people) also found lower cortisol. In one 60-day trial, 240 mg/day of a standardised extract lowered morning cortisol compared with placebo.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: A lower cortisol reading did not always come with feeling less stressed: the 2025 meta-analysis found cortisol fell but perceived stress did not change significantly. Long-term effects are unknown.
claims.limitations: Trials are small and short, with moderate risk of bias; different branded extracts and doses were used.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Standardised ashwagandha extracts. The 2025 meta-analysis included trials using 250 mg/day or more for at least 2 weeks; one cited trial used 240 mg/day for 60 days. NIH ODS describes trials lasting 6–8 weeks.

factors.study_quality: Randomised placebo-controlled trials; moderate risk of bias, some lacking allocation concealment.
factors.consistency: Consistent direction across three meta-analyses.
factors.effect_size: About 1.2 to 2.6 µg/dL lower in two meta-analyses; the 2026 review reports only a standardised difference (SMD -1.18).
factors.clinical_significance: Unclear: a lab change that did not consistently translate into feeling less stressed.
factors.sample_size: Hundreds to about 1,700 participants across reviews, mostly small trials.
factors.population: Mostly stressed adults; NIH ODS notes the trials in one key review were all run in India; generalisability uncertain.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Branded extracts are used in several trials; in one cited trial an author had previously received funding from an extract manufacturer for unrelated studies. Funding of most included trials is not stated in the review abstracts.
factors.reproducibility: Several meta-analyses agree on direction; the abstracts do not say how many trials were independently funded.
factors.formulation_dose: Many different branded extracts with different withanolide content.

claims.claim: Ashwagandha reduces feelings of stress and anxiety
claims.popular_framing: Ashwagandha is the herb that melts stress and anxiety.
claims.question: Does ashwagandha make you feel less stressed or anxious?
claims.outcome: Self-rated stress (Perceived Stress Scale) and anxiety scores
claims.population: Adults with self-reported stress or anxiety.
claims.bottom_line: Maybe. Some reviews find lower stress and anxiety scores, but another found no significant effect on perceived stress, and a 12-week placebo-controlled trial found no difference.
claims.what_research_found: A 2024 meta-analysis of 9 trials (558 people) found lower perceived stress (about 4.7 points) and anxiety scores versus placebo. NIH ODS summarises a 2021 review of 7 Indian studies (491 adults) reporting less stress and anxiety. But a 2025 meta-analysis found no significant effect on perceived stress, and a 12-week trial in overweight adults aged 40–75 found stress improved no more than with placebo.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It is not established that ashwagandha reliably reduces stress across different groups, or that it treats anxiety disorders. Long-term benefits and safety are unknown.
claims.limitations: Small, short trials, many run in India with branded extracts; wide confidence intervals; results differ between reviews.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Branded root or root-and-leaf extracts; cited trials used 240 mg/day for 60 days and 200 mg twice daily for 12 weeks, and the 2025 meta-analysis included doses of 250 mg/day or more. NIH ODS describes trials lasting 6–8 weeks.

factors.study_quality: Randomised placebo-controlled trials, generally moderate risk of bias.
factors.consistency: Inconsistent: some meta-analyses positive, one null for perceived stress, and a null 12-week trial.
factors.effect_size: Moderate where present, with wide confidence intervals.
factors.clinical_significance: Possibly noticeable for some people; uncertain.
factors.sample_size: Under 600 participants per meta-analysis.
factors.population: Stressed adults; mostly Indian populations.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Several trials use branded extracts (for example Shoden and Witholytin); in the null 12-week trial, two of three authors are linked to a contract research organisation funded by nutraceutical companies. Funding is not stated in most abstracts.
factors.reproducibility: Mixed replication across independent groups.
factors.formulation_dose: Different extracts and doses limit comparisons.

claims.claim: Ashwagandha improves sleep
claims.popular_framing: Ashwagandha before bed for better sleep.
claims.question: Does ashwagandha improve sleep?
claims.outcome: Overall sleep quality and quantity
claims.population: Adults with and without insomnia.
claims.bottom_line: Somewhat, mainly in people with insomnia. A meta-analysis of 5 trials found a small overall benefit that was larger in people with insomnia, at higher doses and after 8 weeks or more.
claims.what_research_found: A 2021 meta-analysis of 5 randomised trials (400 adults) found a small but significant improvement in overall sleep. Effects were larger in adults diagnosed with insomnia, at 600 mg/day or more, and with 8 weeks or more of use. It also improved mental alertness on waking and anxiety.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: Clear benefits for good sleepers are not established, and there is little long-term safety data.
claims.limitations: Only five trials with moderate heterogeneity; different extracts and doses.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Ashwagandha extracts; the meta-analysis found larger effects at 600 mg/day or more and with 8 weeks or more of use. NIH ODS lists 250–600 mg/day KSM-66 or 120 mg/day Shoden in sleep trials.

factors.study_quality: Randomised placebo-controlled trials.
factors.consistency: Moderate heterogeneity (I² = 62%).
factors.effect_size: Small overall; larger in insomnia.
factors.clinical_significance: Likely modest for most people.
factors.sample_size: 400 participants.
factors.population: Clearer in insomnia than in healthy sleepers.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Funding of the included trials is not stated in the abstract; the review authors declare no conflicts.
factors.reproducibility: Few trials.
factors.formulation_dose: Effects larger at 600 mg/day and 8 weeks or more.

claims.claim: Ashwagandha raises testosterone in men
claims.popular_framing: Ashwagandha is a natural testosterone booster.
claims.question: Does ashwagandha boost testosterone?
claims.outcome: Blood testosterone levels
claims.population: Men in stress, fatigue or general-health trials; not men with diagnosed low testosterone specifically.
claims.bottom_line: Possibly a modest rise in men, not women. The evidence is limited, and a higher lab number does not by itself show any benefit for strength, mood or libido.
claims.what_research_found: A 2026 hormone meta-analysis found testosterone rose by about 57 ng/dL in men but not in women. A 2024 review of 'testosterone boosters' rated ashwagandha 'possibly effective' for healthy men, based on 3 studies. In a 12-week trial, free testosterone rose in men compared with placebo; in a 60-day trial the rise in men was not significant versus placebo.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It is not shown that this change produces noticeable effects on muscle, mood or sex drive, or that it helps men with clinically low testosterone.
claims.limitations: Few trials, mixed results between trials, and the number of trials behind the pooled testosterone estimate is not given in the abstract.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Branded extracts, for example 240 mg/day for 60 days or 200 mg of root extract twice daily for 12 weeks.

factors.study_quality: Randomised placebo-controlled trials, mostly small.
factors.consistency: Mixed: some trials significant, one not versus placebo.
factors.effect_size: Modest on average in men.
factors.clinical_significance: Unclear; hormone changes are not outcomes people feel directly.
factors.sample_size: Small numbers for this outcome.
factors.population: Men only; not women.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: In the 12-week trial, two of three authors are linked to a contract research organisation funded by nutraceutical companies; in the 60-day trial, one author had previously received extract-manufacturer funding for unrelated studies.
factors.reproducibility: Limited independent replication.
factors.formulation_dose: Different branded extracts.

claims.claim: Ashwagandha boosts strength and muscle gains from training
claims.popular_framing: Add ashwagandha to your stack for bigger lifts.
claims.question: Does ashwagandha increase strength gains from weight training?
claims.outcome: Maximal strength (1-RM), muscle size and body fat
claims.population: Healthy adults doing structured resistance training.
claims.bottom_line: We don't know yet. Only three small trials could be pooled, and the apparent strength benefit lost significance under stricter analysis.
claims.what_research_found: A 2026 meta-analysis found 4 eligible trials; 3 (161 people) could be pooled. Ashwagandha was linked to larger gains in bench press and lower-body strength, but each result depended on one influential trial and lost significance with a stricter statistical method. There was no dependable effect on body fat. Certainty was low to very low.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: The authors conclude current evidence does not establish that ashwagandha meaningfully enhances resistance-training adaptations.
claims.limitations: Very few, small trials with some risk-of-bias concerns; no direct measures of muscle growth.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Standardised root or root-and-leaf extracts combined with structured resistance training.

factors.study_quality: All pooled trials raised some risk-of-bias concerns.
factors.consistency: Low to moderate heterogeneity, but results depend on one trial.
factors.effect_size: Moderate point estimates that are statistically fragile.
factors.clinical_significance: Uncertain.
factors.sample_size: 161 participants pooled.
factors.population: Healthy adults doing structured resistance training; fits the popular claim.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: The authors call for independently funded trials.
factors.reproducibility: Not robustly replicated.
factors.formulation_dose: Different extracts and training programmes.

profiles.absorption: No verified data on absorption differences between extracts. Products are standardised to different withanolide contents, and trial results for one branded extract may not apply to another.
profiles.side_effects: Appears well tolerated for up to about 3 months in trials. Common side effects are mild: stomach upset, loose stools, nausea and drowsiness. Rare case reports describe liver injury and thyroid problems, including thyrotoxicosis. Long-term safety is unknown.
profiles.interactions: May interact with thyroid hormone medicines, diabetes medicines, blood pressure medicines, immunosuppressants and sedatives (NIH ODS).
profiles.cautions: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: some experts advise against use in pregnancy, Denmark banned ashwagandha in 2023, and France's ANSES advised against use in pregnancy, breastfeeding and endocrine disorders in 2024. Anyone who is pregnant or breastfeeding, or who has a thyroid condition, liver problems, or hormone-sensitive prostate cancer (ashwagandha may raise testosterone), should talk to a clinician first.
profiles.research_doses_summary: Doses used in research: 240 mg/day Shoden for 60 days; 200 mg twice daily Witholytin for 12 weeks; 250 mg/day or more in a 2025 cortisol and stress meta-analysis; larger sleep effects at 600 mg/day or more for 8 weeks or more. NIH ODS describes trials lasting 6–8 weeks. These are not recommendations.

sources.title: Dual impact of Ashwagandha: Significant cortisol reduction but no effects on perceived stress - A systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.authors: Albalawi AA
sources.sample_size: 7 studies on cortisol and 6 on perceived stress (488 participants)
sources.population: Participants in RCTs lasting 2 weeks or more
sources.intervention: Oral ashwagandha at 250 mg/day or more.
sources.findings: Cortisol fell by 1.16 µg/dL compared with placebo (95% CI -1.64 to -0.69). There was no significant effect on perceived stress (Perceived Stress Scale SMD -0.355, 95% CI -1.188 to 0.47; P = 0.40). Risk of bias was generally moderate; some trials lacked allocation concealment. The author notes gaps on long-term safety, dosing and effects across populations.
sources.limitations: Single author; searched Google Scholar among four databases; moderate risk of bias in included trials.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract. Conflict statement: none.
sources.cited_for: ashwagandha-cortisol and ashwagandha-stress: cortisol lower, perceived stress not significantly changed.

sources.title: Effects of Ashwagandha (Withania Somnifera) on stress and anxiety: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.authors: Arumugam V, Vijayakumar V, Balakrishnan A, et al.
sources.population: Patients/adults with stress or anxiety
sources.intervention: Ashwagandha formulations vs placebo.
sources.findings: Compared with placebo, ashwagandha lowered Perceived Stress Scale scores (MD -4.72, 95% CI -8.45 to -0.99), Hamilton Anxiety Scale scores (MD -2.19, 95% CI -3.83 to -0.55) and serum cortisol (MD -2.58, 95% CI -4.99 to -0.16). Four studies reported mild to moderate adverse events. More information is needed on long-term safety.
sources.limitations: Wide confidence intervals; search ended January 2022.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract.
sources.cited_for: ashwagandha-stress and ashwagandha-cortisol: pooled reductions in perceived stress, anxiety and cortisol.

sources.title: Hormonal Modulation with Withania somnifera: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized-controlled Trials.
sources.authors: Fornalik M, Malkiewicz A, Adamczak D, Nawrocki F, Zielinska A, Mondal SA
sources.population: Adults in placebo-controlled trials reporting hormone levels
sources.intervention: Oral ashwagandha vs placebo.
sources.findings: Ashwagandha reduced cortisol (SMD -1.18) and increased testosterone in men (MD 57.43 ng/dL) but not women. T4 rose modestly (MD 0.61 µg/dL) with no effect on TSH or T3. Oestradiol was unchanged. The authors note heterogeneity and limited data for some endpoints.
sources.limitations: Heterogeneity; limited data for some hormones; number of trials per hormone not given in the abstract.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract. Conflict statement: none.
sources.cited_for: ashwagandha-cortisol and ashwagandha-testosterone: hormone changes; thyroid (T4) signal.

sources.title: Effect of Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) extract on sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.authors: Cheah KL, Norhayati MN, Husniati Yaacob L, Abdul Rahman R
sources.population: Adults 18 and over, with and without insomnia
sources.intervention: Ashwagandha extract vs placebo.
sources.findings: Ashwagandha had a small but significant effect on overall sleep (SMD -0.59, 95% CI -0.75 to -0.42; I² = 62%). Effects were more prominent in adults diagnosed with insomnia, at 600 mg/day or more, and with 8 weeks or more of treatment. It also improved mental alertness on rising and anxiety, but not quality of life. No serious side effects were reported, but safety data are limited.
sources.limitations: Only five trials; moderate heterogeneity; limited safety data.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract. Conflict statement: none.
sources.cited_for: ashwagandha-sleep: small overall effect, larger in insomnia.

sources.title: Adjunctive Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) Supplementation and Resistance-Training Adaptations in Healthy Adults: A Systematic Review and Random-Effects Meta-Analysis of Muscular Strength, Chest Circumference, and Body Composition.
sources.authors: Lee JC, Heo AS
sources.population: Healthy adults doing structured resistance training
sources.intervention: Standardised ashwagandha root or root-and-leaf extract plus resistance training vs placebo plus training.
sources.findings: Ashwagandha was associated with greater gains in 1-RM bench press (SMD 0.60) and lower-body 1-RM (SMD 0.52) and chest circumference, but not body fat. Under a stricter statistical adjustment both strength results lost significance, and each depended on one influential trial. GRADE certainty was low for strength and very low for chest circumference. The authors conclude current evidence does not establish that ashwagandha meaningfully enhances resistance-training adaptations, and call for independently funded trials.
sources.limitations: Very small evidence base; all pooled trials had some risk-of-bias concerns; review not registered.
sources.funding: No external funding. Conflict statement: none.
sources.cited_for: ashwagandha-strength: evidence is small, fragile and low certainty.

sources.title: Do "testosterone boosters" really increase serum total testosterone? A systematic review.
sources.authors: Morgado A, Tsampoukas G, Sokolakis I, Schoentgen N, Urkmez A, Sarikaya S
sources.sample_size: 52 studies on 27 products (3 on Withania somnifera)
sources.population: Male athletes, men with late-onset hypogonadism, infertile men and healthy men
sources.intervention: Various marketed 'testosterone boosters' vs placebo.
sources.findings: Most testosterone boosters failed to increase total testosterone. Withania somnifera (ashwagandha) was rated 'possibly effective' for healthy men, based on 3 studies.
sources.limitations: Few ashwagandha studies; no pooled effect size in the abstract.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract.
sources.cited_for: ashwagandha-testosterone: 'possibly effective' in healthy men.

sources.title: Exploring the efficacy and safety of a novel standardized ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) root extract (Witholytin®) in adults experiencing high stress and fatigue in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
sources.authors: Smith SJ, Lopresti AL, Fairchild TJ
sources.population: Overweight or mildly obese men and women aged 40–75 with self-reported stress and fatigue
sources.intervention: 200 mg ashwagandha root extract (Witholytin) twice daily for 12 weeks vs placebo.
sources.findings: Perceived stress (primary outcome) improved but not more than placebo (p = 0.867). Fatigue fell more with ashwagandha (p = 0.016) and heart rate variability rose (p = 0.003). In men, free testosterone (p = 0.048) and luteinising hormone rose compared with placebo.
sources.limitations: One population (overweight, middle-to-older age); sample size not given in the abstract.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract. Conflict statement: one author directs a contract research organisation that has received funding from nutraceutical companies, and a second author is employed by it.
sources.cited_for: ashwagandha-stress: a placebo-controlled trial with no effect on perceived stress; ashwagandha-testosterone: free testosterone in men.

sources.title: An investigation into the stress-relieving and pharmacological actions of an ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) extract: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study.
sources.authors: Lopresti AL, Smith SJ, Malvi H, Kodgule R
sources.population: Stressed, healthy adults
sources.intervention: 240 mg standardised ashwagandha extract (Shoden) once daily for 60 days vs placebo.
sources.findings: Compared with placebo, ashwagandha reduced Hamilton anxiety scores (P = .040) and morning cortisol (P < .001); the DASS-21 reduction was near-significant (P = .096). Testosterone rose in men over time but not significantly versus placebo (P = .158). No adverse events were reported.
sources.limitations: Small, 60-day trial; registered in the Clinical Trials Registry-India.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract. One author has previously received funding from an extract manufacturer for unrelated studies.
sources.cited_for: ashwagandha-cortisol and ashwagandha-testosterone: example trial.

sources.title: Ashwagandha: Is it helpful for stress, anxiety, or sleep? - Health Professional Fact Sheet
sources.authors: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements
sources.findings: Describes ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) root or root-and-leaf extracts, with withanolides as key constituents, and several branded extracts. Summarises trials: a 2021 review of 7 studies (491 adults in India, 6–8 weeks) found reduced stress, anxiety and serum cortisol; a 12-week trial in 120 overweight adults found no reduction in perceived stress. A 2021 sleep meta-analysis found a small benefit, greater in insomnia, at 600 mg/day and with 8 weeks or more. Concludes extracts 'may help reduce anxiety and stress and improve sleep' but that studies were small, short and used different preparations. Safety: appears well tolerated for up to about 3 months; long-term safety unknown; mild side effects (stomach upset, loose stools, nausea, drowsiness); case reports of liver injury and of thyroid effects including thyrotoxicosis; may raise testosterone. Some experts advise against use in pregnancy; Denmark banned ashwagandha in 2023 and France's ANSES advised against use in pregnancy, breastfeeding and endocrine disorders in 2024. Possible interactions with thyroid, diabetes, blood pressure, immunosuppressant and sedative medicines. No upper limit stated. Page last updated May 2, 2025.
sources.limitations: Authoritative summary, not a primary study.
sources.funding: US government (NIH)
sources.cited_for: Background, overall evidence summary, safety, interactions, cautions, research doses.

profiles.name: Biotin
profiles.summary: Biotin is essential, but deficiency is rare, and good-quality research does not show that biotin supplements grow hair in healthy people; high doses can also distort some blood test results.
profiles.description: Biotin is a water-soluble B vitamin, sometimes called vitamin B7. It is found in many foods, including liver, eggs, fish, meat, seeds and nuts. It is sold on its own and is a common ingredient in hair, skin and nail supplements.
profiles.biological_function: Biotin helps enzymes that break down fats, carbohydrates and proteins. True deficiency is uncommon. When it happens, signs include thinning hair, a scaly red rash around the eyes, nose and mouth, and brittle nails. These deficiency signs are the main reason biotin is linked to hair and nails.

formulations.name: Free biotin (D-biotin) tablets or capsules
formulations.notes: NIH ODS reports that oral free biotin is absorbed at close to 100%, even at doses up to 20 mg/day. Many hair, skin and nail products contain doses far above the daily Adequate Intake of 30 mcg.

claims.claim: Biotin supplements improve hair growth in people who are not biotin deficient
claims.popular_framing: Take biotin for thicker, faster-growing hair.
claims.question: Does biotin make your hair grow if you are not deficient?
claims.outcome: Hair growth and hair quality
claims.population: People without known biotin deficiency. The 2024 review's trials included people taking isotretinoin and women after sleeve gastrectomy; the abstract does not describe the population of the placebo-controlled trial.
claims.bottom_line: There is no good evidence that biotin grows hair in people who are not deficient. The few studies that exist are small, and the best one found no difference from placebo.
claims.what_research_found: A 2024 literature review found only three studies of oral biotin and hair that met its criteria. The highest-quality one, a double-blind placebo-controlled trial, found no difference in hair growth between biotin and placebo. The other two studied narrow groups (people taking isotretinoin and women after weight-loss surgery), were open to several possible biases, and neither showed striking results in favour of biotin. A 2017 review found 18 reported cases where biotin helped hair or nails, but every one of those people had an underlying cause of poor hair or nail growth.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: No adequately sized trial has shown that biotin improves hair in healthy people. Because so little research exists, we also cannot say with confidence that it has no effect at all, which is why this is 'not established' rather than 'contradicted'.
claims.limitations: The total number of studies is very small. The reviews were based on published literature that is mostly case reports, which were excluded from the 2024 review because they cannot show cause and effect.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Oral biotin. The reviews read here do not report a single standard dose for the hair studies. NIH ODS describes 3–5 mg/day in case reports of children with uncombable hair syndrome, a rare condition.

factors.study_quality: Only one double-blind placebo-controlled trial was identified in the 2024 review; the other evidence is small studies with possible bias and case reports.
factors.consistency: The evidence in non-deficient people does not point to a benefit. Positive reports come only from people with an underlying cause or deficiency.
factors.effect_size: The best trial found no difference from placebo.
factors.clinical_significance: No meaningful benefit has been shown in people without deficiency.
factors.sample_size: Very small. The 2017 review found 18 cases in total; the 2024 review found 3 studies.
factors.population: Positive case reports involve people with deficiency or rare conditions, not the general public who buy hair supplements.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Not stated in the abstracts read.
factors.reproducibility: No independent replication of any benefit in healthy people.
factors.formulation_dose: Commercial products often contain doses far above the Adequate Intake (30 mcg/day); high doses have not been shown to help hair and can interfere with lab tests.

claims.claim: Biotin supplements help hair and skin problems caused by biotin deficiency or rare inherited conditions
claims.popular_framing: Hair loss can be a sign of low biotin.
claims.question: Does biotin help hair and skin when someone is actually deficient?
claims.outcome: Hair and skin signs of deficiency
claims.population: People with acquired or inherited biotin deficiency (for example biotinidase deficiency), and children with uncombable hair syndrome.
claims.bottom_line: Biotin deficiency can cause hair thinning and rashes, and case reports describe improvement with biotin. But the evidence is case reports, not controlled trials, and true deficiency is rare.
claims.what_research_found: NIH ODS lists thinning hair, a scaly red rash around body openings and brittle nails among the signs of biotin deficiency. A 2017 review found 18 reported cases of biotin use for hair and nail changes; all had an underlying cause, and all improved. NIH ODS describes case reports in children with uncombable hair syndrome (3–5 mg/day improved hair after 3–4 months) and in infants (100 mcg to 10 mg/day improved rash and hair loss).
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: There are no controlled trials. Case reports cannot show how often biotin helps, or by how much.
claims.limitations: Evidence is limited to case reports in uncommon conditions, mostly in children and infants.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Oral biotin; 100 mcg to 10 mg/day in infant case reports and 3–5 mg/day in children with uncombable hair syndrome (NIH ODS).

factors.study_quality: Case reports only; no randomised trials.
factors.consistency: Reported cases consistently describe improvement, but positive cases are more likely to be published.
factors.effect_size: Not measurable from case reports.
factors.clinical_significance: Improvement described in individual cases may be meaningful, but cannot be generalised.
factors.sample_size: 18 cases in the 2017 review.
factors.population: Rare conditions and deficiency, mostly in children; not representative of healthy adults.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Not stated in the sources read.
factors.reproducibility: Multiple separate case reports, but no controlled replication.
factors.formulation_dose: Doses varied widely across case reports.

claims.claim: Biotin supplements strengthen brittle nails
claims.popular_framing: Biotin gives you stronger nails.
claims.question: Does biotin help brittle nails?
claims.outcome: Nail hardness and thickness
claims.population: Adults with brittle, splitting or soft nails.
claims.bottom_line: A few small studies without a placebo group reported firmer nails with biotin. That is not enough to know whether biotin itself caused the change.
claims.what_research_found: NIH ODS describes three small studies without a placebo group, all using 2.5 mg/day. In one, nail thickness rose 25% in 8 patients with before-and-after samples, but only 7% (not statistically significant) in 14 others. In another, 41 of 45 patients (91%) had firmer, harder nails after an average of 5.5 months. In a retrospective study, 22 of 35 patients (63%) improved.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: Without a placebo group, these studies cannot separate the effect of biotin from natural improvement or other factors. No placebo-controlled trial of biotin for brittle nails was found in the sources read.
claims.limitations: Small, uncontrolled studies; one was retrospective. The 2017 review notes brittle nail syndrome as a condition where biotin may help, but describes the overall evidence as insufficient for healthy people.
claims.formulation_and_dose: 2.5 mg/day oral biotin for about 5.5 to 15 months (as described by NIH ODS).

factors.study_quality: No placebo control; one retrospective study.
factors.consistency: All three studies reported some improvement, though one key measure was not statistically significant.
factors.effect_size: Reported improvements are large in percentage terms but are uncontrolled.
factors.clinical_significance: Unclear without a comparison group.
factors.sample_size: Roughly 100 people across three studies.
factors.population: People with brittle nails; not people with normal nails.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Not stated in the sources read.
factors.reproducibility: Three separate studies, but none controlled.
factors.formulation_dose: 2.5 mg/day, which is much higher than the 30 mcg/day Adequate Intake.

claims.claim: High-dose biotin supplements can cause falsely high or falsely low results on some blood tests
claims.popular_framing: Biotin is harmless, so it doesn't matter how much you take.
claims.question: Can biotin supplements affect blood test results?
claims.outcome: Accuracy of laboratory tests (for example thyroid tests and troponin, a heart-attack marker)
claims.population: Healthy adults taking 10 mg/day in a controlled study; case reports and FDA adverse event reports in patients.
claims.bottom_line: Yes. High doses of biotin can make some lab tests read wrongly, including thyroid tests and troponin. The FDA has received reports of falsely low troponin results, and NIH ODS reports a death following a troponin test in a person with a high biotin intake.
claims.what_research_found: In a 2017 study, 6 healthy adults took 10 mg/day of biotin for 7 days. Biotin was associated with potentially important interference in 9 of 23 biotin-based assays (39%) and in none of 14 control assays. Results could be falsely high (5 of 8 competitive assays) or falsely low (4 of 15 sandwich assays). NIH ODS reports that a single 10 mg dose has interfered with thyroid tests done within 24 hours, and describes case reports of falsely indicated Graves' disease. The FDA states that biotin can significantly interfere with certain lab tests and that it continues to receive reports of falsely low troponin results.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: Not every test is affected; only tests that use biotin-streptavidin technology. The sources read do not give a single safe cut-off dose, and some manufacturers have changed their tests since 2017.
claims.limitations: The controlled study had only 6 participants. Much of the remaining evidence is case reports and adverse event reports, though the mechanism is well understood.
claims.formulation_and_dose: 10 mg/day for 7 days in the controlled study; case reports at 10–300 mg/day (NIH ODS).

factors.study_quality: A small non-randomised crossover study in healthy adults (with non-biotin assays as controls), plus regulator (FDA) reports and case reports.
factors.consistency: Consistent across the experimental study, case reports and FDA reports.
factors.effect_size: Large enough to be potentially clinically important in 39% of biotin-based assays tested.
factors.clinical_significance: High: a falsely low troponin result could cause a missed heart attack; falsely abnormal thyroid tests have led to misdiagnosis.
factors.sample_size: Small controlled study (6 people), supported by wider adverse event reporting.
factors.population: Healthy adults at doses common in hair and nail supplements.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: The 2017 study lists NIH (NCATS) funding.
factors.reproducibility: Reported by independent researchers, case reports and the FDA.
factors.formulation_dose: Interference was shown at 10 mg/day, a dose found in some supplements.

research_doses.note: 2.5 mg/day in the brittle-nail studies described by NIH ODS; 10 mg/day in the lab-interference study. These are far above food amounts.

reference_intake.label: Adequate Intake, adults 19+ (35 mcg during breastfeeding)

food_vs_supplement.comparison_note: A cooked egg provides about 10 mcg, a third of the adult Adequate Intake. Research doses of 2,500–10,000 mcg are roughly 80–330 times the Adequate Intake, so food and these supplements are not comparable.
food_vs_supplement.food_advantages: Food provides biotin alongside other nutrients, at amounts that have not been linked to lab-test interference.
food_vs_supplement.when_supplement_may_help: NIH ODS lists people with biotinidase deficiency, people with chronic alcohol exposure, and pregnant and breastfeeding women as groups at risk of inadequate biotin. Long-term use of some anticonvulsant medicines is linked to lower biotin levels. Any decision should be made with a clinician.

profiles.absorption: NIH ODS reports that oral free biotin is absorbed at close to 100%, even at doses up to 20 mg/day. Avidin, a protein in raw egg white, binds biotin and blocks its absorption; cooking the egg white stops this.
profiles.side_effects: NIH ODS reports no toxicity in several studies at 10–50 mg/day, and none at up to 200 mg/day orally in people with biotinidase deficiency. The main known risk of high intakes is interference with laboratory tests.
profiles.interactions: Lab tests: high-dose biotin can cause falsely high or falsely low results on tests that use biotin-streptavidin technology, including some thyroid and troponin tests (FDA; NIH ODS). Anticonvulsants: long-term use of carbamazepine, primidone, phenytoin or phenobarbital is associated with lower blood biotin levels (NIH ODS).
profiles.cautions: Tell your clinician and the lab if you take biotin before any blood test, especially thyroid or heart tests. FDA advises health care providers to ask patients about biotin-containing supplements. People taking anticonvulsants, and pregnant or breastfeeding women, should speak to a clinician about their biotin needs.
profiles.upper_limit: No upper limit set. The Food and Nutrition Board found no evidence that biotin is toxic in humans at high intakes (NIH ODS).
profiles.research_doses_summary: Doses used in research and case reports range from 100 mcg/day (infant case reports) to 2.5 mg/day (brittle-nail studies), 3–5 mg/day (children with uncombable hair syndrome) and 10 mg/day (lab-interference study). These describe research only and are not recommendations.

sources.title: Biotin: Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
sources.authors: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements
sources.population: General population; groups at risk of inadequacy
sources.findings: Adequate Intake 30 mcg/day for adults (35 mcg lactation). Food content table. No upper limit set. Free biotin absorbed at ~100% up to 20 mg/day. Hair, skin and nail benefit claims supported 'at best' by a few case reports and small studies; three small uncontrolled brittle-nail studies at 2.5 mg/day. High intakes can interfere with biotin-streptavidin lab assays; FDA reports a death after a falsely low troponin test. Anticonvulsants linked to lower biotin levels.
sources.limitations: Summary document; the fetched page did not show a last-updated date.
sources.funding: US government (NIH)
sources.cited_for: Food amounts, AI, upper limit, absorption, brittle-nail studies, deficiency signs, lab interference, anticonvulsant interaction.

sources.title: Biotin Interference with Troponin Lab Tests - Assays Subject to Biotin Interference
sources.authors: US Food and Drug Administration
sources.population: Patients having troponin tests
sources.findings: Biotin, often found in dietary supplements, can significantly interfere with certain lab tests and cause incorrect results that may go undetected. Since FDA's 2017 safety communication some test makers have reduced the interference but others have not, and FDA continues to receive adverse event reports of falsely low troponin results. Lists 17 troponin assays still subject to interference.
sources.limitations: Page last updated 21 June 2022. The linked 2017/updated safety communication itself could not be opened in this session.
sources.funding: US government (FDA)
sources.cited_for: Lab-test interference claim: FDA statement and continuing reports of falsely low troponin results.

sources.title: Association of Biotin Ingestion With Performance of Hormone and Nonhormone Assays in Healthy Adults.
sources.authors: Li D, Radulescu A, Shrestha RT, et al.
sources.sample_size: 6 healthy adults; 37 immunoassays for 11 analytes on 4 diagnostic systems
sources.population: Healthy adults, mean age 38 years
sources.intervention: Biotin 10 mg/day for 7 days
sources.findings: Potentially clinically important interference in 9 of 23 biotinylated assays (39%) vs 0 of 14 non-biotinylated controls. Falsely high results in 5 of 8 competitive immunoassays (63%); falsely low in 4 of 15 sandwich immunoassays (27%). Authors advise clinicians to consider biotin use before ordering or interpreting tests.
sources.limitations: Very small preliminary crossover study.
sources.funding: NIH NCATS grant UL1 TR000114 listed
sources.cited_for: Lab-test interference claim: size and direction of interference at 10 mg/day.

sources.title: Biotin for Hair Loss: Teasing Out the Evidence.
sources.authors: Yelich A, Jenkins H, Holt S, Miller R
sources.population: People studied for hair growth or quality with oral biotin
sources.intervention: Oral biotin
sources.findings: Only three studies qualified. The highest-quality, double-blind placebo-controlled study found no difference in hair growth between biotin and placebo. The other two (isotretinoin users; women after sleeve gastrectomy) were susceptible to multiple potential biases and neither had striking results in favour of biotin. Public belief exceeds the evidence; high-quality studies do not support biotin for hair.
sources.limitations: Limited by the small number of available studies; case reports excluded.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: Hair-growth claim in non-deficient people.

sources.title: A Review of the Use of Biotin for Hair Loss.
sources.authors: Patel DP, Swink SM, Castelo-Soccio L
sources.population: Case reports and trials of biotin for hair and nail changes
sources.intervention: Biotin supplementation
sources.findings: All 18 reported cases had an underlying cause of poor hair or nail growth, and all improved with biotin. Biotin may help people with acquired or inherited biotin deficiency, brittle nail syndrome or uncombable hair, but these are uncommon, and evidence is insufficient to support supplementation in healthy people.
sources.limitations: Evidence base is case reports.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: Hair claims (non-deficient and deficient) and brittle-nail context.

profiles.name: Caffeine
profiles.summary: Caffeine reliably gives a small boost to exercise performance and a small-to-moderate boost to attention and reaction time, even in regular coffee drinkers; for most healthy adults up to about 400 mg a day is not generally linked to harm.
profiles.description: Caffeine is a natural stimulant found in coffee, tea, cacao and guarana, and added to energy drinks, gels and pre-workout products. It is also sold as pills and as pure powder.
profiles.biological_function: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors in the brain, which reduces feelings of tiredness and increases arousal. It may also lower perceived effort and pain during exercise. Blood levels peak within about 45 minutes, and its half-life is about 4–5 hours (NIH ODS).

formulations.name: Caffeine pills / anhydrous caffeine
formulations.notes: Gives a measured dose, as used in performance research.

formulations.name: Coffee, tea and energy drinks
formulations.notes: Caffeine content varies widely by drink and brand (FDA).

formulations.name: Pure or highly concentrated powder
formulations.notes: FDA warns these can cause serious harm including death; NIH ODS notes one tablespoon contains about 10 g.

formulations.name: Caffeinated gum, gels and chews
formulations.notes: ISSN reports these improve performance, mainly in aerobic exercise; gum may act faster than capsules.

claims.claim: Caffeine taken before exercise improves exercise performance in healthy adults
claims.popular_framing: A coffee or pre-workout before training makes you perform better.
claims.question: Does caffeine improve exercise performance?
claims.outcome: Endurance, strength, power, sprint and jump performance
claims.population: Healthy adults, mostly young men; trained and untrained.
claims.bottom_line: Yes. Caffeine gives a small but reliable performance boost, most clearly for endurance exercise. Moderate doses worked in research; very high doses have not been shown to add benefit.
claims.what_research_found: An umbrella review of 21 meta-analyses found caffeine improved aerobic endurance, muscle strength and endurance, power, jumping and speed, with mostly moderate-quality evidence. Effects were generally larger for aerobic exercise. A 2022 meta-analysis of 60 studies found an overall small effect (SMD 0.25); effects were significant at doses below 3 mg/kg and at 3–6 mg/kg, but not above 6 mg/kg. NIH ODS describes benefits at about 2–6 mg/kg; the ISSN reports consistent benefits at 3–6 mg/kg, with a minimum effective dose possibly as low as 2 mg/kg.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: Higher doses (above 6 mg/kg) were not shown to work better and raise side effects. Evidence is thinner for women, middle-aged and older adults.
claims.limitations: Effects are small on average and vary between people. Most studies were short, lab-based and in young men. Not every meta-analysis gave a definite direction once prediction intervals were considered.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Caffeine at about 2–6 mg/kg body mass (about 210–420 mg for a 70 kg person), usually 15–60 minutes before exercise (NIH ODS); the ISSN notes 60 minutes before is the most common timing. Gum, gels, energy drinks and pre-workouts were also studied.

factors.study_quality: Placebo-controlled studies pooled in many meta-analyses; the umbrella review rated the reviews moderate to high in methodological quality and the evidence as generally moderate quality (some low to very low).
factors.consistency: Benefit found across 21 meta-analyses and many exercise types, though not every analysis gave a definite direction once prediction intervals were considered.
factors.effect_size: Small (SMD about 0.25 overall); larger for endurance.
factors.clinical_significance: Small percentages can matter in competition; less noticeable in casual exercise.
factors.sample_size: Large: 60 studies in one meta-analysis alone; 21 meta-analyses in the umbrella review.
factors.population: Mostly young men; fewer data in women and older adults.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: The umbrella review authors declare none; the ISSN position stand authors report many industry ties.
factors.reproducibility: Replicated across many studies and meta-analyses; consistent with NIH ODS and ISSN summaries.
factors.formulation_dose: Studied doses (about 210–420 mg for a 70 kg person) are similar to the caffeine in one to three 12-oz cups of brewed coffee, using FDA content figures.

claims.claim: Regular coffee drinkers lose caffeine's performance benefit
claims.popular_framing: If you drink coffee every day, caffeine won't help your workout anymore.
claims.question: Does daily caffeine use cancel out the performance boost?
claims.outcome: Acute exercise performance in habitual vs low caffeine users
claims.population: Men and women, trained and untrained, with varied habitual caffeine intake.
claims.bottom_line: No. Across 60 studies, habitual caffeine intake did not change caffeine's performance benefit.
claims.what_research_found: A 2022 meta-analysis of 60 studies found caffeine improved performance (SMD 0.25) regardless of how much caffeine people normally consumed. This held for endurance, power and strength exercise, for men and women, and for trained and untrained people. Caffeine still helped whether people had stopped caffeine for under 24 hours, 24–48 hours or more than 48 hours beforehand, and whether the test dose was above or below their usual daily intake. A 2025 attention meta-analysis also found no link with habitual intake.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: The abstract does not report results for very heavy daily users separately, and individual responses still vary.
claims.limitations: Only the 60 studies that reported participants' habitual intake could be included, and habitual intake was taken from what each study reported. The ISSN position stand notes habitual intake may still play a role in differences between individuals.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Acute caffeine doses below 3, 3–6 and above 6 mg/kg body mass.

factors.study_quality: Placebo-controlled studies analysed with three-level meta-analysis and meta-regression.
factors.consistency: No influence of habitual intake across exercise types and groups; the ISSN notes habitual intake may play a role in individual differences.
factors.effect_size: Benefit similar whether the dose was above or below the person's usual intake.
factors.clinical_significance: Habitual users still benefit in practice.
factors.sample_size: 60 studies.
factors.population: Broad: men, women, trained and untrained.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Not stated in abstract.
factors.reproducibility: Consistent with the separate attention meta-analysis.
factors.formulation_dose: Typical acute doses.

claims.claim: Caffeine improves alertness and attention in adults
claims.popular_framing: Coffee wakes you up and sharpens your focus.
claims.question: Does caffeine make you more alert and focused?
claims.outcome: Attention (reaction time and accuracy), vigilance, performance after sleep loss
claims.population: Rested healthy adults, and sleep-deprived adults.
claims.bottom_line: Yes. Caffeine reliably improves reaction time and attention by a small-to-moderate amount, and effects looked larger in studies of people short on sleep. The studies do not show it fully makes up for lost sleep.
claims.what_research_found: A 2025 meta-analysis of 31 double-blind trials (1,455 rested adults) found caffeine improved attention accuracy and reaction time (g about 0.27–0.28). Doses of 200 mg or more worked better than lower doses, though accuracy declined at the highest doses. In sleep-deprived people, a meta-analysis of 45 publications found improvements in attention, reaction time, executive function, information processing and simulated driving, mostly with larger effect sizes than in rested adults (the two meta-analyses used different tasks, so they are not directly comparable).
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: These studies show short-term effects, not that caffeine fully reverses sleep loss or improves long-term cognitive health.
claims.limitations: Effects in rested people are small to moderate. Accuracy may drop at high doses. Sleep-loss studies varied widely in tasks and designs.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Single doses of pure caffeine; benefits were larger at 200 mg or more in rested adults.

factors.study_quality: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in the attention meta-analysis.
factors.consistency: Consistent across meta-analyses and agreed by the ISSN.
factors.effect_size: Small to moderate in rested adults (g about 0.27); moderate to large after sleep loss.
factors.clinical_significance: Small in rested adults; the larger effects seen after sleep loss are more likely to be noticeable.
factors.sample_size: 1,455 participants in 31 trials, plus 45 sleep-loss publications.
factors.population: Healthy adults; sleep-deprived adults.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Attention meta-analysis authors declare no conflicts.
factors.reproducibility: Replicated across many independent labs.
factors.formulation_dose: Benefits were larger at 200 mg or more, roughly one to two 12-oz cups of brewed coffee by FDA figures.

claims.claim: Up to about 400 mg of caffeine a day is not generally linked to harmful effects in healthy adults
claims.popular_framing: Up to 400 mg of caffeine a day is safe.
claims.question: How much caffeine is too much?
claims.outcome: Adverse effects (heart, behaviour, bone, reproduction, acute toxicity)
claims.population: Healthy adults. Different limits apply to pregnancy, children and adolescents.
claims.bottom_line: For most healthy adults, up to about 400 mg a day is not generally linked to harm. That is a general figure, not a target. Lower amounts are cited for pregnancy, children and teens, and some people are more sensitive.
claims.what_research_found: A systematic review of 381 studies found that up to 400 mg/day in healthy adults is not associated with overt harmful effects on the heart, behaviour, bones, reproduction or acute toxicity. It supported up to 300 mg/day in healthy pregnant women and 2.5 mg/kg/day for children and adolescents. The FDA cites 400 mg/day for most adults, about two to three 12-oz cups of coffee, and warns that rapidly taking about 1,200 mg can cause seizures.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It does not mean 400 mg is safe for everyone. People with heart conditions, those on certain medicines, and sensitive individuals were not the focus.
claims.limitations: The systematic review covered studies to mid-2015 and found limited data for children and teens. Individual sensitivity varies widely.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Total daily caffeine from all sources (coffee, tea, energy drinks, supplements).

factors.study_quality: Large systematic review with risk-of-bias rating, backed by FDA guidance.
factors.consistency: Consistent across agencies (FDA, Health Canada reference values used in the review).
factors.effect_size: Not applicable (safety threshold).
factors.clinical_significance: Practical guidance for daily intake.
factors.sample_size: 381 studies.
factors.population: Healthy adults; separate values for pregnancy and young people.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Most review authors work for a consulting firm; funding not stated in the abstract.
factors.reproducibility: Agrees with FDA and NIH ODS figures.
factors.formulation_dose: Applies to total caffeine from all sources; pure powders are especially risky.

research_doses.note: Single doses before exercise; about 210–420 mg for a 70 kg person (NIH ODS). Doses above 6 mg/kg showed no added benefit. Attention studies found larger effects at 200 mg or more.

reference_intake.label: Daily amount FDA cites as not generally associated with negative effects in most healthy adults (not a target)

food_vs_supplement.comparison_note: One 12-oz cup of brewed coffee (113–247 mg) can fall within the range used in performance research for many adults (about 210–420 mg for 70 kg). Coffee caffeine varies a lot by brew and brand, while pills deliver a measured dose.
food_vs_supplement.food_advantages: Coffee and tea deliver caffeine in amounts that are harder to overshoot than concentrated powders. FDA warns pure and highly concentrated caffeine products can be dangerous because a safe dose is hard to measure.
food_vs_supplement.when_supplement_may_help: Research used measured doses before endurance or high-intensity exercise, and after sleep loss. The ISSN reports that other caffeine sources, such as gum, gels, energy drinks and pre-workouts, have also improved performance.

profiles.absorption: Caffeine is absorbed quickly; blood levels peak within about 45 minutes and the half-life is about 4–5 hours (NIH ODS). The ISSN notes caffeinated gum may act faster than capsules. How strongly people respond varies: the ISSN links this partly to genetic differences in caffeine metabolism, and FDA notes some medications and medical conditions can increase sensitivity.
profiles.side_effects: Too much caffeine can cause a fast heart rate, palpitations, high blood pressure, insomnia, anxiety, jitters, upset stomach, nausea and headache (FDA). Intakes of 500 mg/day or more may impair performance and disturb sleep (NIH ODS). Rapidly taking about 1,200 mg can cause seizures (FDA).
profiles.interactions: FDA notes some medications and medical conditions can make people more sensitive to caffeine. Combining caffeine with other stimulants may increase adverse effects (NIH ODS).
profiles.cautions: People who are pregnant, trying to conceive or breastfeeding should talk with a health care provider about limiting caffeine (FDA); a systematic review supported up to 300 mg/day in healthy pregnant women. Children and teens: NIH ODS cites no more than 100 mg/day for teenagers. FDA warns that pure and highly concentrated caffeine powders can cause serious harm, including death. People with heart conditions, anxiety or sleep problems, or on medications, should speak to a clinician.
profiles.upper_limit: No formal upper limit set. FDA cites 400 mg/day as an amount not generally associated with negative effects in most healthy adults; a systematic review supports up to 300 mg/day in healthy pregnancy and 2.5 mg/kg/day for children and adolescents.
profiles.research_doses_summary: Doses used in research: about 2–6 mg/kg body mass (about 210–420 mg for a 70 kg person), usually 15–60 minutes before exercise. Doses above 6 mg/kg showed no added benefit in a large meta-analysis. Attention studies used single doses, with larger effects at 200 mg or more.

sources.title: Wake up and smell the coffee: caffeine supplementation and exercise performance-an umbrella review of 21 published meta-analyses.
sources.authors: Grgic J, Grgic I, Pickering C, Schoenfeld BJ, Bishop DJ, Pedisic Z.
sources.population: Mostly young men
sources.intervention: Caffeine ingestion before exercise
sources.findings: Caffeine was ergogenic for aerobic endurance, muscle strength, muscle endurance, power, jumping and exercise speed. Evidence quality was generally moderate (some low to very low). Effects were generally larger for aerobic than anaerobic exercise. Not all analyses gave a definite direction when 95% prediction intervals were considered.
sources.limitations: Few studies in women, middle-aged and older adults.
sources.funding: Authors declare no competing interests.
sources.cited_for: caffeine-exercise-performance: breadth and quality of performance evidence.

sources.title: Can I Have My Coffee and Drink It? A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis to Determine Whether Habitual Caffeine Consumption Affects the Ergogenic Effect of Caffeine.
sources.authors: Carvalho A, Marticorena FM, Grecco BH, Barreto G, Saunders B.
sources.population: Men and women, trained and untrained
sources.intervention: Acute caffeine vs placebo at <3, 3–6 and >6 mg/kg body mass; various withdrawal periods
sources.findings: Overall positive effect of caffeine (SMD 0.25, 95% CI 0.20–0.30), not influenced by habitual caffeine intake. Significant effects at <3 mg/kg and 3–6 mg/kg, but not at >6 mg/kg (SMD 0.11, 95% CI −0.07 to 0.30). Effective for endurance, power and strength exercise; habitual intake did not modify effects in men, women, trained or untrained people. Effects were significant whether the dose was above or below habitual intake (SMD 0.26 and 0.21) and whatever the withdrawal period (<24 h, 24–48 h, >48 h).
sources.limitations: Only studies reporting habitual intake were included.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: caffeine-habitual-users and caffeine-exercise-performance: effect size, dose and habituation.

sources.title: International society of sports nutrition position stand: caffeine and exercise performance.
sources.authors: Guest NS, VanDusseldorp TA, Nelson MT, Grgic J, Schoenfeld BJ, Jenkins NDM, Arent SM, Antonio J, Stout JR, Trexler ET, Smith-Ryan AE, Goldstein ER, Kalman DS, Campbell BI.
sources.population: Trained and untrained exercising individuals
sources.intervention: Caffeine at 3–6 mg/kg body mass, commonly 60 min before exercise
sources.findings: Caffeine acutely enhances many aspects of exercise performance in many but not all studies, with small to moderate benefits; aerobic endurance shows the most consistent moderate-to-large benefits. Consistent benefits at 3–6 mg/kg; minimal effective dose may be as low as 2 mg/kg. Very high doses (e.g. 9 mg/kg) bring a high incidence of side effects and do not seem required. Caffeine is ergogenic for attention and vigilance in most individuals. Individual differences may relate to genetics and habitual intake.
sources.limitations: Position stand by a society that receives supplement-industry funding.
sources.funding: Several authors report ties to supplement companies; ISSN has received grants from companies selling caffeine products.
sources.cited_for: caffeine-exercise-performance and caffeine-alertness: expert consensus and dose range; caffeine-habitual-users: note that habitual intake may affect individual responses.

sources.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of the acute effect of caffeine on attention.
sources.authors: Kløve K, Petersen A.
sources.population: Rested, healthy adults
sources.intervention: Single doses of pure caffeine vs placebo in randomised, double-blind trials
sources.findings: Caffeine improved attention accuracy (g = 0.27) and reaction time (g = 0.28). Doses of 200 mg or more improved both more than lower doses. Reaction time kept improving with dose, but accuracy improved only up to a point before declining. Effects did not depend on habitual caffeine use.
sources.limitations: Only tests of attention; short-term effects.
sources.funding: Authors declare no conflicts of interest.
sources.cited_for: caffeine-alertness: effect in rested adults and dose-response.

sources.title: Effects of acute caffeine consumption following sleep loss on cognitive, physical, occupational and driving performance: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.authors: Irwin C, Khalesi S, Desbrow B, McCartney D.
sources.population: Sleep-deprived or sleep-restricted individuals
sources.intervention: Acute caffeine
sources.findings: Caffeine improved attention (response time g = 0.86; accuracy g = 0.68), executive function (g = 0.35), reaction time (g = 1.11), information processing and simulated driving control (g about 1.6–1.7). Authors conclude caffeine is an effective counter-measure to cognitive and physical impairment from sleep loss.
sources.limitations: Effect estimates pooled from varied tasks and designs. The abstract's 95% CI for attention response time (0.53–0.83) does not contain its point estimate (g = 0.86), so one of these figures is likely a typo.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: caffeine-alertness: larger effects after sleep loss.

sources.title: Systematic review of the potential adverse effects of caffeine consumption in healthy adults, pregnant women, adolescents, and children.
sources.authors: Wikoff D, Welsh BT, Henderson R, Brorby GP, Britt J, Myers E, Goldberger J, Lieberman HR, O'Brien C, Peck J, Tenenbein M, Weaver C, Harvey S, Urban J, Doepker C.
sources.population: Healthy adults, pregnant women, adolescents and children
sources.intervention: Caffeine intake compared with Health Canada reference intakes (400 mg/day adults, 300 mg/day pregnancy, 2.5 mg/kg/day children and adolescents)
sources.findings: Evidence generally supports that up to 400 mg/day in healthy adults is not associated with overt adverse cardiovascular, behavioural, reproductive, acute or bone effects; up to 300 mg/day in healthy pregnant women is generally not associated with adverse reproductive and developmental effects; 2.5 mg/kg/day remains appropriate for children and adolescents (limited data). Calls for more research on sensitive groups.
sources.limitations: Covers literature 2001–June 2015; limited data for children and adolescents.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract (most authors affiliated with a consulting firm, ToxStrategies).
sources.cited_for: caffeine-safety-400mg: systematic review behind the 400 mg/day figure.

sources.title: Spilling the Beans: How Much Caffeine is Too Much?
sources.authors: U.S. Food and Drug Administration
sources.population: Adults, pregnant and breastfeeding people, children and teens
sources.findings: For most adults, FDA has cited 400 mg/day (about two to three 12-oz cups of coffee) as an amount not generally associated with negative effects. Rapid consumption of about 1,200 mg can cause toxic effects such as seizures. Pure and highly concentrated caffeine products can cause serious harm, including death. Sensitivity varies with medications, medical conditions and individual factors. Pregnant, trying-to-conceive and breastfeeding people should talk to a provider. Lists caffeine content of common drinks.
sources.limitations: Consumer guidance; page last updated 28 August 2024.
sources.funding: US government (FDA)
sources.cited_for: Safety limits, side effects, caffeine content of drinks.

sources.title: Dietary Supplements for Exercise and Athletic Performance — Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
sources.authors: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements
sources.population: Athletes and exercisers
sources.intervention: Caffeine about 2–6 mg/kg (210–420 mg for a 70 kg person) 15–60 minutes before exercise
sources.findings: Many studies show performance benefits at about 2–6 mg/kg; higher intakes are unlikely to help further and raise side-effect risk. In a review of time trials, 30 of 33 showed improvement but only about half were statistically significant. Benefit is greater for endurance and long intermittent activity than short intense efforts. Peak blood levels within about 45 minutes; half-life about 4–5 hours. 500 mg/day or more might impair performance and disturb sleep. Caffeine does not cause diuresis enough to impair performance. One tablespoon of pure powder contains 10 g; 10–14 g can be fatal. AMA: adolescents limit to 100 mg/day.
sources.limitations: Summary document; last-updated date not captured.
sources.funding: US government (NIH)
sources.cited_for: Doses used in research, timing, side effects and safety notes.

sources.title: Dietary Supplements for Exercise and Athletic Performance — Fact Sheet for Consumers
sources.authors: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements
sources.population: Athletes and exercisers
sources.intervention: Caffeine 2–6 mg/kg, 15–60 minutes before exercise
sources.findings: Up to 400–500 mg/day appears safe for adults; teenagers no more than 100 mg/day. 500 mg or more daily can reduce performance, disturb sleep and cause irritability and anxiety. A cup of coffee has about 85–100 mg.
sources.limitations: Consumer summary.
sources.funding: US government (NIH)
sources.cited_for: Plain-language safety and dose summary.

profiles.name: Collagen
profiles.summary: Collagen may modestly help osteoarthritis symptoms, but skin benefits are uncertain because they show up mainly in company-funded studies, and there is no evidence that swallowed collagen goes straight to your skin.
profiles.description: Collagen supplements are usually sold as hydrolyzed collagen, also called collagen peptides. They come as powders, capsules and drinks and are marketed mainly for skin and joints.
profiles.biological_function: When you eat collagen, it is digested. Studies in people found small fragments, mainly a two-amino-acid piece called Pro-Hyp, in the blood within 1 to 2 hours. Whether these fragments do anything for skin or joints is not established.

formulations.name: Hydrolyzed collagen / collagen peptides
formulations.notes: The form tested in most skin and joint trials cited here.

formulations.name: Collagen tripeptide preparations
formulations.notes: In one absorption study, preparations rich in tripeptides such as Gly-Pro-Hyp raised blood levels of these peptides more than a collagen peptide without tripeptides. This does not show better health effects.

claims.claim: Collagen supplements improve skin hydration and elasticity
claims.popular_framing: A daily scoop of collagen for plumper, bouncier, hydrated skin.
claims.question: Does taking collagen improve skin hydration and elasticity?
claims.outcome: Skin hydration and elasticity measured with instruments
claims.population: Mostly healthy adult women
claims.bottom_line: Unclear. Pooled studies look positive, but in one review, studies without company funding and higher-quality studies showed no significant effect.
claims.what_research_found: Several meta-analyses report better skin hydration and elasticity with collagen than placebo. A 2026 review of 35 trials (2,534 people) found statistically significant improvements in instrument-measured hydration and elasticity, with elasticity gains needing at least 12 weeks. But a 2025 review of 23 trials found the benefit only in studies funded by pharmaceutical companies; studies without that funding, and high-quality studies, showed no effect.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It has not been shown that independent, high-quality trials find a benefit. A 2026 re-analysis found errors in earlier meta-analyses and no benefit once dose was accounted for.
claims.limitations: Many trials are small and use different measuring tools. Results are mainly in women. Only abstracts were read.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Oral hydrolyzed collagen or collagen peptides, for about 12 weeks (90 days). In one review, effects depended on time (at least 12 weeks for elasticity) rather than dose.

factors.study_quality: High-quality studies showed no significant effect in the 2025 review; positive results came mainly from lower-quality studies.
factors.consistency: Reviews disagree. Pooled results are positive, but subgroup analyses and a 2026 re-analysis are negative.
factors.effect_size: Small to moderate in one review (SMD 0.44 for hydration, 0.62 for elasticity), with wide confidence intervals.
factors.clinical_significance: Unclear whether instrument-measured changes are visible to the person.
factors.sample_size: Up to 35 trials and 2,534 participants in total; a 2022 review noted that many trials are limited by sample size.
factors.population: Mostly women; about 95% of participants in one review.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Major concern. In the 2025 review, benefits appeared only in company-funded studies.
factors.reproducibility: Independent trials have not reproduced the benefit, according to the 2025 subgroup analysis.
factors.formulation_dose: Products vary in source, peptide size and dose; one review found time mattered more than dose.

claims.claim: Collagen supplements reduce wrinkles and reverse skin aging
claims.popular_framing: Drink collagen to erase wrinkles and turn back the clock.
claims.question: Does collagen get rid of wrinkles?
claims.outcome: Wrinkles, roughness and dermal density
claims.population: Mostly healthy adult women
claims.bottom_line: Not shown. Recent analyses suggest earlier wrinkle benefits were statistical artifacts or tied to industry funding.
claims.what_research_found: Earlier meta-analyses reported fewer wrinkles with hydrolyzed collagen. A 2026 review of 35 trials found that apparent improvements in wrinkles, roughness and dermal density were driven by outliers and high heterogeneity. A 2025 review found no wrinkle benefit in studies without pharmaceutical-company funding or in high-quality studies.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: No reliable evidence shows that collagen supplements visibly reduce wrinkles or reverse skin aging.
claims.limitations: Wrinkle measurements differ between studies, which makes pooling unreliable. Only abstracts were read.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Oral hydrolyzed collagen or collagen peptides; doses varied across trials.

factors.study_quality: High-quality studies showed no significant effect (2025 review).
factors.consistency: Inconsistent; the 2026 review found high heterogeneity.
factors.effect_size: Positive pooled effects did not survive sensitivity analysis in the 2026 review.
factors.clinical_significance: No verified evidence of a visible change.
factors.sample_size: Up to 35 trials and 2,534 participants pooled in one review.
factors.population: Mostly women.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Benefits were limited to company-funded studies in the 2025 review.
factors.reproducibility: Not reproduced by independent or high-quality studies.
factors.formulation_dose: Products and doses vary widely.

claims.claim: Collagen you swallow goes straight to your skin and joints and becomes new collagen there
claims.popular_framing: Eat collagen, and it goes straight to your skin.
claims.question: Does swallowed collagen go straight to your skin?
claims.outcome: What happens to collagen after it is eaten
claims.population: Healthy volunteers in absorption studies
claims.bottom_line: Not shown. Swallowed collagen is digested. What reaches the blood is small fragments, and no study cited here shows they are sent to the skin or rebuilt into skin collagen.
claims.what_research_found: Absorption studies in healthy people found small collagen fragments in the blood after eating collagen hydrolysate. The main one was a two-amino-acid fragment called Pro-Hyp, which peaked 1 to 2 hours after eating and halved by 4 hours. How much reaches the blood depends on the product's peptide form.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: These studies did not track fragments to the skin or joints, and did not show that eaten collagen becomes new body collagen. A 2022 review said the physiologic mechanism still needs to be established.
claims.limitations: Absorption studies used single doses, and their size is not stated in the abstracts read. In one, the authors' listed affiliation was a company (Jellice Co., Ltd.).
claims.formulation_and_dose: Single doses of 9.4 to 23 g gelatin hydrolysate; collagen tripeptide preparations in another study.

factors.study_quality: Short, single-dose absorption studies of blood levels; size and design details are not given in the abstracts read.
factors.consistency: Studies agree that small peptides like Pro-Hyp appear in blood.
factors.effect_size: Not applicable; these measured blood levels, not health outcomes.
factors.clinical_significance: Blood fragments do not by themselves show any effect on skin.
factors.sample_size: Small; numbers not stated in the abstracts read.
factors.population: Healthy volunteers.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: In one absorption study, the authors' listed affiliation was a company (Jellice Co., Ltd.).
factors.reproducibility: Appearance of collagen peptides in blood was reported by separate groups.
factors.formulation_dose: Absorption differed by peptide form (tripeptide vs other collagen peptides).

claims.claim: Collagen supplements reduce symptoms of osteoarthritis
claims.popular_framing: Collagen rebuilds your joints and stops arthritis pain.
claims.question: Does collagen help osteoarthritis pain?
claims.outcome: Pain, stiffness and function scores
claims.population: Adults with osteoarthritis, mainly of the knee
claims.bottom_line: Possibly a modest help for osteoarthritis symptoms, but the trials are few and at high risk of bias. It has not been shown to rebuild joints.
claims.what_research_found: A 2019 meta-analysis found collagen lowered total WOMAC scores (a standard osteoarthritis questionnaire), visual analog pain scores and stiffness. WOMAC pain and function subscores did not differ from placebo. A 2023 meta-analysis of 4 trials (507 people with knee osteoarthritis) found more pain relief than placebo.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: These studies did not show collagen rebuilds cartilage. They did not test healthy people.
claims.limitations: All four trials in the 2023 review were at high risk of bias. Results within the 2019 review were mixed across subscores.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Oral collagen, collagen peptides or hydrolyzed collagen. Doses and durations were not stated in the abstracts read.

factors.study_quality: All trials in the 2023 review rated high risk of bias.
factors.consistency: Both reviews favour collagen on some measures, but not on WOMAC pain or function subscores.
factors.effect_size: Moderate (SMD -0.58) for pain in the 2023 review, with a wide confidence interval.
factors.clinical_significance: Uncertain; a total WOMAC difference of 8 points was reported.
factors.sample_size: 4 trials, 507 people in the 2023 review.
factors.population: People with osteoarthritis only.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Not stated for the underlying trials in the abstracts read.
factors.reproducibility: Two reviews agree in direction; how many trials they share is not stated in the abstracts.
factors.formulation_dose: Different collagen products pooled together.

claims.claim: Collagen supplements reduce joint pain in healthy, active people
claims.popular_framing: Athletes should take collagen to protect their knees.
claims.question: Does collagen help sore knees if you don't have arthritis?
claims.outcome: Activity-related knee pain
claims.population: Physically active adults without diagnosed joint disease
claims.bottom_line: Mixed. One trial in young active adults found a small benefit; another in older active adults found none.
claims.what_research_found: In 180 active adults aged 18 to 30, 5 g/day of specific collagen peptides for 12 weeks reduced exercise-related knee pain slightly more than placebo (about 6 mm more on a 100 mm scale). In 167 active adults with a median age of 63, 10 g/day for 12 weeks did no better than placebo. A 2021 systematic review of 15 trials, mostly in recreational athletes, judged joint pain and function as the most likely benefits.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It has not been shown that collagen prevents joint injury or protects joints long term.
claims.limitations: Few trials, short duration, and different doses (5 g vs 10 g a day). In the positive trial, one author had given lectures partly supported by GELITA AG.
claims.formulation_and_dose: 5 to 10 g/day collagen peptides for 12 weeks in the trials cited.

factors.study_quality: Randomized, placebo-controlled trials, but few of them.
factors.consistency: Conflicting results between trials.
factors.effect_size: Small where positive (about 6 mm on a 100 mm pain scale).
factors.clinical_significance: A 6 mm difference may not be noticeable.
factors.sample_size: 167 to 180 people per trial.
factors.population: Young versus older active adults gave different results.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: In the positive trial, one author had lectures partly supported by GELITA AG, one listed affiliation was the Collagen Research Institute, and another author joined that institute after the study.
factors.reproducibility: The positive trial was designed to confirm an earlier result with the same peptides; a trial of 10 g/day collagen peptides in older active adults was null.
factors.formulation_dose: Specific bioactive collagen peptides (type I collagen, mean molecular weight 3 kDa; 5 g/day) in the positive trial vs collagen peptides (10 g/day; product details not given in the abstract) in the null trial.

profiles.absorption: Collagen is broken down during digestion. After a dose of gelatin hydrolysate, collagen peptides (mainly Pro-Hyp) rose in the blood, peaked at 1 to 2 hours and halved by 4 hours. Blood levels varied with the peptide form of the product.
profiles.side_effects: In a 2023 meta-analysis of knee osteoarthritis trials, adverse events did not differ significantly between collagen peptides and placebo, but the result was borderline (OR 1.66; 95% CI 0.99 to 2.78; p = 0.05) and the evidence was rated very low quality. Other side-effect data were not verified for this draft.
profiles.interactions: No interaction data were found in the sources verified for this draft.
profiles.cautions: Talk to a clinician before starting any supplement, especially if pregnant, breastfeeding, taking medication or managing a health condition. Collagen is an animal product; the absorption study cited used gelatin hydrolysates from pig skin, chicken feet and cartilage, which may matter for allergies or dietary choices. Check the label for the source.
profiles.upper_limit: No upper limit was found in the sources verified for this draft.
profiles.research_doses_summary: Doses used in research: 5 to 10 g/day of collagen peptides for 12 weeks in joint trials; skin reviews reported effects after about 12 weeks (90 days). Absorption studies used single doses of 9.4 to 23 g gelatin hydrolysate.
