sources.title: Effects of Collagen Supplements on Skin Aging: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
sources.authors: Myung SK, Park Y.
sources.population: Adults in collagen skin-aging RCTs
sources.intervention: Oral collagen supplements vs control in RCTs (comparator not described in the abstract)
sources.findings: Pooled over all 23 RCTs, collagen improved skin hydration, elasticity and wrinkles. But studies without pharmaceutical-company funding showed no effect on any of these, while company-funded studies did. High-quality studies showed no significant effect in any category; low-quality studies showed improved elasticity. Authors concluded there is currently no clinical evidence to support collagen supplements to prevent or treat skin aging.
sources.limitations: Effect sizes not given in the abstract.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract (the review itself analysed trial funding).
sources.cited_for: collagen-skin and collagen-wrinkles: funding-source and study-quality subgroup results.

sources.title: Effects of hydrolyzed collagen supplementation on skin aging: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.authors: de Miranda RB, Weimer P, Rossi RC.
sources.population: Adults aged 20 to 70; 95% women
sources.intervention: Oral hydrolyzed collagen vs placebo
sources.findings: Hydrolyzed collagen gave favourable results compared with placebo for skin hydration, elasticity and wrinkles; hydration and elasticity findings were confirmed in subgroup analysis. Authors concluded 90 days of intake is effective in reducing skin aging.
sources.limitations: Effect sizes, heterogeneity and funding not given in the abstract; mostly women.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: collagen-skin, collagen-wrinkles: earlier positive pooled result.

sources.title: Oral Collagen Peptides and Skin Rejuvenation: A Systematic Review and an Updated Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
sources.authors: Batool A, Abbas MS, Farooq R, et al.
sources.population: Healthy adults
sources.intervention: Oral collagen supplementation vs control in RCTs (comparator not described in the abstract)
sources.findings: Improvements in instrument-measured skin hydration (SMD 0.44; 95% CI 0.15 to 0.73), elasticity (SMD 0.62; 95% CI 0.15 to 1.10) and transepidermal water loss (SMD -0.39; 95% CI -0.62 to -0.16). Effects appeared time-dependent rather than dose-dependent; elasticity and barrier changes needed at least 12 weeks. Apparent improvements in wrinkles, roughness and dermal density were judged statistical artifacts driven by outliers and heterogeneity.
sources.limitations: Trial funding not analysed in the abstract.
sources.funding: Authors declare no conflicts of interest; funding not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: collagen-skin: hydration and elasticity estimates and 12-week timing; collagen-wrinkles: wrinkle results judged artifacts.

sources.title: Hydrolyzed Collagen for Skin Aging Meta-Analyses Are Unreliable.
sources.authors: Grimes DR, Mahto A.
sources.population: Re-analysis of existing collagen skin meta-analyses and their primary trials
sources.intervention: Methodological re-analysis and dose-adjusted meta-regression
sources.findings: Found inaccurate reporting of primary-study data and inappropriate combining of different measures in two existing meta-analyses. A meta-regression accounting for dose found no evidence of benefit from collagen supplementation.
sources.limitations: A methods critique and re-analysis rather than a new trial.
sources.funding: Authors declare no conflicts of interest; funding not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: collagen-skin, collagen-wrinkles: concerns about reliability of positive meta-analyses.

sources.title: Myths and media in oral collagen supplementation for the skin, nails, and hair: A review.
sources.authors: Rustad AM, Nickles MA, McKenney JE, et al.
sources.population: Collagen claims on Instagram, YouTube and by companies, compared with the literature
sources.intervention: Narrative review
sources.findings: Some studies show collagen can enhance skin elasticity and hydration, but dermatologic claims in the media go beyond what the literature supports. More research is needed on effects and on the physiologic mechanism.
sources.limitations: Review, not a quantitative synthesis.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: collagen-straight-to-skin and collagen-skin: media claims exceed evidence; mechanism not established.

sources.title: Identification of food-derived collagen peptides in human blood after oral ingestion of gelatin hydrolysates.
sources.authors: Iwai K, Hasegawa T, Taguchi Y, et al.
sources.population: Healthy volunteers after a 12-hour fast
sources.intervention: Single doses of gelatin hydrolysate, 9.4 to 23 g, from porcine skin, chicken feet and cartilage
sources.findings: After ingestion, the peptide form of hydroxyproline in blood rose, peaking at 20 to 60 nmol/mL plasma at 1 to 2 hours and halving by 4 hours. The main food-derived collagen peptide in blood was the dipeptide Pro-Hyp; small amounts of other di- and tripeptides were also found.
sources.limitations: Absorption study only; number of volunteers not captured; does not measure skin.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: collagen-straight-to-skin: ingested collagen appears in blood as small peptides such as Pro-Hyp.

sources.title: Absorption and Urinary Excretion of Peptides after Collagen Tripeptide Ingestion in Humans.
sources.authors: Yamamoto S, Deguchi K, Onuma M, et al.
sources.population: Humans
sources.intervention: Collagen tripeptide preparations vs a collagen peptide without tripeptides
sources.findings: Plasma Gly-Pro-Hyp and Pro-Hyp rose after collagen tripeptide preparations, more with greater Gly-Pro-Hyp intake, and these peptides were also found in urine. Authors conclude tripeptides from collagen are absorbed efficiently.
sources.limitations: Absorption study; does not measure skin or joints; sample size not stated in abstract.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract; first author affiliated with Jellice Co., Ltd. (a company)
sources.cited_for: collagen-straight-to-skin: absorption depends on peptide form; fragments circulate in blood.

sources.title: Effect of collagen supplementation on osteoarthritis symptoms: a meta-analysis of randomized placebo-controlled trials.
sources.authors: García-Coronado JM, Martínez-Olvera L, Elizondo-Omaña RE, et al.
sources.population: People with osteoarthritis
sources.intervention: Oral collagen vs placebo
sources.findings: Collagen reduced total WOMAC score (WMD -8.00; 95% CI -13.04 to -2.95) and VAS pain score (WMD -16.57; 95% CI -26.24 to -6.89) and the WOMAC stiffness subscore (WMD -0.41). WOMAC pain (WMD -0.22; 95% CI -1.58 to 1.13) and function subscores did not differ from placebo.
sources.limitations: Number of trials and participants not stated in the abstract.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: collagen-osteoarthritis: symptom score changes.

sources.title: Analgesic efficacy of collagen peptide in knee osteoarthritis: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
sources.authors: Lin CR, Tsai SHL, Huang KY, et al.
sources.population: Adults with knee osteoarthritis
sources.intervention: Collagen peptides or hydrolyzed collagen vs placebo
sources.findings: Collagen peptides gave more pain relief than placebo (SMD -0.58; 95% CI -0.98 to -0.18; I2 68%; moderate-quality evidence). Adverse event risk did not differ significantly (OR 1.66; 95% CI 0.99 to 2.78; very low-quality evidence).
sources.limitations: All four trials judged at high risk of bias.
sources.funding: Authors report no conflicts of interest
sources.cited_for: collagen-osteoarthritis: pain relief and high risk of bias; side_effects.

sources.title: The effects of collagen peptide supplementation on body composition, collagen synthesis, and recovery from joint injury and exercise: a systematic review.
sources.authors: Khatri M, Naughton RJ, Clifford T, et al.
sources.population: 12 studies in recreational athletes, 2 in older adults, 1 in untrained pre-menopausal women
sources.intervention: Collagen peptides with exercise
sources.findings: Collagen peptides appeared most beneficial for joint function and joint pain. Collagen synthesis rates rose with 15 g/day but muscle protein synthesis was not improved compared with higher-quality protein.
sources.limitations: Narrative synthesis; authors call for larger studies and more precise outcome measures.
sources.funding: Conflict statement says 'the company' had no involvement in conception or writing; details not in abstract
sources.cited_for: collagen-active-joints: overview of trials in active people.

sources.title: The Influence of Specific Bioactive Collagen Peptides on Knee Joint Discomfort in Young Physically Active Adults: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
sources.authors: Zdzieblik D, Brame J, Oesser S, et al.
sources.population: Active adults aged 18 to 30 with exercise-related knee pain, no diagnosed joint disease
sources.intervention: 5 g/day specific collagen peptides vs placebo for 12 weeks
sources.findings: Exercise-induced knee pain fell more with collagen (-21.9 mm) than placebo (-15.6 mm) on a 100 mm scale (p = 0.024). Pain at rest and after squats did not differ between groups.
sources.limitations: Difference between groups was about 6 mm on a 100 mm scale.
sources.funding: Authors declare no conflict of interest; one author has given lectures partly supported by GELITA AG; one listed affiliation is the Collagen Research Institute (Kiel), and another author joined it after the study
sources.cited_for: collagen-active-joints: positive trial in young active adults.

sources.title: Effectiveness of collagen supplementation on pain scores in healthy individuals with self-reported knee pain: a randomized controlled trial.
sources.authors: Bongers CCWG, Ten Haaf DSM, Catoire M, et al.
sources.population: Healthy, physically active adults (median age 63) with self-reported knee pain
sources.intervention: 10 g/day collagen peptides vs placebo for 12 weeks
sources.findings: Knee pain fell similarly in both groups (VAS -1.6 vs -1.9; p = 0.42). Knee function scores and inflammatory, cartilage and bone markers did not differ between groups.
sources.limitations: Middle-aged to older participants.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: collagen-active-joints: null trial in active middle-aged and older adults.

profiles.name: Creatine
profiles.summary: Creatine monohydrate reliably boosts strength gains from resistance training; research does not support fears about kidney damage in healthy people or hair loss, and brain benefits are unproven.
profiles.description: Creatine is a compound stored mostly in skeletal muscle. The body makes about 1 g a day, and meat and fish supply more. Supplements are almost always creatine monohydrate, the form used in nearly all research.
profiles.biological_function: Creatine helps muscles quickly regenerate ATP, the cell's energy supply, during short, hard efforts. Supplements raise muscle phosphocreatine stores and may speed their recovery between efforts. That is why the benefits show up mainly in repeated bursts, such as lifting or sprinting, rather than endurance exercise.

formulations.name: Creatine monohydrate
formulations.notes: The form used in almost all research. It is 88% creatine by weight. NIH ODS states other forms have not been proven superior.

claims.claim: Creatine increases muscle strength and lean mass when combined with resistance training in adults
claims.popular_framing: Creatine is the most proven supplement for getting stronger in the gym.
claims.question: Does creatine help you get stronger when you lift weights?
claims.outcome: Muscle strength and lean tissue mass
claims.population: Adults doing resistance training: mainly men under 50, and men and women with average ages of 57–70.
claims.bottom_line: Yes. Taken alongside resistance training, creatine leads to larger strength gains than training alone. It works with training, not instead of it.
claims.what_research_found: In adults under 50, a 2024 meta-analysis of 23 studies found creatine plus training added about 4.4 kg to upper-body and 11.4 kg to lower-body strength compared with placebo. In older adults (average ages 57–70 across studies), a meta-analysis of 22 trials (721 people) found about 1.4 kg more lean tissue mass and greater chest and leg press strength. The under-50 meta-analysis measured strength only, so the lean-mass figures read here come from older adults. NIH ODS reports that several sports nutrition bodies agree creatine enhances repeated high-intensity exercise.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: Part of the lean-mass gain may be water, since creatine causes water retention. Gains in directly measured muscle size are small (see the muscle-size claim). Creatine adds little for endurance sports.
claims.limitations: Most young-adult studies were in men; in the under-50 meta-analysis, women did not show significant strength gains, but only a few small female studies existed. Both meta-analyses read share an author (Candow), who declared creatine-industry ties in the 2024 paper.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Creatine monohydrate. Common research protocols: about 20 g/day for 5–7 days then 3–5 g/day, or 3–6 g/day without loading. Older-adult trials lasted 7–52 weeks with training 2–3 days a week.

factors.study_quality: Randomised, placebo-controlled trials pooled in several meta-analyses.
factors.consistency: Strength benefit in both meta-analyses (under-50s and older adults). In under-50s, women's gains were not statistically significant, but there were few female studies.
factors.effect_size: Meaningful: about 4.4 kg upper-body and 11.4 kg lower-body strength in under-50s; SMD 0.24–0.35 in older adults.
factors.clinical_significance: Large enough to matter for people training for strength.
factors.sample_size: Over 1,200 participants across the two meta-analyses read, plus many short-term trials summarised by NIH ODS.
factors.population: Applies to people doing resistance training. Evidence in younger women is thin.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: One author of the under-50 meta-analysis reports industry-sponsored creatine research and advisory roles with creatine makers; the older-adult meta-analysis, which shares that author, reports no conflicts.
factors.reproducibility: Many trials pooled in two meta-analyses (which share one author); NIH ODS reports that several sports nutrition bodies agree creatine enhances repeated high-intensity exercise.
factors.formulation_dose: NIH ODS says monohydrate is the form used in almost all research and research doses match common products; the meta-analysis abstracts do not state form or dose.

claims.claim: Creatine substantially increases directly measured muscle size on top of resistance training
claims.popular_framing: Creatine makes your muscles grow much bigger.
claims.question: Does creatine actually make muscles bigger, not just heavier?
claims.outcome: Muscle size measured directly by MRI, CT or ultrasound
claims.population: Healthy adults doing resistance training for at least 6 weeks.
claims.bottom_line: Only a little. When muscle is measured directly, the extra growth from creatine is very small. Some of the weight people gain on creatine is water.
claims.what_research_found: A 2023 meta-analysis of 10 trials (44 outcomes) found a very small effect favouring creatine on directly measured muscle size (pooled estimate 0.11). Muscle thickness grew about 0.10–0.16 cm more in the upper and lower body. The benefit was slightly larger in younger than older adults, though the uncertainty range for that difference included zero.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It did not show a large extra gain in muscle size. The uncertainty range for the pooled effect included zero.
claims.limitations: Only 10 trials used direct muscle imaging. Several authors report ties to creatine companies. Only the abstract was read.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Creatine monohydrate with resistance training for 6 weeks or more; doses were not detailed in the abstract.

factors.study_quality: Randomised controlled trials with direct imaging of muscle.
factors.consistency: Small effects in the same direction for upper and lower body.
factors.effect_size: Very small (pooled 0.11; 0.10–0.16 cm muscle thickness).
factors.clinical_significance: Unlikely to be noticeable by itself.
factors.sample_size: 10 trials; participant total not stated in the abstract.
factors.population: Healthy training adults; slightly larger effect in younger people.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Several authors report advisory roles or industry-funded creatine research.
factors.reproducibility: One meta-analysis read for this specific outcome.
factors.formulation_dose: Monohydrate, matching common products.

claims.claim: Creatine causes hair loss by raising DHT
claims.popular_framing: Creatine will make you go bald.
claims.question: Does creatine cause hair loss?
claims.outcome: Hair loss, hair follicle measures and DHT (dihydrotestosterone)
claims.population: Young men: rugby players (2009) and resistance-trained men aged 18–40 (2025).
claims.bottom_line: No study has shown that creatine causes hair loss. The worry comes from one small 2009 study that found higher DHT. A 2025 trial that measured hair directly found no difference from placebo in DHT or hair measures.
claims.what_research_found: In a 2009 crossover study of 20 rugby players, DHT rose 56% after a week of high-dose creatine and stayed 40% above baseline after two more weeks; hair was not measured. In a 2025 randomised trial, 38 trained men completed 12 weeks of 5 g/day creatine or placebo. There were no differences in testosterone, DHT, the DHT-to-testosterone ratio, hair density, follicle count or hair thickness.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: No study has followed hair over years. The 2009 rise in DHT has not been shown to cause hair loss, and it was not repeated in the 2025 trial.
claims.limitations: Both studies are small, short and only in young men. People already prone to hair loss and women were not specifically studied. The 2025 trial's authors include advisors to creatine brands. There is not enough data yet to rate this as 'evidence against'.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Creatine monohydrate: 25 g/day for 7 days then 5 g/day for 14 days (2009); 5 g/day for 12 weeks (2025).

factors.study_quality: Both placebo-controlled; the 2025 trial was randomised and measured hair directly.
factors.consistency: Conflicting on DHT; no study shows hair loss.
factors.effect_size: No difference in hair outcomes in the only trial that measured them.
factors.clinical_significance: The 2009 DHT rise was a blood-test change without any hair measurement.
factors.sample_size: Small: 20 and 38 participants.
factors.population: Young men only.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: 2025 trial authors report advisory roles with supplement and creatine brands.
factors.reproducibility: The 2009 DHT finding was not reproduced in 2025.
factors.formulation_dose: Monohydrate at common research doses.

claims.claim: Creatine harms the kidneys of healthy people
claims.popular_framing: Creatine wrecks your kidneys.
claims.question: Is creatine bad for your kidneys?
claims.outcome: Kidney injury and kidney function (creatinine, measured and estimated GFR, urea, protein in urine)
claims.population: Healthy adults. People with existing kidney disease are a separate question.
claims.bottom_line: In healthy people, trials have not found kidney damage. Creatine does raise blood creatinine, which can make a standard kidney blood test look worse even when the kidneys are fine.
claims.what_research_found: A 2026 meta-analysis of 26 randomised trials (1,036 people, including some with chronic kidney disease) found creatine raised serum creatinine by about 0.14 mg/dL and lowered creatinine-based kidney function estimates. But when kidney filtration was measured directly with a tracer (Cr-EDTA), there was no significant drop. Blood urea, and albumin and protein in the urine, did not differ. The authors concluded the creatinine changes likely reflect creatinine metabolism, not kidney injury. A 2019 meta-analysis also concluded creatine did not cause kidney damage at the doses and durations studied, and NIH ODS describes creatine as safe for healthy adults in the short term.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: These studies do not show that creatine is safe for people who already have kidney disease. Data covering many years of use are more limited.
claims.limitations: Serum creatinine results varied widely between trials. Fewer trials measured filtration directly. The 2019 meta-analysis abstract reports confidence intervals that conflict with its 'no significant change' wording. The 2026 meta-analysis pooled healthy people with people who have chronic kidney disease, and its abstract does not give healthy-only results. Only abstracts were read.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Creatine monohydrate at doses used in research; doses and durations were not detailed in the abstracts read.

factors.study_quality: Randomised, placebo-controlled trials pooled in a registered meta-analysis.
factors.consistency: Direct measures and urine markers consistently show no harm; creatinine-based markers shift for a known reason.
factors.effect_size: No significant change in directly measured filtration (Cr-EDTA: +5.89 mL/min, 95% CI −0.30 to 12.08), so a meaningful drop is unlikely.
factors.clinical_significance: No sign of kidney injury in healthy people at research doses.
factors.sample_size: 26 trials, 1,036 participants (healthy and with chronic kidney disease) in the latest meta-analysis; the abstract does not say how many trials measured filtration directly.
factors.population: Healthy people and people with chronic kidney disease were pooled in the latest meta-analysis; it does not settle safety for people with kidney disease.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: 2026 meta-analysis authors declare no competing interests.
factors.reproducibility: Two meta-analyses by different groups (2019 and 2026) conclude there is no kidney damage, although the 2019 abstract's own numbers show significant rises in creatinine and urea.
factors.formulation_dose: Monohydrate at common research doses.

claims.claim: Creatine improves cognitive function (memory, attention, processing speed) in adults
claims.popular_framing: Creatine is a brain booster.
claims.question: Does creatine help you think better?
claims.outcome: Memory, attention, processing speed and overall cognition
claims.population: Adults aged about 21–76, healthy and with specific diseases.
claims.bottom_line: Maybe a small effect on memory, but it is not settled. One meta-analysis found small benefits; the EU food safety authority (EFSA) reviewed the evidence and concluded a cause-and-effect link has not been established.
claims.what_research_found: A 2024 meta-analysis of 16 trials (492 adults) found small improvements in memory (SMD 0.31), attention time and processing speed. There was no effect on overall cognition or executive function. Benefits were larger in people with diseases. In 2024, EFSA's panel noted that a working-memory effect appeared only at 20 g/day for 5–7 days, not at lower doses or with longer use, and concluded that a cause-and-effect relationship was not established.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It is not established that creatine improves thinking in healthy people at usual doses. Nothing here shows creatine prevents or treats dementia or any other disease.
claims.limitations: Certainty was moderate for memory and low for other outcomes. Trials were small and mixed healthy and ill participants. The two authoritative reviews disagree in emphasis.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Creatine monohydrate. EFSA described studies at 20 g/day for 5–7 days, 2.2–14 g/day, and 5 g/day for 6 weeks after loading.

factors.study_quality: Randomised trials; risk of bias rated low to moderate.
factors.consistency: Inconsistent: positive in some domains and some doses, null in others; EFSA judged the evidence insufficient.
factors.effect_size: Small (SMD about 0.3–0.5).
factors.clinical_significance: Unclear whether a healthy person would notice a difference.
factors.sample_size: 492 participants across 16 trials.
factors.population: Mixed healthy and ill adults; larger effects in people with diseases.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: The EFSA application came from a creatine manufacturer; the meta-analysis authors declare no conflicts.
factors.reproducibility: Several small independent trials, but low GRADE certainty for most outcomes.
factors.formulation_dose: Effects may depend on high loading doses rather than usual 3–5 g/day.

research_doses.note: Per day. 3–5 g/day maintenance or 3–6 g/day without loading; about 20 g/day for 5–7 days in loading protocols (NIH ODS). The hair-loss trial used 5 g/day.

food_vs_supplement.comparison_note: NIH ODS lists about 2 g of creatine per pound of beef or salmon, and the body makes about 1 g a day. Reaching a 3–5 g research dose from food alone would take roughly 1.5–2.5 lb of meat or fish a day, so food and supplement amounts are not directly comparable at research doses.
food_vs_supplement.food_advantages: Meat and fish also provide protein and other nutrients. The creatine amounts per pound come from NIH ODS; the cooking state was not specified.
food_vs_supplement.when_supplement_may_help: Research benefits are mainly in people doing resistance training or repeated high-intensity exercise. NIH ODS notes vegetarians, who have lower muscle creatine, may respond more.

profiles.absorption: Creatine monohydrate raises muscle creatine stores. A loading phase (about 20 g/day for 5–7 days) raises stores faster; 3–6 g/day without loading was used over 3–4 weeks in research (NIH ODS). Other forms have not been proven better than monohydrate.
profiles.side_effects: The most consistent effect is weight gain from water retention: 1–2 kg in the first month in several studies (NIH ODS). Anecdotal reports include nausea, diarrhoea, muscle cramps and heat intolerance. Rare muscle stiffness has been reported.
profiles.interactions: No specific drug interactions were described in the sources read for this profile.
profiles.cautions: People with kidney disease, and those who are pregnant or breastfeeding, should speak to a clinician first; the research cited here does not settle safety for them. Creatine raises blood creatinine, which can make creatinine-based kidney tests look worse, so whoever interprets those tests should know about it. Water weight gain may matter for weight-class or endurance athletes.
profiles.research_doses_summary: Doses used in research: creatine monohydrate at about 20 g/day (four 5 g portions) for 5–7 days then 3–5 g/day, or 3–6 g/day without loading. Older-adult trials ran 7–52 weeks alongside resistance training.

sources.title: Effects of Creatine Supplementation and Resistance Training on Muscle Strength Gains in Adults <50 Years of Age: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
sources.authors: Wang Z, Qiu B, Li R, Han Y, Petersen C, Liu S, Zhang Y, Liu C, Candow DG, Del Coso J.
sources.population: Adults under 50 doing resistance training (mostly men)
sources.intervention: Creatine vs placebo combined with resistance training
sources.findings: Creatine plus training increased upper-body strength by 4.43 kg and lower-body strength by 11.35 kg more than placebo. Men showed significant gains; women did not show significant gains (few female studies). Trend toward larger lower-body gains with higher doses.
sources.limitations: Very few studies in women; trends in subgroup analyses were not significant.
sources.funding: One author (Candow) reports industry-sponsored creatine research and advisory roles with creatine manufacturers.
sources.cited_for: creatine-strength-lean-mass: strength gains in adults under 50; sex difference.

sources.title: Effect of creatine supplementation during resistance training on lean tissue mass and muscular strength in older adults: a meta-analysis.
sources.authors: Chilibeck PD, Kaviani M, Candow DG, Zello GA.
sources.population: Men and women, mean age 57–70 years, doing resistance training
sources.intervention: Creatine vs placebo during resistance training 2–3 days/week for 7–52 weeks
sources.findings: Creatine gave greater gains in lean tissue mass (mean difference 1.37 kg, 95% CI 0.97–1.76), chest press strength (SMD 0.35) and leg press strength (SMD 0.24).
sources.limitations: Authors note results across individual studies had been equivocal; mechanisms not extensively evaluated.
sources.funding: Authors report no conflicts of interest.
sources.cited_for: creatine-strength-lean-mass: lean mass and strength gains in older adults.

sources.title: The Effects of Creatine Supplementation Combined with Resistance Training on Regional Measures of Muscle Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis.
sources.authors: Burke R, Piñero A, Coleman M, Mohan A, Sapuppo M, Augustin F, Aragon AA, Candow DG, Forbes SC, Swinton P, Schoenfeld BJ.
sources.population: Healthy adults doing resistance training for at least 6 weeks
sources.intervention: Creatine plus resistance training vs resistance training plus placebo; muscle measured by MRI, CT or ultrasound
sources.findings: Pooled estimate 0.11 (95% credible interval −0.02 to 0.25): a very small effect favouring creatine. Upper- and lower-body muscle thickness gains were 0.10–0.16 cm larger. Slightly larger benefit in younger than older adults (0.17, 95% CrI −0.09 to 0.45).
sources.limitations: Small number of trials; the credible interval includes zero.
sources.funding: Several authors report current or past advisory roles with supplement or creatine companies, industry-sponsored creatine research, or creatine donations.
sources.cited_for: creatine-muscle-size: directly measured muscle growth is small.

sources.title: Does creatine cause hair loss? A 12-week randomized controlled trial.
sources.authors: Lak M, Forbes SC, Ashtary-Larky D, Dadkhahfar S, Robati RM, Nezakati F, Khajevandi M, Naseri S, Gerafiani A, Haghighat N, Antonio J, Tinsley GM.
sources.population: Resistance-trained men aged 18–40
sources.intervention: Creatine monohydrate 5 g/day vs maltodextrin 5 g/day for 12 weeks
sources.findings: No group-by-time differences for total or free testosterone, DHT, DHT-to-testosterone ratio, or hair density, follicular unit count and cumulative hair thickness. Authors describe it as the first study to directly assess hair follicle health after creatine.
sources.limitations: Small, short, men only.
sources.funding: Several authors report advisory or consulting roles with supplement brands, including creatine brands, and creatine donations.
sources.cited_for: creatine-hair-loss: direct test of hair outcomes found no effect.

sources.title: Three weeks of creatine monohydrate supplementation affects dihydrotestosterone to testosterone ratio in college-aged rugby players.
sources.authors: van der Merwe J, Brooks NE, Myburgh KH.
sources.population: College-aged male rugby players, during competitive season
sources.intervention: Double-blind placebo-controlled crossover: 25 g/day creatine (with glucose) for 7 days, then 5 g/day for 14 days; 6-week washout
sources.findings: Testosterone did not change. DHT rose 56% after 7 days of loading and stayed 40% above baseline after 14 days of maintenance. The DHT:T ratio rose 36%, then stayed 22% above baseline. Hair was not measured.
sources.limitations: Small; short; no hair outcomes. The abstract describes a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover but does not say allocation was randomised.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: creatine-hair-loss: origin of the DHT concern.

sources.title: Impact of creatine supplementation on kidney health: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.authors: de Souza Almeida A, da Silva LOD, Takahasi BNA, Terada BD, Gonçalves FGA, Porto BC, da Silva Sardenberg RA, Passerotti CC, Maia RS, Samaan F, Thoman M, Molina WR, Shiomi da Cruz JA.
sources.population: Healthy individuals and patients with chronic kidney disease (including a hemodialysis subgroup)
sources.intervention: Creatine vs placebo; RCTs to March 2025
sources.findings: Creatine raised serum creatinine (MD 0.14 mg/dL, 95% CI 0.05–0.22; I² 93.9%) and lowered creatinine-based GFR estimates (MD −10.75 mL/min). GFR measured with Cr-EDTA did not change significantly (MD 5.89 mL/min, 95% CI −0.30 to 12.08), and there were no differences in serum urea, albuminuria, proteinuria or urinary creatinine. Authors conclude the changes likely reflect altered creatinine metabolism rather than kidney injury.
sources.limitations: Very high heterogeneity for serum creatinine; mixed healthy and CKD populations.
sources.funding: Authors declare no competing interests.
sources.cited_for: creatine-kidney-harm: no sign of kidney injury on direct measures; creatinine-based tests are affected.

sources.title: Effects of Creatine Supplementation on Renal Function: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
sources.authors: de Souza E Silva A, Pertille A, Reis Barbosa CG, Aparecida de Oliveira Silva J, de Jesus DV, Ribeiro AGSV, Baganha RJ, de Oliveira JJ.
sources.population: Not detailed in abstract
sources.intervention: Creatine supplementation; doses and durations not stated in abstract
sources.findings: Authors conclude creatine does not induce renal damage in the amounts and durations studied. Reported SMDs: serum creatinine 0.48 (95% CI 0.24–0.73), plasma urea 1.10 (95% CI 0.34–1.85).
sources.limitations: Only 6 studies pooled. The abstract calls these changes non-significant, yet the confidence intervals exclude zero; this should be checked in the full text.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: creatine-kidney-harm: earlier meta-analysis reaching the same conclusion.

sources.title: The effects of creatine supplementation on cognitive function in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.authors: Xu C, Bi S, Zhang W, Luo L.
sources.population: Adults aged 20.8–76.4, healthy and with specific diseases
sources.intervention: Creatine monohydrate; short (<4 weeks) and longer (≥4 weeks) interventions
sources.findings: Improved memory (SMD 0.31, 95% CI 0.18–0.44), attention time (SMD −0.31) and processing speed time (SMD −0.51). No significant effect on overall cognitive function or executive function. Larger benefit in people with diseases, ages 18–60, and females. GRADE certainty moderate for memory, low for the rest.
sources.limitations: Mostly low-certainty evidence; small trials; mixed populations.
sources.funding: Authors declare no conflicts of interest.
sources.cited_for: creatine-cognition: pooled cognitive effects and certainty.

sources.title: Creatine and improvement in cognitive function: Evaluation of a health claim pursuant to article 13(5) of regulation (EC) No 1924/2006.
sources.authors: EFSA Panel on Nutrition, Novel Foods and Food Allergens (NDA); Turck D, Bohn T, Cámara M, et al.
sources.sample_size: 21 human intervention studies identified by the applicant, plus 2 later studies
sources.population: Healthy individuals (10 studies) and diseased individuals (3 studies), among others
sources.intervention: Creatine at various doses, including 20 g/day for 5–7 days and 2.2–14 g/day
sources.findings: A working-memory effect seen in two studies at 20 g/day for 5–7 days was not seen at lower doses (2.2–14 g/day) or with 5 g/day for 6 weeks after loading. A response-inhibition effect was an isolated finding among 10 studies in healthy people. Studies in diseased people did not support an effect. The panel concluded a cause-and-effect relationship between creatine and improved cognitive function has not been established.
sources.limitations: Regulatory assessment of a specific health-claim application.
sources.funding: Application submitted by Alzchem Trostberg GmbH (a creatine manufacturer); assessed by the independent EFSA panel.
sources.cited_for: creatine-cognition: authoritative body found cause-and-effect not established.

sources.title: Dietary Supplements for Exercise and Athletic Performance — Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
sources.authors: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements
sources.population: Athletes and exercisers
sources.intervention: Creatine monohydrate: about 20 g/day for 5–7 days then 3–5 g/day; or 3–6 g/day without loading
sources.findings: Short-term creatine often improved strength, power and repeated high-intensity work in men and women; little value for endurance sports. Liver and kidneys make about 1 g/day. Beef has about 2 g/lb, pork about 2.3 g/lb, salmon about 2 g/lb. Most consistent side effect is 1–2 kg weight gain in a month from water retention; anecdotal nausea, diarrhoea, cramps, heat intolerance. Considered safe short term in healthy adults; multi-year use reported as safe. Monohydrate is 88% creatine; other forms not proven superior. Vegetarians may respond more. Several sports bodies agree it enhances repeated high-intensity exercise.
sources.limitations: Summary document; last-updated date not captured.
sources.funding: US government (NIH)
sources.cited_for: Food creatine content, research doses, side effects, safety, agency consensus on performance.

sources.title: Dietary Supplements for Exercise and Athletic Performance — Fact Sheet for Consumers
sources.authors: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements
sources.population: Athletes and exercisers
sources.intervention: Creatine about 20 g/day in four portions for 5–7 days, then 3–5 g/day
sources.findings: Creatine can increase strength and power in repeated short bursts of intense activity lasting up to about 2.5 minutes; little value for endurance. Appears safe for healthy adults for weeks to months and seemingly for several years. Often causes some weight gain from water retention; rare muscle stiffness, cramps and stomach upset.
sources.limitations: Consumer summary.
sources.funding: US government (NIH)
sources.cited_for: Plain-language safety and performance summary.

profiles.name: Electrolytes (sodium & potassium)
profiles.summary: For everyday life, water hydrates you well and there is no good evidence electrolyte drinks are better for daily health; during long, continuous exercise some carbohydrate-electrolyte drinks may help keep you hydrated, but extra sodium tablets have not been shown to improve performance, and on average Americans already eat more sodium than recommended.
profiles.description: Electrolytes are minerals that carry an electrical charge in body fluids. The main ones in hydration products are sodium (usually as salt, sodium chloride) and potassium. They are sold as powders, tablets and capsules to add to water, as ready-made sports drinks, and as oral rehydration solutions.
profiles.biological_function: Sodium and potassium help control fluid balance, nerve signals and muscle contraction. The kidneys keep blood levels in a tight range by adjusting how much is lost in urine. Sweat contains sodium, and losses vary a lot between people (ACSM). Diets low in potassium and high in sodium are linked to higher blood pressure (NIH ODS).

formulations.name: Oral rehydration solution (ORS)
formulations.notes: Higher in electrolytes than typical sports drinks. In a trial in rested men, an ORS reduced urine output over 4 hours compared with water.

formulations.name: Sports drinks (carbohydrate-electrolyte drinks)
formulations.notes: Contain sugar plus some sodium and potassium. Can be hypotonic, isotonic or hypertonic; a meta-analysis found hypotonic versions were most likely to support hydration during continuous exercise.

formulations.name: Electrolyte tablets and powders
formulations.notes: Dissolved in water; usually low or no sugar. Formulations vary widely; one brand was tested in a small trial at rest.

formulations.name: Salt (sodium) tablets or capsules
formulations.notes: Used by some endurance athletes. Trials cited here used about 620 mg salt tablets, 700 mg salt per hour, or 1,800 mg sodium over 2 hours.

formulations.name: Potassium supplements
formulations.notes: Potassium chloride is the most common form. Many products contain no more than 99 mg potassium per serving because of FDA concerns about gut lesions with higher-dose potassium drugs (NIH ODS).

claims.claim: Electrolyte drinks hydrate you better than water for everyday, day-to-day hydration
claims.popular_framing: Water isn't enough — add electrolytes to every bottle to stay properly hydrated.
claims.question: Are electrolyte drinks better than water for daily hydration?
claims.outcome: Hydration status / fluid retention in rested, non-exercising people
claims.population: Healthy, well-hydrated adults at rest.
claims.bottom_line: Not established. Drinks with more electrolytes can keep slightly more fluid in your body for a few hours after drinking, but results for sports-drink-style carbohydrate-electrolyte drinks were mixed (no difference from water in one study, slightly more fluid kept in another), and there is no evidence this matters for everyday health.
claims.what_research_found: In a trial of 72 rested men, an oral rehydration solution, full-fat milk and skimmed milk led to less urine over 4 hours than water, but a sports drink and other common drinks did not differ from water. In 19 young adults, electrolytes alone did not consistently improve fluid retention versus water, while electrolytes with carbohydrate did. In 18 active adults, electrolyte tablets in water reduced urine output over 4 hours compared with water. Over a full 24 hours, 34 healthy men had the same hydration status whether they drank water only or water combined with cola, diet cola or orange juice.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: No study we found showed that daily electrolyte drinks improve health, energy, thinking or wellbeing in people who are not exercising heavily or unwell. Short-term fluid retention is a lab measure, not a health outcome.
claims.limitations: Small, short (4–24 hour) studies; mostly young men; drinks varied widely in electrolyte content. One trial tested a single commercial brand.
claims.formulation_and_dose: 1 litre of drink (taken over 30 minutes in two of the fluid-retention studies); 24-hour fluid intake of about 35 ml/kg in the 24-hour study.

factors.study_quality: Randomised crossover trials with objective urine and body-weight measures.
factors.consistency: Mixed: higher-electrolyte ORS and electrolyte tablets improved short-term retention; electrolytes alone did not consistently; a sports drink matched water in one study while a carbohydrate-electrolyte drink beat water in another; 24-hour hydration did not differ across the (non-electrolyte) beverages tested.
factors.effect_size: Modest: e.g. about 300 g less urine over 4 hours with ORS than water (1,038 g vs 1,337 g).
factors.clinical_significance: Unclear for everyday life, where people can drink when thirsty.
factors.sample_size: Small to moderate (18–72 per trial).
factors.population: Healthy, rested, well-hydrated adults, mostly men.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: The carbohydrate/dipeptide-electrolyte study lists a Coca-Cola grant in its PubMed record and one author has consulted for Coca-Cola; the electrolyte-tablet study lists a grant from Nuun & Company, maker of the tablets tested. Both say the sponsor had no role in running the study or interpreting the data.
factors.reproducibility: The beverage hydration index method has been used by several independent groups with somewhat different results.
factors.formulation_dose: Results depend on electrolyte content: higher-sodium solutions like ORS retained more fluid than typical sports drinks.

claims.claim: During prolonged continuous exercise, carbohydrate-electrolyte drinks maintain hydration better than water
claims.popular_framing: For long workouts, a sports drink hydrates you better than plain water.
claims.question: Do sports drinks hydrate better than water during long exercise?
claims.outcome: Change in plasma volume (blood fluid) during exercise
claims.population: People doing continuous exercise for up to 3 hours in lab studies.
claims.bottom_line: Partly. Hypotonic (more dilute) carbohydrate-electrolyte drinks were likely better than water at maintaining blood volume during continuous exercise, but isotonic and hypertonic drinks were not clearly better than water.
claims.what_research_found: A meta-analysis of 28 studies found hypotonic carbohydrate-electrolyte drinks were very likely superior to isotonic drinks and likely superior to hypertonic drinks and water for maintaining plasma volume during continuous exercise. Water performed similarly to hypertonic drinks. The American College of Sports Medicine says drinks with electrolytes and carbohydrate can provide benefits over water alone under certain circumstances, and recommends individual plans because sweat rates and sweat sodium vary between people.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: The meta-analysis measured plasma volume, not race times or health outcomes. The differences between drinks were small (around 1–2 percentage points of plasma volume).
claims.limitations: Surrogate outcome; results were adjusted with modelling assumptions; one author previously received funding from sports-drink companies. The ACSM statement is from 2007.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Carbohydrate-electrolyte drinks with sodium below 50 mmol/L, grouped by osmolality (hypotonic <275, isotonic 275–300, hypertonic >300 mOsmol/kg), drunk continuously during 0–180 minutes of exercise.

factors.study_quality: Systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis of 28 studies.
factors.consistency: Benefit was specific to hypotonic drinks; other drink types did not beat water.
factors.effect_size: Small: about 1.1 percentage points of plasma volume for hypotonic drinks vs water.
factors.clinical_significance: Uncertain; the analysis measured plasma volume, not performance or health outcomes.
factors.sample_size: 28 studies with 68 drink comparisons; participant total not given in the abstract.
factors.population: Exercising adults in lab settings.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Lead author previously funded by Frucor and Lucozade-Ribena-Suntory to report on hypotonic drink effects.
factors.reproducibility: Pooled across many studies; consistent with ACSM guidance that electrolyte-carbohydrate drinks can help in some circumstances.
factors.formulation_dose: Effect depends on drink concentration (osmolality); check a product's osmolality rather than assuming it matches the drinks studied.

claims.claim: Taking extra sodium (salt tablets) during endurance exercise improves performance
claims.popular_framing: Salt tablets are the secret to better long-distance performance in the heat.
claims.question: Do salt tablets improve endurance performance?
claims.outcome: Endurance performance and heat tolerance
claims.population: Trained endurance athletes (cyclists, triathletes).
claims.bottom_line: Not shown. In the trials we found, extra sodium did not improve performance, sweat rate or heat strain, but the trials were small.
claims.what_research_found: In 9 trained cyclists doing a 72 km time trial in cool conditions, 700 mg of salt per hour did not change finishing time (171 vs 172 minutes). In 11 endurance athletes exercising for 2 hours under moderate heat stress, 1,800 mg of sodium did not change sweat rate, heart-rate drift, skin temperature, effort ratings or time to exhaustion. In 413 Ironman triathletes, finishing times did not differ between sodium tablets, placebo and no supplement.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: These small trials cannot rule out a modest benefit for some people, such as very salty sweaters in very long events in extreme heat. No trial we read tested performance in very hot conditions specifically.
claims.limitations: Very small crossover trials; the Ironman trial let athletes take tablets as they wished and was designed around blood sodium rather than performance.
claims.formulation_and_dose: 700 mg salt per hour (capsules); 1,800 mg sodium over 2 hours; 620 mg salt tablets taken 1–4 per hour (Ironman).

factors.study_quality: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trials, plus a large randomised field trial.
factors.consistency: All trials found no performance benefit.
factors.effect_size: None detected.
factors.clinical_significance: No meaningful performance gain shown.
factors.sample_size: Small in the lab trials (9 and 11 athletes); 413 in the field trial.
factors.population: Trained endurance athletes; not tested in everyday exercisers.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Ironman trial authors declared no competing interests; others not stated in abstracts.
factors.reproducibility: Independent groups in New Zealand, the US and South Africa reached similar results.
factors.formulation_dose: Salt capsules or tablets at doses typical of athlete use.

claims.claim: Endurance athletes need sodium supplements to prevent dangerously low blood sodium (hyponatraemia)
claims.popular_framing: Take salt during long races or you'll get hyponatraemia.
claims.question: Do salt tablets prevent hyponatraemia in endurance events?
claims.outcome: Blood sodium concentration and exercise-associated hyponatraemia
claims.population: Ironman triathletes and other endurance athletes.
claims.bottom_line: The evidence does not support this. In a large Ironman trial, sodium tablets did not change blood sodium, and a recent review says drinking too much fluid and a hormone released during exercise (vasopressin) are key causes of exercise-related hyponatraemia, with sweat salt loss playing a less important role.
claims.what_research_found: In 413 Ironman triathletes randomised to sodium tablets, placebo or nothing, blood sodium before and after the roughly 12-hour race did not differ between groups, even though the sodium group took about 3.6 g extra sodium. A 2026 review states that exercise-associated hyponatraemia has several causes, including excessive fluid intake and hormone (vasopressin) release during exercise, that sweat sodium loss appears to play a less important role, and that 'drinking when thirsty' should replace drinking ahead of thirst.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: One field trial is not enough to rule out benefit in every situation, such as ultra-long events in extreme heat. The abstract reports blood sodium levels; it does not give the number of hyponatraemia cases in each group.
claims.limitations: Single randomised trial with self-dosed tablets; the review is narrative, not a systematic review.
claims.formulation_and_dose: 620 mg salt tablets taken as desired, 1–4 per hour (about 15 tablets on average).

factors.study_quality: Large randomised field trial with placebo arm; narrative expert review.
factors.consistency: The trial and the review point in the same direction.
factors.effect_size: No difference in blood sodium.
factors.clinical_significance: Hyponatraemia can be life-threatening; the review emphasises avoiding overdrinking.
factors.sample_size: 413 athletes.
factors.population: Ironman finishers in Cape Town (2001).
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Trial authors and review authors declared no competing interests.
factors.reproducibility: Only one randomised trial in the sources we read.
factors.formulation_dose: Salt tablets.

claims.claim: Eating less sodium lowers blood pressure, and on average Americans already eat more than recommended
claims.popular_framing: Salt is an electrolyte, so more of it is healthy.
claims.question: Is extra sodium from electrolyte products good for me?
claims.outcome: Blood pressure
claims.population: Adults with and without high blood pressure.
claims.bottom_line: Cutting sodium lowers blood pressure in people with and without high blood pressure. Americans already average about 3,400 mg a day, above the recommended limit of 2,300 mg, so adding sodium through daily electrolyte products works against that for most people.
claims.what_research_found: A Cochrane meta-analysis of 34 trials (3,230 people) found that reducing salt by about 4.4 g a day for at least four weeks lowered blood pressure by about 4.2/2.1 mmHg on average: about 5.4/2.8 mmHg in people with high blood pressure and 2.4/1.0 mmHg in people with normal blood pressure. Larger reductions gave larger falls. FDA reports that Americans eat about 3,400 mg of sodium a day, while the Dietary Guidelines advise adults to stay under 2,300 mg, and links high-sodium diets to high blood pressure, a major cause of heart disease and stroke.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: These trials did not test electrolyte products specifically, and they measured blood pressure rather than heart attacks or strokes. People who lose a lot of sodium in sweat during long, hot exercise may have different needs.
claims.limitations: Results varied between trials (I² 68–75%), though age, ethnicity, blood-pressure status and size of salt reduction explained much of it.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Modest salt reduction (average 4.4 g salt, about 75 mmol sodium, per day) for at least four weeks.

factors.study_quality: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials.
factors.consistency: Blood pressure fell in both men and women, white and black people, and people with and without hypertension.
factors.effect_size: Moderate at population level (about 4 mmHg systolic); bigger with bigger reductions.
factors.clinical_significance: Authors describe the falls as important from a population viewpoint.
factors.sample_size: 34 trials, 3,230 participants.
factors.population: Adults with and without high blood pressure.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Not stated in the abstract.
factors.reproducibility: Consistent across subgroups; consistent with FDA and Dietary Guidelines advice.
factors.formulation_dose: Dietary salt reduction, not supplements.

research_doses.note: No potassium-dose trials were reviewed for this profile. The exercise trials cited tested sodium, not potassium: 620 mg salt tablets taken 1–4 per hour, 700 mg salt per hour, or 1,800 mg sodium over 2 hours. NIH ODS notes most potassium supplements contain no more than 99 mg per serving and add a mean of only 87 mg/day among users.

food_vs_supplement.comparison_note: A single serving of many fruits, vegetables, beans and dairy foods gives 300–750 mg of potassium, several times more than a typical potassium supplement serving (99 mg or less). NIH ODS reports average US intakes from food of about 3,016 mg/day for men and 2,320 mg/day for women, below the AIs. For sodium, FDA reports average US intake of about 3,400 mg/day, above the recommended limit of under 2,300 mg/day, so on average people are not short of sodium.
food_vs_supplement.food_advantages: Whole foods supply potassium in much larger amounts than supplements, along with fibre and other nutrients. Over 70% of dietary sodium comes from packaged and prepared foods (FDA), so food choices, not electrolyte products, drive most people's sodium intake.
food_vs_supplement.when_supplement_may_help: ACSM notes that during exercise, drinks with electrolytes and carbohydrate can help more than water under certain circumstances, and that sweat losses vary between people. Oral rehydration solutions retained more fluid than water in rested adults. NIH ODS notes people taking loop or thiazide diuretics, people with inflammatory bowel disease, and people using laxatives heavily can lose potassium; potassium supplementation in these situations should be guided by a clinician.

profiles.absorption: Sodium and potassium are both well absorbed, and the kidneys regulate blood levels by adjusting urine losses. In healthy people, NIH ODS states that high dietary potassium does not pose a health risk because the kidneys remove the excess. How much fluid a drink helps you keep depends on its electrolyte, carbohydrate and protein content: in rested adults, oral rehydration solution and milk led to less urine over 4 hours than water.
profiles.side_effects: Too much potassium (hyperkalaemia) can cause muscle weakness, palpitations and dangerous heart rhythms, mainly in people with kidney disease or on certain medicines; very large doses of supplements or salt substitutes can cause it even in healthy people (NIH ODS). Diets high in sodium are linked to high blood pressure (FDA). In one trial, sodium capsules during exercise increased thirst.
profiles.interactions: ACE inhibitors and ARBs (e.g. benazepril, losartan) and potassium-sparing diuretics (e.g. spironolactone, amiloride) reduce potassium loss and can cause hyperkalaemia with extra potassium. Loop and thiazide diuretics (e.g. furosemide) increase potassium loss (NIH ODS).
profiles.cautions: People with kidney disease, heart failure, type 1 diabetes, adrenal insufficiency or liver disease, or who take ACE inhibitors, ARBs or potassium-sparing diuretics, should talk to a clinician before using potassium-containing products or salt substitutes (NIH ODS). People with high blood pressure or advised to limit salt should check the sodium content of electrolyte products. During long endurance events, drinking far beyond thirst can cause dangerous hyponatraemia; a recent review advises drinking when thirsty.
profiles.upper_limit: No upper limit has been set for potassium (NIH ODS). For sodium, the Dietary Guidelines advise adults to keep intake below 2,300 mg/day, which is also the Daily Value on food labels (FDA); this is a recommended limit rather than a supplement-specific upper limit.
profiles.research_doses_summary: Doses used in research: in endurance trials, salt tablets of 620 mg (1–4 per hour) during an Ironman, 700 mg salt per hour during a 72 km time trial, and 1,800 mg sodium during 2 hours of exercise. In hydration studies, 1 litre of an oral rehydration solution, sports drink or electrolyte-tablet drink taken over 30 minutes at rest. These are research doses, not recommendations.

sources.title: A randomized trial to assess the potential of different beverages to affect hydration status: development of a beverage hydration index.
sources.authors: Maughan RJ, Watson P, Cordery PA, Walsh NP, Oliver SJ, Dolci A, Rodriguez-Sanchez N, Galloway SD.
sources.population: Euhydrated, fasted healthy men at rest.
sources.intervention: 1 L of still water or one of 13 common drinks (including ORS, milk, sports drink, cola, tea, coffee, lager, orange juice) over 30 minutes; urine collected for 4 hours.
sources.findings: Urine over 4 hours was lower than water (1,337 g) after ORS (1,038 g), full-fat milk (1,052 g) and skimmed milk (1,049 g), all P<0.001. Cola, diet cola, hot tea, iced tea, coffee, lager, orange juice, sparkling water and a sports drink did not differ from water. BHI at 2 h: ORS 1.54, full-fat milk 1.50, skimmed milk 1.58.
sources.limitations: Men only; rested and euhydrated; short-term measure.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract.
sources.cited_for: ORS retained more fluid than water; a sports drink did not differ from water.

sources.title: The Beverage Hydration Index: Influence of Electrolytes, Carbohydrate and Protein.
sources.authors: Millard-Stafford M, Snow TK, Jones ML, Suh H.
sources.population: Healthy young adults at rest.
sources.intervention: 1 L of deionised water, electrolytes only, carbohydrate-electrolytes, or dipeptide-electrolytes, in random order.
sources.findings: Electrolytes alone (in the range of sports drinks) did not consistently improve BHI versus water; carbohydrate-electrolyte (BHI 1.15 at 120 min) and dipeptide-electrolyte drinks increased fluid retention. Electrolytes made the largest contribution to hydration properties at rest.
sources.limitations: Small; rested participants; short-term.
sources.funding: Coca-Cola grant listed in the PubMed record; authors say the sponsor had no role in execution or interpretation; one author has consulted for The Coca-Cola Company.
sources.cited_for: Electrolytes alone did not consistently beat water for fluid retention at rest.

sources.title: Impact of Nuun Electrolyte Tablets on Fluid Balance in Active Men and Women.
sources.authors: Pence J, Bloomer RJ.
sources.population: Healthy, exercise-trained adults at rest, fasted and euhydrated.
sources.intervention: 1 L of water alone or water with electrolyte tablets at single or double strength, over 30 minutes, in random order.
sources.findings: Electrolyte tablets lowered urine output and improved fluid balance compared with water from 2 hours onward; body-weight loss was 0.38 kg (single dose) vs 0.57 kg (water). Results were similar at both strengths, suggesting extra electrolytes are not needed at rest.
sources.limitations: Small; one commercial product; rested state only.
sources.funding: Nuun & Company, Inc. (maker of the tablets tested) grant listed in the PubMed record; authors declared no conflicts and say the sponsor had no role in execution or interpretation.
sources.cited_for: Electrolyte tablets modestly improved short-term fluid retention at rest.

sources.title: Hydration Status over 24-H Is Not Affected by Ingested Beverage Composition.
sources.authors: Tucker MA, Ganio MS, Adams JD, Brown LA, Ridings CB, Burchfield JM, Robinson FB, McDermott JL, Schreiber BA, Moyen NE, Washington TA, Bermudez AC, Bennett MP, Buyckx ME.
sources.population: Healthy, free-living adult men over a sedentary 24 hours.
sources.intervention: Randomised repeated-measures: water only, water+cola, water+diet cola, or water+cola+diet cola+orange juice; total fluid about 35 ml/kg.
sources.findings: 24-hour hydration status (urine osmolality and volume, serum osmolality, total body water) did not differ between treatments; one small difference in urine specific gravity. Authors conclude beverages of varying composition are equally effective in hydrating the body.
sources.limitations: Men only; did not include an electrolyte drink.
sources.funding: Listed in PubMed as non-US government supported; details not in abstract.
sources.cited_for: Over 24 hours, everyday hydration did not depend on beverage type.

sources.title: The Hydrating Effects of Hypertonic, Isotonic and Hypotonic Sports Drinks and Waters on Central Hydration During Continuous Exercise: A Systematic Meta-Analysis and Perspective.
sources.authors: Rowlands DS, Kopetschny BH, Badenhorst CE.
sources.population: People performing continuous exercise.
sources.intervention: Hypertonic, isotonic and hypotonic carbohydrate-electrolyte drinks (sodium <50 mmol/L) vs water, over 0–180 minutes of exercise.
sources.findings: Plasma volume change: hypertonic −7.4%, isotonic −8.7%, hypotonic −6.3%, water −7.5%. Hypotonic drinks were very likely superior to isotonic and likely superior to hypertonic drinks and water. Metabolic rate, ingestion rate, carbohydrate and electrolyte concentration modified effects.
sources.limitations: Surrogate outcome (plasma volume); modelling assumptions.
sources.funding: Lead author previously received funding from Frucor Ltd and Lucozade-Ribena-Suntory to report on hypotonic drink effects.
sources.cited_for: Hypotonic carbohydrate-electrolyte drinks best maintained hydration during continuous exercise.

sources.title: American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Exercise and fluid replacement.
sources.authors: American College of Sports Medicine; Sawka MN, Burke LM, Eichner ER, Maughan RJ, Montain SJ, Stachenfeld NS.
sources.population: People performing physical activity.
sources.intervention: Guidance on fluid and electrolyte replacement before, during and after exercise.
sources.findings: Aim to prevent excessive dehydration (>2% body weight loss) and excessive electrolyte changes. Sweat rates and sweat electrolyte content vary considerably between people, so customised plans are recommended. Drinks containing electrolytes and carbohydrates can provide benefits over water alone under certain circumstances.
sources.limitations: Position statement from 2007; abstract only read.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract.
sources.cited_for: Electrolyte-carbohydrate drinks can help in some exercise circumstances; individual variation in sweat losses.

sources.title: Sodium supplementation is not required to maintain serum sodium concentrations during an Ironman triathlon.
sources.authors: Hew-Butler TD, Sharwood K, Collins M, Speedy D, Noakes T.
sources.population: Finishers of the 2001 Cape Town Ironman triathlon.
sources.intervention: Sodium tablets (620 mg table salt), placebo (596 mg starch), or no supplement; tablets taken ad libitum, suggested 1–4 per hour.
sources.findings: The sodium group took an extra 3.6 g sodium on average. No differences between groups in finishing time, serum sodium before and after the race, weight change, rectal temperature or blood pressure. Authors conclude ad libitum sodium supplementation was not necessary to preserve serum sodium over about 12 hours.
sources.limitations: Self-dosed tablets; not designed primarily for performance.
sources.funding: Competing interests: none declared.
sources.cited_for: Sodium supplements did not change blood sodium or finishing time in an Ironman; research doses.

sources.title: Sodium supplementation has no effect on endurance performance during a cycling time-trial in cool conditions: a randomised cross-over trial.
sources.authors: Cosgrove SD, Black KE.
sources.population: Well-trained cyclists (5 men, 4 women).
sources.intervention: 700 mg/h salt capsule or placebo during a 72 km road time trial in cool conditions (about 13.8°C), water ad libitum; double-blind crossover.
sources.findings: No effect on time-trial performance (171 vs 172 min; p=0.46) or on plasma sodium change. Plasma volume change differed and thirst increased with sodium.
sources.limitations: Very small; cool conditions only.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract.
sources.cited_for: Salt capsules did not improve endurance performance.

sources.title: Effects of oral sodium supplementation on indices of thermoregulation in trained, endurance athletes.
sources.authors: Earhart EL, Weiss EP, Rahman R, Kelly PV.
sources.population: Trained endurance athletes.
sources.intervention: 1,800 mg sodium or placebo during 2 hours of exercise at 60% heart rate reserve, then a time-to-exhaustion test; double-blind randomised-sequence crossover.
sources.findings: No differences in sweat rate, heat-stress ratings (moderate, 'warm/hot'), cardiovascular drift, skin temperature, effort ratings or time to exhaustion (6.88 vs 6.96 min). Authors advise athletes to interpret sodium recommendations with caution given possible adverse effects such as hypertension.
sources.limitations: Very small; moderate heat stress only; no DOI listed in the PubMed record.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract.
sources.cited_for: High-dose sodium did not improve thermoregulation or performance.

sources.title: Pathophysiology and treatment of exercise-associated hyponatremia.
sources.authors: Altieri B, Aini I, Cannavale G, Magnelli C, Mancini C, Zamponi V, Isidori AM, Colao A, Faggiano A, Peri A; NIKE group.
sources.population: Athletes in endurance and other sports.
sources.intervention: Narrative review.
sources.findings: Exercise-associated hyponatraemia occurs in endurance and shorter events; its causes are multifactorial, including excessive fluid intake and non-osmotic vasopressin release, with sweat sodium loss appearing to play a less important role. Symptoms range from nausea and headache to coma and death. Recommends 'drinking when thirsty' rather than drinking ahead of thirst.
sources.limitations: Narrative review, not a systematic review.
sources.funding: Authors declared no conflicts of interest.
sources.cited_for: Overdrinking and vasopressin release contribute more than sweat sodium loss to exercise-associated hyponatraemia; 'drink when thirsty'.

sources.title: Effect of longer term modest salt reduction on blood pressure: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials.
sources.authors: He FJ, Li J, Macgregor GA.
sources.population: Adults with and without hypertension.
sources.intervention: Modest salt reduction for at least four weeks (mean urinary sodium −75 mmol/24 h, about 4.4 g/day salt).
sources.findings: Blood pressure fell by 4.18 mmHg systolic (95% CI −5.18 to −3.18) and 2.06 mmHg diastolic. In hypertension: −5.39/−2.82 mmHg; normal blood pressure: −2.42/−1.00 mmHg. A 6 g/day salt reduction was associated with a 5.8 mmHg systolic fall. No significant change in lipids.
sources.limitations: High heterogeneity (I² 68–75%), partly explained by age, ethnicity, blood-pressure status and size of reduction.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract.
sources.cited_for: Reducing sodium lowers blood pressure in people with and without hypertension.

sources.title: Sodium in Your Diet
sources.authors: US Food and Drug Administration
sources.population: US general population.
sources.findings: Dietary Guidelines advise adults to keep sodium below 2,300 mg/day (also the Daily Value); Americans eat about 3,400 mg/day; over 70% of sodium comes from packaged and prepared foods; higher-sodium diets are linked to high blood pressure, a major cause of heart disease and stroke; children under 14 have lower limits.
sources.limitations: Consumer summary; content current as of 03/05/2024.
sources.funding: US federal government (FDA).
sources.cited_for: Sodium limit, average US intake, sources of sodium, health effects of excess.

sources.title: Potassium: Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
sources.authors: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements
sources.population: General population; groups at risk of low or high potassium.
sources.findings: AIs (3,400 mg men, 2,600 mg women); no UL set; food-content table; average US intakes below AIs; supplements usually ≤99 mg per serving; hyperkalaemia risks with kidney disease and certain drugs; interactions with ACE inhibitors, ARBs and diuretics; low potassium raises hypertension risk especially with high sodium.
sources.limitations: Summary document; last-updated date not recorded at time of reading.
sources.funding: US federal government (NIH).
sources.cited_for: Potassium food table, AI, no UL, intakes, supplement content, safety, interactions, cautions.

profiles.name: Fish oil (omega-3s)
profiles.summary: Fish oil reliably lowers triglycerides, but standard supplements make little or no difference to major heart events, strokes or deaths in most people, do not protect memory in older adults, and are linked to more atrial fibrillation, especially at higher doses.
profiles.description: Fish oil supplies the omega-3 fats EPA and DHA, which are also found in fatty fish such as salmon, mackerel, tuna, herring and sardines. A highly purified form of EPA (icosapent ethyl) has been tested at high doses in heart trials; those results do not apply to ordinary fish oil supplements.
profiles.biological_function: EPA and DHA are long-chain omega-3 fats. Taking more of them lowers blood triglycerides in a dose-dependent way. Experts have set a recommended intake only for ALA, the plant omega-3, not for EPA or DHA.

formulations.name: Fish oil capsules (EPA + DHA)
formulations.notes: Typically about 1 g/day in large prevention trials such as VITAL and ASCEND.

formulations.name: Icosapent ethyl (highly purified EPA)
formulations.notes: 4 g/day in REDUCE-IT, studied in high-risk patients on statins.

formulations.name: Omega-3 carboxylic acids (EPA + DHA)
formulations.notes: 4 g/day in STRENGTH, which found no cardiovascular benefit compared with corn oil.

claims.claim: Fish oil supplements prevent heart attacks, strokes and heart disease deaths in the general population
claims.popular_framing: Take fish oil every day to protect your heart.
claims.question: Do fish oil supplements prevent heart disease?
claims.outcome: Major cardiovascular events and deaths
claims.population: Adults at usual or moderately raised risk, including older adults and people with diabetes
claims.bottom_line: For most people, no meaningful benefit. Large trials and a Cochrane review found standard fish oil supplements made little or no difference to major cardiovascular events, strokes and deaths overall; a small reduction in coronary heart disease events is possible but uncertain.
claims.what_research_found: A 2020 Cochrane review of 86 trials (162,796 people) found high-certainty evidence that EPA/DHA had little or no effect on cardiovascular events or deaths from any cause. The VITAL trial (25,871 adults, 1 g/day for 5.3 years) and the ASCEND trial (15,480 people with diabetes, 1 g/day for 7.4 years) found no reduction in major cardiovascular events.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: A small benefit for coronary heart disease cannot be ruled out: Cochrane found a possible slight reduction (about 1 in 167 people helped, low certainty), and VITAL saw fewer heart attacks as a secondary result.
claims.limitations: Trials used different doses and populations. Secondary results like VITAL's heart-attack finding need confirmation.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Mostly 1 g/day fish oil capsules; Cochrane trials ranged from 0.5 g to more than 5 g/day for 1 to 7 years.

factors.study_quality: Large, randomized, placebo-controlled trials; Cochrane found 28 trials at low risk of bias.
factors.consistency: Consistent lack of effect on major cardiovascular events.
factors.effect_size: RR 0.96 for cardiovascular events (Cochrane); HR 0.92 in VITAL, not significant.
factors.clinical_significance: Any benefit for coronary events is small (NNTB 167, low certainty).
factors.sample_size: Over 140,000 people for cardiovascular events in the Cochrane review.
factors.population: General population, older adults and people with diabetes.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: VITAL was funded by the National Institutes of Health and others, and ASCEND by the British Heart Foundation and others; Cochrane authors declared no known conflicts.
factors.reproducibility: Multiple independent large trials agree.
factors.formulation_dose: Effects did not differ by dose or duration in the Cochrane review.

claims.claim: High-dose, highly purified EPA (icosapent ethyl) reduces cardiovascular events in high-risk patients with high triglycerides
claims.popular_framing: High-dose omega-3 is proven to cut heart attacks.
claims.question: Does high-dose purified omega-3 help people at high heart risk?
claims.outcome: Major cardiovascular events
claims.population: Statin-treated adults with heart disease or diabetes plus risk factors, and raised triglycerides
claims.bottom_line: One large trial funded by a pharmaceutical company found that 4 g/day of highly purified EPA (icosapent ethyl) cut events in high-risk patients; a similar trial of a high-dose EPA+DHA formulation did not. This does not apply to ordinary fish oil.
claims.what_research_found: In REDUCE-IT (8,179 statin-treated high-risk patients), 4 g/day of icosapent ethyl lowered the main cardiovascular outcome from 22.0% to 17.2% over about 5 years (HR 0.75). In STRENGTH (13,078 similar patients), 4 g/day of an EPA+DHA formulation (omega-3 carboxylic acids) did no better than corn oil (HR 0.99) and the trial stopped early.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It has not been shown that over-the-counter fish oil, or omega-3 in people without high risk, gives this benefit.
claims.limitations: The positive trial was funded by Amarin Pharma. The two trials tested different formulations, and the REDUCE-IT abstract does not describe what its placebo contained (STRENGTH used corn oil). Only abstracts were read.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Icosapent ethyl (highly purified EPA ethyl ester) 4 g/day; STRENGTH used 4 g/day omega-3 carboxylic acids (EPA + DHA).

factors.study_quality: Both were large, randomized, double-blind trials.
factors.consistency: Conflicting: REDUCE-IT positive, STRENGTH null.
factors.effect_size: 25% relative reduction in REDUCE-IT; none in STRENGTH.
factors.clinical_significance: About 5 percentage points fewer events over about 5 years in REDUCE-IT.
factors.sample_size: 8,179 and 13,078 patients.
factors.population: High-risk, statin-treated patients with raised triglycerides only.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: REDUCE-IT was funded by Amarin Pharma. In STRENGTH, several authors reported AstraZeneca funding during the study and two listed AstraZeneca affiliations.
factors.reproducibility: Not reproduced by the STRENGTH trial of a different omega-3 formulation (EPA + DHA).
factors.formulation_dose: Highly purified EPA at 4 g/day; not comparable to typical fish oil supplements.

claims.claim: Omega-3 (EPA and DHA) lowers blood triglycerides
claims.popular_framing: Fish oil lowers your blood fats.
claims.question: Does fish oil lower triglycerides?
claims.outcome: Blood triglyceride levels
claims.population: Adults, including people with high blood lipids
claims.bottom_line: Yes. EPA and DHA reliably lower triglycerides, and higher doses lower them more.
claims.what_research_found: A 2020 Cochrane review found EPA/DHA lowered triglycerides by about 15% in a dose-dependent way, with high-certainty evidence. A 2023 meta-analysis of 90 trials (72,598 people) found a near-linear dose response, clearest in people with high lipids or overweight taking more than 2 g/day. NIH ODS agrees that more EPA and DHA lowers triglycerides.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: Lower triglycerides have not been shown to mean fewer heart events for most people: the same Cochrane review found little or no effect on cardiovascular events overall.
claims.limitations: Exact size depends on dose and starting level. Only abstracts were read.
claims.formulation_and_dose: EPA, DHA or both; the dose response was clearest above 2 g/day in people with high lipids or overweight.

factors.study_quality: High-certainty evidence per Cochrane GRADE.
factors.consistency: Consistent across reviews.
factors.effect_size: About 15% reduction on average.
factors.clinical_significance: Meaningful lab change; outcome benefit not shown for typical users.
factors.sample_size: 90 trials and 72,598 people in one review.
factors.population: Broad; stronger in people with high lipids.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Cochrane authors declared no known conflicts; funding not stated for the 2023 review's abstract.
factors.reproducibility: Replicated across many trials and reviews.
factors.formulation_dose: Dose-dependent; clearest above 2 g/day in people with high lipids or overweight.

claims.claim: Fish oil improves depression and mood
claims.popular_framing: Omega-3s are a natural antidepressant.
claims.question: Does fish oil help depression?
claims.outcome: Depressive symptoms; new cases of depression
claims.population: Adults with major depression; older adults without depression
claims.bottom_line: Not established. In people with major depression, the average effect is small and probably not noticeable; in adults aged 50 and over, fish oil did not prevent depression.
claims.what_research_found: A 2021 Cochrane review of 34 placebo-controlled studies (1,924 people with major depression) found a small effect on symptoms, about 2.5 points on a scale where 3 points is the smallest meaningful change, with very low-certainty evidence. Remission and response rates did not differ. In VITAL-DEP (18,353 adults aged 50+), 1 g/day for 5.3 years slightly increased depression risk (HR 1.13) and did not change mood scores.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It is not shown that fish oil works as a treatment for depression or improves mood in healthy people.
claims.limitations: Depression trials were small, highly varied and possibly biased toward positive results.
