claims.formulation_and_dose: Various omega-3 doses in depression trials; 1 g/day (465 mg EPA + 375 mg DHA) in VITAL-DEP.

factors.study_quality: Very low certainty in the Cochrane review; VITAL-DEP was large and well run.
factors.consistency: Considerable heterogeneity among depression trials.
factors.effect_size: SMD -0.40, likely below clinical relevance.
factors.clinical_significance: Unlikely to be clinically meaningful (Cochrane).
factors.sample_size: 1,924 people in treatment trials; 18,353 in the prevention trial.
factors.population: Major depression vs older adults without depression.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Cochrane review authors declared no known conflicts. In VITAL-DEP, one author reported nonfinancial support from Pronova BioPharma/BASF; trial funding is not stated in the abstract.
factors.reproducibility: Treatment results inconsistent.
factors.formulation_dose: Doses and EPA:DHA ratios varied.

claims.claim: Fish oil supplements protect memory and prevent cognitive decline
claims.popular_framing: Omega-3s are brain food — take fish oil to stay sharp.
claims.question: Does fish oil protect your brain as you age?
claims.outcome: Cognitive function, cognitive impairment and dementia
claims.population: Mostly older adults without dementia
claims.bottom_line: No. Large reviews of randomized trials found little or no effect on memory, thinking or new cognitive problems in older adults.
claims.what_research_found: A 2020 meta-analysis of 38 trials (49,757 people) found little or no effect of long-chain omega-3 on new cognitive illness, new cognitive impairment or global cognition, with moderate-quality evidence and no difference by dose or duration. A 2012 Cochrane review of three high-quality trials in healthy people aged 60+ also found no benefit.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: These reviews mostly studied older adults; they do not answer whether omega-3 affects brain function in young adults. The 2012 review found no trial that measured dementia itself.
claims.limitations: Cognitive decline was small in both groups in some trials, which makes changes harder to detect.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Omega-3 capsules or enriched spreads for 6 months to several years.

factors.study_quality: Moderate-quality evidence; the 2012 trials were high quality.
factors.consistency: Consistent null results.
factors.effect_size: RR 0.98 to 0.99 for new cognitive problems.
factors.clinical_significance: No meaningful effect.
factors.sample_size: 38 trials and 49,757 participants in the 2020 review; about 33,000 for new cognitive illness or impairment.
factors.population: Mainly older adults.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: One 2012 author led an included trial.
factors.reproducibility: Two reviews by different author groups agree.
factors.formulation_dose: No difference by dose or duration.

claims.claim: Omega-3 supplements raise the risk of atrial fibrillation, especially at higher doses
claims.popular_framing: Fish oil is good for your heart rhythm.
claims.question: Can fish oil raise the risk of an irregular heartbeat?
claims.outcome: Atrial fibrillation (AF)
claims.population: Adults in large cardiovascular outcome trials, mean age about 65
claims.bottom_line: Yes, modestly. In large heart trials, omega-3 supplements were linked to more AF, with higher risk above 1 g/day.
claims.what_research_found: A 2021 meta-analysis of 7 trials (81,210 people) found a 25% higher AF risk (HR 1.25). Risk was higher in trials using more than 1 g/day (HR 1.49) than 1 g/day or less (HR 1.12). A second meta-analysis of 8 trials (83,112 people) found AF in 4.0% vs 3.3%, with no increase in stroke. In REDUCE-IT, 4 g/day icosapent ethyl led to more hospitalizations for AF or atrial flutter (3.1% vs 2.1%).
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: These trials enrolled mostly older or higher-risk adults; the risk in young healthy people is not known.
claims.limitations: In some trials, AF was recorded as an adverse event or a cause of hospitalization rather than a planned outcome. The two reviews probably include many of the same trials; trial lists were not in the abstracts.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Omega-3 supplements and high-dose purified omega-3 products, from 1 g/day or less to 4 g/day.

factors.study_quality: Pooled data from large randomized trials.
factors.consistency: Both reviews agree, with a clear dose pattern.
factors.effect_size: About 12% higher at ≤1 g/day and about 50% higher at >1 g/day.
factors.clinical_significance: Absolute rates were low (4.0% vs 3.3%).
factors.sample_size: Over 80,000 participants.
factors.population: Older or higher-risk adults.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Some trials were industry funded.
factors.reproducibility: Two meta-analyses by different groups, which probably share many trials.
factors.formulation_dose: Risk rose by about 11% per extra 1 g/day.

research_doses.note: About 1 g/day of fish oil in large prevention trials (VITAL, ASCEND); 4 g/day of highly purified EPA in REDUCE-IT and of omega-3 carboxylic acids in STRENGTH.

reference_intake.label: No recommended intake set for EPA or DHA (only for ALA: 1.6 g men, 1.1 g women)

food_vs_supplement.comparison_note: One 3 oz serving of farmed Atlantic salmon or herring provides roughly 1.7 to 1.8 g of EPA + DHA. That is about twice the 0.84 g of EPA + DHA (465 mg EPA + 375 mg DHA) in the 1 g/day fish oil used in VITAL (dose breakdown from the VITAL-DEP report). Fish amounts vary by species and are calculated from USDA per-100 g data.
food_vs_supplement.food_advantages: NIH ODS says eating fatty fish and other seafood as part of a healthy diet may help protect the heart. The supplement trial findings in this profile do not test eating fish.
food_vs_supplement.when_supplement_may_help: Omega-3 lowers triglycerides. As summarised by NIH ODS, the American Heart Association does not recommend omega-3 supplements for people without high cardiovascular risk. The high-dose purified products tested in heart trials were studied in high-risk patients already on statins; whether they suit any individual is a decision for a clinician.

profiles.absorption: Not covered by the sources verified for this draft.
profiles.side_effects: Usually mild: unpleasant taste, bad breath, heartburn, nausea, stomach discomfort, diarrhea, headache and smelly sweat (NIH ODS). In STRENGTH, gastrointestinal side effects occurred in 24.7% on 4 g/day vs 14.7% on corn oil. Higher doses are linked to more atrial fibrillation. In REDUCE-IT, serious bleeding was 2.7% vs 2.1% (not statistically significant); VITAL found no excess bleeding at 1 g/day.
profiles.interactions: High doses of omega-3s may cause bleeding problems when taken with warfarin or other anticoagulant medicines (NIH ODS).
profiles.cautions: People taking blood thinners, and people with or at risk of atrial fibrillation, should talk to a clinician first. The 4 g/day purified omega-3 products in heart trials were studied in high-risk patients, not the general public. Talk to a clinician before starting any supplement, especially if pregnant, breastfeeding, taking medication or managing a health condition.
profiles.upper_limit: No formal upper limit is listed in the sources verified; FDA recommends no more than 5 g/day of EPA and DHA combined from supplements (NIH ODS).
profiles.research_doses_summary: Doses used in research: about 1 g/day of fish oil (for example 465 mg EPA + 375 mg DHA) for 5 to 7 years in large prevention trials; 4 g/day of highly purified EPA or omega-3 carboxylic acids in high-risk patients; 0.5 g to more than 5 g/day across trials in the Cochrane review.

sources.title: Omega-3 fatty acids for the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease.
sources.authors: Abdelhamid AS, Brown TJ, Brainard JS, et al.
sources.population: Adults at varying cardiovascular risk, mainly in high-income countries
sources.intervention: Mostly long-chain omega-3 (EPA/DHA) capsules, 0.5 g to more than 5 g/day, for 12 to 88 months
sources.findings: Increasing EPA/DHA had little or no effect on all-cause mortality (RR 0.97; high certainty), cardiovascular events (RR 0.96; high certainty), cardiovascular mortality (RR 0.92; moderate certainty), stroke (RR 1.02) or arrhythmia (RR 0.99; low certainty). It may slightly reduce coronary heart disease deaths (RR 0.90; NNTB 334) and events (RR 0.91; NNTB 167), both low certainty. EPA/DHA reduced triglycerides by about 15% in a dose-dependent way (high certainty). Effects did not differ by dose or duration.
sources.limitations: Trials varied in population, dose and design.
sources.funding: Authors declare none known
sources.cited_for: fish-oil-heart-general (main evidence); fish-oil-triglycerides (about 15% reduction, high certainty).

sources.title: Marine n-3 Fatty Acids and Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer.
sources.authors: Manson JE, Cook NR, Lee IM, et al.; VITAL Research Group.
sources.population: US men 50+ and women 55+ (general population, usual risk)
sources.intervention: Marine omega-3 1 g/day vs placebo; median 5.3 years
sources.findings: Major cardiovascular events: HR 0.92 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.06), not significant. Invasive cancer: HR 1.03. Secondary analyses: total heart attack HR 0.72 (0.59 to 0.90); stroke HR 1.04; cardiovascular death HR 0.96. No excess bleeding or other serious adverse events.
sources.limitations: Heart-attack result was a secondary outcome.
sources.funding: Funded by the National Institutes of Health and others
sources.cited_for: fish-oil-heart-general: no reduction in major cardiovascular events in a general population; side_effects (no excess bleeding).

sources.title: Effects of n-3 Fatty Acid Supplements in Diabetes Mellitus.
sources.authors: ASCEND Study Collaborative Group; Bowman L, Mafham M, Wallendszus K, et al.
sources.population: Adults with diabetes but no known atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease
sources.intervention: 1 g/day omega-3 capsules vs olive oil placebo; mean 7.4 years
sources.findings: Serious vascular events: 8.9% vs 9.2% (rate ratio 0.97; 95% CI 0.87 to 1.08). Death from any cause: rate ratio 0.95 (0.86 to 1.05). No significant differences in nonfatal serious adverse events.
sources.limitations: Adherence 76%.
sources.funding: Funded by the British Heart Foundation and others
sources.cited_for: fish-oil-heart-general: no reduction in serious vascular events in people with diabetes.

sources.title: Cardiovascular Risk Reduction with Icosapent Ethyl for Hypertriglyceridemia.
sources.authors: Bhatt DL, Steg PG, Miller M, et al.; REDUCE-IT Investigators.
sources.population: Statin-treated patients with cardiovascular disease, or diabetes plus other risk factors, with triglycerides 135-499 mg/dL
sources.intervention: Icosapent ethyl (highly purified EPA ethyl ester) 4 g/day vs placebo; median 4.9 years
sources.findings: Primary end point: 17.2% vs 22.0% (HR 0.75; 95% CI 0.68 to 0.83). Cardiovascular death: 4.3% vs 5.2% (HR 0.80). More hospitalization for atrial fibrillation or flutter (3.1% vs 2.1%). Serious bleeding 2.7% vs 2.1% (P = 0.06).
sources.limitations: Single trial; industry funded; placebo composition not described in the abstract.
sources.funding: Funded by Amarin Pharma
sources.cited_for: fish-oil-prescription-epa: positive outcome trial; fish-oil-afib and side_effects: AF hospitalization and bleeding.

sources.title: Effect of High-Dose Omega-3 Fatty Acids vs Corn Oil on Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events in Patients at High Cardiovascular Risk: The STRENGTH Randomized Clinical Trial.
sources.authors: Nicholls SJ, Lincoff AM, Garcia M, et al.
sources.population: Statin-treated patients at high cardiovascular risk with high triglycerides and low HDL
sources.intervention: 4 g/day omega-3 carboxylic acids (EPA + DHA) vs corn oil
sources.findings: Stopped early for low probability of benefit. Primary end point 12.0% vs 12.2% (HR 0.99; 95% CI 0.90 to 1.09). Gastrointestinal adverse events 24.7% vs 14.7%.
sources.limitations: Stopped early.
sources.funding: Several authors report grants or fees from AstraZeneca during the study, and two list AstraZeneca affiliations; funding statement not in abstract
sources.cited_for: fish-oil-prescription-epa: high-dose EPA+DHA did not reduce events; side_effects (GI events).

sources.title: Association Between Omega-3 Fatty Acid Intake and Dyslipidemia: A Continuous Dose-Response Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
sources.authors: Wang T, Zhang X, Zhou N, et al.
sources.population: General population and subgroups with hyperlipidemia or overweight/obesity
sources.intervention: DHA, EPA or both, various doses
sources.findings: Omega-3 intake lowered triglycerides and non-HDL cholesterol in a roughly linear, dose-dependent way, more clearly in people with high lipids or overweight given more than 2 g/day.
sources.limitations: Exact effect sizes not in abstract.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: fish-oil-triglycerides: dose-response.

sources.title: Effect of Long-Term Marine ɷ-3 Fatty Acids Supplementation on the Risk of Atrial Fibrillation in Randomized Controlled Trials of Cardiovascular Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
sources.authors: Gencer B, Djousse L, Al-Ramady OT, et al.
sources.population: Adults in cardiovascular outcome trials; mean age 65; 39% women
sources.intervention: Marine omega-3 supplements; ≤1 g/day or >1 g/day; weighted mean follow-up 4.9 years
sources.findings: Omega-3 supplements were linked to higher AF risk (HR 1.25; 95% CI 1.07 to 1.46). Risk was greater in trials of >1 g/day (HR 1.49) than ≤1 g/day (HR 1.12). AF risk rose per extra 1 g/day (HR 1.11).
sources.limitations: Included trials reported AF as a prespecified outcome, an adverse event or a cause of hospitalization, so AF was not always a planned outcome.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: fish-oil-afib: AF risk and dose relationship.

sources.title: Association Between Omega-3 Fatty Acid Treatment and Atrial Fibrillation in Cardiovascular Outcome Trials: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
sources.authors: Jia X, Gao F, Pickett JK, et al.
sources.population: Adults in large cardiovascular outcome trials
sources.intervention: Omega-3 ≤1 g/day (5 trials) or >1 g/day (3 trials)
sources.findings: AF 4.0% vs 3.3% (RR 1.24; 95% CI 1.11 to 1.38). RR 1.12 at ≤1 g/day and 1.51 at >1 g/day. No increase in stroke (RR 1.04).
sources.limitations: Probably overlaps with trials in the Gencer review; trial lists not in abstract.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: fish-oil-afib: confirms dose-related AF risk; overall AF rates low.

sources.title: Omega-3 fatty acids for depression in adults.
sources.authors: Appleton KM, Voyias PD, Sallis HM, et al.
sources.population: Adults with major depressive disorder
sources.intervention: Omega-3 supplements vs placebo (34 studies) or vs antidepressant (1 study)
sources.findings: Small-to-modest benefit on depressive symptoms (SMD -0.40; 95% CI -0.64 to -0.16; very low certainty), about 2.5 points on the HDRS scale where 3 points is the minimal clinically important change, so unlikely to be clinically meaningful. No difference in remission or response rates. Estimate may be biased towards a positive finding.
sources.limitations: Very limited, heterogeneous and potentially biased evidence.
sources.funding: Authors declare none known (with editorial-role disclosures)
sources.cited_for: fish-oil-depression: treatment of major depression.

sources.title: Effect of Long-term Supplementation With Marine Omega-3 Fatty Acids vs Placebo on Risk of Depression or Clinically Relevant Depressive Symptoms and on Change in Mood Scores: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
sources.authors: Okereke OI, Vyas CM, Mischoulon D, et al.
sources.population: US adults 50+ without clinically relevant depressive symptoms at baseline (VITAL-DEP)
sources.intervention: 1 g/day fish oil (465 mg EPA + 375 mg DHA) vs placebo; median 5.3 years
sources.findings: Depression risk was slightly higher with omega-3 (HR 1.13; 95% CI 1.01 to 1.26). No difference in mood scores (PHQ-8 difference 0.03). Authors: findings do not support omega-3 to prevent depression.
sources.limitations: Older adults only.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract; one author reported nonfinancial support from Pronova BioPharma/BASF, another from Nordic Naturals outside the submitted work
sources.cited_for: fish-oil-depression: no prevention benefit in the general older population.

sources.title: Omega-3, Omega-6, and Polyunsaturated Fat for Cognition: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Trials.
sources.authors: Brainard JS, Jimoh OF, Deane KHO, et al.
sources.population: Adults, trials lasting at least 24 weeks
sources.intervention: Increased long-chain omega-3 vs lower intake
sources.findings: Little or no effect of long-chain omega-3 on new neurocognitive illness (RR 0.98), new cognitive impairment (RR 0.99) or MMSE (MD 0.10), all moderate-quality evidence. No differences by dose or duration. Authors: long-chain omega-3 supplements do not help older adults protect against cognitive decline.
sources.limitations: Mainly older adults.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: fish-oil-cognition: main evidence.

sources.title: Omega 3 fatty acid for the prevention of cognitive decline and dementia.
sources.authors: Sydenham E, Dangour AD, Lim WS.
sources.population: Cognitively healthy adults aged 60+
sources.intervention: Omega-3 capsules or enriched margarine for 6 to 40 months
sources.findings: No difference in MMSE score (MD -0.07) or other cognitive tests. No study examined dementia incidence. All three trials of high methodological quality. Main side effect was mild gastrointestinal problems.
sources.limitations: Few trials; dementia not studied.
sources.funding: One author was principal investigator of an included trial
sources.cited_for: fish-oil-cognition: no benefit in healthy older people; side_effects.

sources.title: Omega-3 Fatty Acids — Fact Sheet for Consumers
sources.authors: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements
sources.findings: Food sources include fatty fish (salmon, mackerel, tuna, herring, sardines), nuts and seeds, and plant oils. Recommended amounts are set only for ALA (Adequate Intake 1.6 g men, 1.1 g women). More EPA and DHA from food or supplements lowers triglycerides. The American Heart Association does not recommend omega-3 supplements for people without high cardiovascular risk. FDA recommends no more than 5 g/day of EPA and DHA combined from supplements. Side effects include unpleasant taste, bad breath, heartburn, nausea, stomach discomfort, diarrhea, headache and smelly sweat. High doses may cause bleeding problems with warfarin or other anticoagulants.
sources.limitations: Consumer summary; the Health Professional fact sheet could not be loaded in this session.
sources.funding: Government agency
sources.cited_for: fish-oil-triglycerides; upper_limit; side_effects; interactions; reference intake; food_advantages (seafood and heart, AHA seafood advice).

sources.title: USDA FoodData Central, SR Legacy: EPA (20:5 n-3) and DHA (22:6 n-3) in cooked fish
sources.authors: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Agricultural Research Service
sources.findings: Per 100 g, EPA / DHA (g): salmon, Atlantic, farmed, cooked, dry heat (FDC 175168) 0.69 / 1.46; salmon, Atlantic, wild, cooked (171998) 0.411 / 1.43; salmon, chinook, cooked (171999) 1.01 / 0.727; salmon, sockeye, cooked (173692) 0.299 / 0.56; herring, Atlantic, cooked (175117) 0.909 / 1.1; shrimp, cooked (175180) 0.015 / 0.015. Per-serving values in this profile are calculated for 85 g (3 oz).
sources.limitations: Per-serving amounts are calculated from per-100 g values; the ODS food table could not be loaded in this session.
sources.funding: Government agency
sources.cited_for: food_vs_supplement food amounts.

profiles.name: Glutathione
profiles.summary: Daily oral glutathione may raise blood levels over months, but skin lightening and detox claims are not established, and injectable glutathione carries real safety concerns.
profiles.description: Glutathione is a small molecule made of three amino acids that the body makes itself. It is sold as capsules, liposomal liquids, films and, in clinics, as injections, mainly for skin lightening and detox.
profiles.biological_function: Glutathione is one of the body's main antioxidants and is involved in protecting cells from oxidative stress. Your body makes it, and one study concluded that glutathione in the diet is not a major factor in blood levels. Whether swallowing it adds to the body's supply has been debated, because enzymes in the gut and liver break it down.

formulations.name: Reduced glutathione (L-glutathione)
formulations.notes: The standard form in most trials. A single 3 g dose did not raise blood levels; 6 months of daily use did in one trial.

formulations.name: Liposomal glutathione
formulations.notes: One small, open-label, company-authored study found higher peak blood levels than plain glutathione after one dose.

formulations.name: Orally dissolving film
formulations.notes: Gave higher blood levels than a tablet at 4 and 6 hours in one study.

formulations.name: S-acetyl glutathione
formulations.notes: In one 12-week trial, lowered a skin pigment measure faster than reduced glutathione, but blood glutathione did not differ between groups.

formulations.name: Intravenous glutathione
formulations.notes: Used in clinics for skin lightening without trial evidence of safety for long-term use. FDA has warned about supplement-grade ingredients in injectables.

claims.claim: Taking glutathione by mouth raises glutathione levels in the body
claims.popular_framing: Take glutathione daily to boost your body's master antioxidant.
claims.question: Does oral glutathione actually raise your glutathione levels?
claims.outcome: Glutathione levels in blood and cells
claims.population: Healthy adults
claims.bottom_line: Possibly, with daily use over months. A 6-month placebo-controlled trial found higher levels; a single dose and a 4-week placebo-controlled trial did not.
claims.what_research_found: In a 6-month randomized trial of 54 adults, 250 or 1,000 mg/day raised glutathione in blood and cells, by 30-35% in several blood compartments at the high dose. Levels returned to baseline a month after stopping. A single dose of about 3 g in 7 people did not raise blood levels, and 1,000 mg/day for 4 weeks in 40 adults did not change red-cell glutathione. A 4-week study without a placebo group reported that 100 mg/day of glutathione as a film or tablet increased circulating glutathione.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It has not been shown that higher blood glutathione from supplements leads to any health benefit.
claims.limitations: All studies are small. Results differ by duration and measurement method. Only abstracts were read.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Reduced glutathione 250 to 1,000 mg/day for 4 weeks to 6 months; one single dose of about 3 g; 100 mg/day film or tablet for 4 weeks in a study without placebo.

factors.study_quality: Two randomized, placebo-controlled trials, one small uncontrolled single-dose absorption study, and one 4-week film-vs-tablet study without a placebo group.
factors.consistency: Inconsistent: the 6-month trial was positive; the 4-week placebo-controlled trial and single-dose study were negative; a 4-week study without placebo reported increases.
factors.effect_size: 30-35% increases in blood compartments at 1,000 mg/day after 6 months.
factors.clinical_significance: Unknown; only biomarkers were measured.
factors.sample_size: 7 to 54 people per study (size not stated in the abstract of the film study).
factors.population: Healthy adults only.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Not stated in the abstracts read.
factors.reproducibility: The positive 6-month result has not been replicated in the sources verified here.
factors.formulation_dose: Results may depend on duration; standard reduced glutathione was used.

claims.claim: Liposomal or other special forms of glutathione are absorbed much better than regular glutathione
claims.popular_framing: Only liposomal glutathione actually works.
claims.question: Is liposomal or film glutathione better absorbed?
claims.outcome: Blood glutathione after a dose
claims.population: Healthy adults
claims.bottom_line: Unproven. Small company-linked or open-label studies suggest higher blood levels with some forms, but no health benefit has been shown.
claims.what_research_found: In an open-label study of 12 people, a branded liposomal product gave a peak blood level about 6 times higher than plain glutathione; all authors worked at a company. An orally dissolving film gave higher blood levels than a tablet at 4 and 6 hours. In a 12-week trial, S-acetyl glutathione lowered a skin pigment measure faster, but blood glutathione did not differ between groups.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: No verified trial shows that any special form leads to better health or skin outcomes.
claims.limitations: Small or short studies; the liposomal and film single-dose studies were open-label.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Liposomal glutathione 1 g single dose; film or tablet 300 mg single dose and 100 mg/day for 4 weeks; S-acetyl glutathione 200 mg/day for 12 weeks.

factors.study_quality: Open-label single-dose studies, plus one 12-week double-blind trial.
factors.consistency: Absorption results point the same way, but a 12-week trial found no difference in glutathione levels.
factors.effect_size: Up to 6-fold peak difference in one 12-person study.
factors.clinical_significance: Not shown.
factors.sample_size: 6 per group in the liposomal study.
factors.population: Healthy adults.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Liposomal study authors were all from one company. In the film study, two authors listed company affiliations, though authors declared no competing interests.
factors.reproducibility: Not independently replicated in the sources verified.
factors.formulation_dose: Each study tested a different form; results do not transfer between products.

claims.claim: Glutathione pills lighten skin
claims.popular_framing: Glutathione capsules for brighter, lighter skin.
claims.question: Does oral glutathione lighten skin?
claims.outcome: Melanin index and skin tone
claims.population: Healthy adults, mostly in Asia
claims.bottom_line: Not established. Small trials give mixed results, and a systematic review called the evidence inconclusive.
claims.what_research_found: In 60 medical students in Thailand, 500 mg/day for 4 weeks lowered the melanin index more than placebo at 2 of 6 skin sites. A 12-week trial of a glutathione combination product in 83 adults found no significant difference from placebo. A 2019 systematic review of four studies concluded the whitening evidence is inconclusive, with a possible trend in sun-exposed skin.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: No large or long-term trial shows that oral glutathione lightens skin or that long-term use is safe.
claims.limitations: Few, small, short trials with different products and measurement tools.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Oral glutathione 250 to 500 mg/day for 4 to 12 weeks; some products combined it with vitamin C, alpha-lipoic acid and zinc.

factors.study_quality: Some randomized placebo-controlled trials, but small; the review cited quality concerns.
factors.consistency: Inconsistent across trials and skin sites.
factors.effect_size: Small; significant at only some skin sites.
factors.clinical_significance: Uncertain whether changes are visible.
factors.sample_size: 60 to 90 people per trial.
factors.population: Trials in Thailand and Indonesia and in people with darker skin types (Fitzpatrick IV and V); one trial in medical students.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Not stated or none declared in abstracts read.
factors.reproducibility: Positive finding not consistently reproduced.
factors.formulation_dose: Products differ (single ingredient vs combinations).

claims.claim: Glutathione injections or IV drips safely lighten skin
claims.popular_framing: Glutathione drips for glowing, whiter skin.
claims.question: Are glutathione injections a safe way to lighten skin?
claims.outcome: Skin lightening and safety of intravenous use
claims.population: People using IV glutathione cosmetically
claims.bottom_line: No good evidence that IV glutathione works for skin lightening, and there are real safety concerns, including adverse events reported by FDA, some needing hospital care.
claims.what_research_found: A 2016 review found no studies of IV glutathione for skin lightening and no data on its long-term safety. A 2026 review found only limited, modest and varied pigment changes from small studies, often mixed with vitamin C. In August 2026, FDA reported at least 30 patients with adverse events after IV glutathione, including signs of shock and sepsis-like symptoms. FDA said dietary-supplement-grade glutathione is not an appropriate ingredient for injectable drugs, and two pharmacies recalled glutathione injectables over high endotoxin levels.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: No adequately sized, long-term trial has shown IV glutathione to be effective or safe for cosmetic use.
claims.limitations: Evidence on benefit is sparse. Safety concerns come from reviews and FDA reports, not from large trials.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Intravenous glutathione, often given with vitamin C; doses not standardized in the sources read.

factors.study_quality: Small studies with short follow-up.
factors.consistency: Varied results.
factors.effect_size: Described as modest at best.
factors.clinical_significance: Unclear benefit; potential serious harms.
factors.sample_size: Small.
factors.population: Cosmetic users.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Not stated.
factors.reproducibility: Not established.
factors.formulation_dose: Co-use of vitamin C makes glutathione's own effect hard to judge.

claims.claim: Glutathione supplements detox your body
claims.popular_framing: Glutathione is the master detoxifier — take it to flush out toxins.
claims.question: Do glutathione supplements detox your body?
claims.outcome: Detoxification or oxidative stress in healthy people
claims.population: Healthy adults
claims.bottom_line: No evidence. We found no human trial that measured detox outcomes, and trials of oxidative stress markers were mostly negative.
claims.what_research_found: Glutathione is part of the body's own antioxidant and detox systems, but that does not mean extra glutathione from pills does more. In healthy adults, 1,000 mg/day for 4 weeks did not change oxidative stress markers, and a 4-week film or tablet study also found no change in oxidative stress markers. A 6-month trial found a lower ratio of oxidized to reduced glutathione in blood.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: No verified human study shows that glutathione supplements remove toxins or improve liver detox in healthy people.
claims.limitations: Few small trials measured only lab markers.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Oral glutathione 100 to 1,000 mg/day for 4 weeks to 6 months.

factors.study_quality: Small trials of surrogate markers only.
factors.consistency: Mostly no change in oxidative stress markers.
factors.effect_size: None shown for detox outcomes.
factors.clinical_significance: Not shown.
factors.sample_size: Small.
factors.population: Healthy adults.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Not stated in the abstracts read.
factors.reproducibility: Not applicable; no detox outcome studied.
factors.formulation_dose: Standard oral forms.

profiles.absorption: Absorption is debated. A 1992 study found a single 3 g dose did not raise blood glutathione, likely because gut and liver enzymes break it down. A 6-month placebo-controlled trial found daily doses raised levels, while a 4-week placebo-controlled trial did not; a 4-week study without placebo reported increases with 100 mg/day film or tablet. Small studies suggest film and liposomal forms may give higher short-term blood levels.
profiles.side_effects: In small oral trials, glutathione was well tolerated; mild, temporary side effects were reported in a combination-product trial, and a review noted some non-serious adverse events. A 4-week film and tablet study reported no adverse events. Long-term safety of oral use has not been established. For intravenous use, FDA has reported adverse events including fever, chills, dizziness, signs of shock and sepsis-like symptoms, and has said dietary-supplement-grade glutathione is not an appropriate ingredient for injectable drugs.
profiles.interactions: No interaction data were found in the sources verified for this draft.
profiles.cautions: Injectable or IV glutathione for skin lightening has no long-term safety data, and FDA reported at least 30 people with adverse events in 2026, some needing hospital care. Talk to a clinician before starting any supplement, especially if pregnant, breastfeeding, taking medication or managing a health condition.
profiles.upper_limit: No upper limit was found in the sources verified for this draft.
profiles.research_doses_summary: Doses used in research: oral reduced glutathione 250 to 1,000 mg/day for 4 weeks to 6 months; 500 mg/day for skin trials of 4 to 12 weeks; S-acetyl glutathione 200 mg/day; 100 mg/day film or tablet for 4 weeks.

sources.title: Randomized controlled trial of oral glutathione supplementation on body stores of glutathione.
sources.authors: Richie JP Jr, Nichenametla S, Neidig W, et al.
sources.population: Healthy non-smoking adults
sources.intervention: Oral glutathione 250 or 1,000 mg/day vs placebo for 6 months
sources.findings: Blood glutathione rose at 1, 3 and 6 months at both doses. At 6 months the high dose raised levels 30-35% in red cells, plasma and lymphocytes and 260% in cheek cells; the low dose raised blood and red-cell levels 17% and 29%. Increases were mostly dose- and time-dependent and returned to baseline after a 1-month washout. The oxidized-to-reduced glutathione ratio fell in both dose groups.
sources.limitations: Small trial; biomarker outcomes, not health outcomes.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: glutathione-oral-levels: 6-month RCT showing raised body stores; glutathione-detox: oxidized/reduced ratio.

sources.title: Effects of oral glutathione supplementation on systemic oxidative stress biomarkers in human volunteers.
sources.authors: Allen J, Bradley RD.
sources.population: Healthy adults
sources.intervention: Oral glutathione 500 mg twice daily vs placebo for 4 weeks
sources.findings: No significant changes in oxidative stress markers (urinary F2-isoprostanes, 8-OHdG) or in red-cell glutathione status compared with placebo.
sources.limitations: Short (4 weeks) and small.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: glutathione-oral-levels and glutathione-detox: null 4-week trial.

sources.title: The systemic availability of oral glutathione.
sources.authors: Witschi A, Reddy S, Stofer B, et al.
sources.population: Healthy volunteers
sources.intervention: Single oral dose of glutathione, 0.15 mmol/kg (about 3 g)
sources.findings: Plasma glutathione, cysteine and glutamate did not rise significantly over 270 minutes. Authors concluded systemic availability of a single oral dose is negligible because glutathione is broken down by enzymes in the gut and liver.
sources.limitations: Very small, single-dose study.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: glutathione-oral-levels: single dose did not raise blood glutathione; absorption.

sources.title: Formulation-dependent differences in systemic glutathione availability: Comparative pharmacokinetics of orally dissolving film and tablet formulations in healthy adults.
sources.authors: Jung ES, Jang HY, Jung SJ, et al.
sources.population: Healthy adults
sources.intervention: Single 300 mg dose crossover (film vs tablet); then 100 mg/day film or tablet for 4 weeks
sources.findings: Plasma glutathione was higher with the orally dissolving film at 4 and 6 hours. Over 4 weeks both forms increased circulating glutathione, with no significant changes in oxidative stress markers. No adverse events were reported.
sources.limitations: Single-dose part was open-label; no placebo group described in the abstract; sample size not stated in abstract.
sources.funding: Authors declare no competing interests; two authors list company affiliations (Bio360 Co., Ltd.; ESTHER FORMULA USA Corp.); funding not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: glutathione-formulations; glutathione-oral-levels (4-week increase without placebo); glutathione-detox (no change in oxidative stress markers); side_effects.

sources.title: Liposomal glutathione outperforms plain glutathione in uptake, cell regeneration and systemic availability: evidence from cellular and human models.
sources.authors: Prasad KN, Chandrashekar C, Karthik Y, et al.
sources.sample_size: 12 healthy people (6 per group) in the human part
sources.population: Healthy subjects (age not stated in abstract)
sources.intervention: Single 1 g oral dose of a branded liposomal glutathione (LipoDuo) vs plain glutathione; open-label
sources.findings: The liposomal product reached a peak plasma level of about 1,800 ng/mL, about 6 times higher than plain glutathione, and stayed above 500 ng/mL at 24 hours.
sources.limitations: Very small, open-label, single dose; tests one branded product.
sources.funding: All authors affiliated with Samarth Biorigins LLP (a company); funding not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: glutathione-formulations: liposomal absorption claim and its limits; glutathione-detox: background statement that glutathione is involved in redox balance and detoxification.

sources.title: The clinical effect of glutathione on skin color and other related skin conditions: A systematic review.
sources.authors: Dilokthornsakul W, Dhippayom T, Dilokthornsakul P.
sources.population: Healthy volunteers
sources.intervention: Oral glutathione 250-500 mg/day, or topical 2% oxidized glutathione
sources.findings: Oral glutathione 500 mg/day and topical 2% oxidized glutathione could brighten skin in sun-exposed areas by melanin index; no difference in sun-protected areas. Authors concluded the evidence for skin whitening is inconclusive because of study quality and inconsistent findings. Some non-serious adverse events were reported.
sources.limitations: Only four small studies.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: glutathione-skin-oral: overall evidence inconclusive; also notes limited oral absorption as a concern.

sources.title: Glutathione as an oral whitening agent: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study.
sources.authors: Arjinpathana N, Asawanonda P.
sources.population: Healthy medical students in Thailand
sources.intervention: Oral glutathione 500 mg/day for 4 weeks vs placebo
sources.findings: Melanin index fell at all six sites with glutathione, but the difference from placebo was significant at only two sites (right face and sun-exposed left forearm). Both glutathione and placebo were well tolerated. Long-term safety not established.
sources.limitations: Small and short.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: glutathione-skin-oral: small positive trial; side_effects.

sources.title: Evaluating Oral Glutathione Plus Ascorbic Acid, Alpha-lipoic Acid, and Zinc Aspartate as a Skin-lightening Agent: An Indonesian Multicenter, Randomized, Controlled Trial.
sources.authors: Sitohang IBS, Anwar AI, Jusuf NK, et al.
sources.population: Adults aged 33 to 50 in Indonesia
sources.intervention: Combination supplement (glutathione, vitamin C, alpha-lipoic acid, zinc) vs placebo for 12 weeks
sources.findings: Reductions in spots and skin tone were greater with the supplement but not statistically significant. Only mild side effects were reported in both groups in the first four weeks.
sources.limitations: Combination product, so glutathione's own effect cannot be separated.
sources.funding: Authors report no conflicts of interest relevant to the article
sources.cited_for: glutathione-skin-oral: null 12-week trial; side_effects.

sources.title: Skin Lightening and Evenness Effects of Oral Supplementation With S-Acetyl Glutathione in Comparison With Reduced Glutathione: A Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Clinical Trial.
sources.authors: Kusumawardani A, Norawati L, Veronica S, et al.
sources.population: Participants with Fitzpatrick skin types IV and V
sources.intervention: S-acetyl glutathione 200 mg/day vs reduced glutathione 500 mg/day vs placebo for 12 weeks
sources.findings: S-acetyl glutathione reduced the melanin index faster than reduced glutathione or placebo. However, no group showed significant pigmentation reduction on the facial skin analyzer, and glutathione levels did not differ significantly between groups.
sources.limitations: Mixed outcomes; the abstract reports few numbers.
sources.funding: Authors declare no conflicts of interest; funding not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: glutathione-skin-oral and glutathione-formulations: mixed results; no difference in glutathione levels.

sources.title: Intravenous glutathione for skin lightening: Inadequate safety data.
sources.authors: Davids LM, Van Wyk JC, Khumalo NP.
sources.population: Literature review (MEDLINE to September 2015)
sources.intervention: Review of glutathione for skin lightening and its safety across medical uses
sources.findings: Found no studies of intravenous glutathione for skin lightening, and no studies of its safety for long-term use for any indication. Most trials reviewed reported no or minimal adverse effects, but treatment lasted only a few doses (IV) or 4 to 12 weeks. Authors raised a concern that shifting melanin type could increase sun-induced skin cancer risk, and called for regulatory assessment.
sources.limitations: Review; skin-cancer concern is the authors' hypothesis, not a measured outcome.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: glutathione-skin-iv: absence of efficacy and long-term safety data.

sources.title: Glutathione for skin lightening via intravenous, oral, and topical routes: a critical narrative review of current evidence, safety, and the evidence-practice gap.
sources.authors: Aloraini K, Alangari A, Arif J, et al.
sources.population: Mechanistic, preclinical and clinical studies to March 2026
sources.intervention: Intravenous, oral and topical glutathione
sources.findings: Evidence shows limited, modest and varied pigmentation improvements, with small samples, non-standard outcomes and short follow-up. Common co-use of vitamin C makes the effect of IV glutathione alone hard to judge. Safety concerns for IV use include liver toxicity, hypersensitivity reactions and possible kidney and hormonal effects. Authors conclude evidence is too limited to justify routine cosmetic use.
sources.limitations: Narrative review.
sources.funding: Authors declare no conflicts of interest
sources.cited_for: glutathione-skin-iv: limited efficacy evidence and safety concerns.

sources.title: FDA reminds compounders not to use dietary supplement grade glutathione for injectables
sources.authors: U.S. Food and Drug Administration
sources.sample_size: At least 30 patients with reported adverse events
sources.population: Patients receiving compounded IV glutathione
sources.intervention: Intravenous glutathione made from dietary-supplement-grade ingredient
sources.findings: Dated 27 August 2026. FDA reported at least 30 patients with adverse events after IV glutathione, including fever, chills, pain, dizziness, signs of shock and sepsis-like symptoms, some needing hospital care. Two pharmacies recalled glutathione injectables over high endotoxin levels. FDA said dietary-supplement-grade glutathione is not an appropriate ingredient for injectable drugs, and that it had raised the same concern in 2019.
sources.limitations: Concerns contamination and ingredient quality, not glutathione's effectiveness.
sources.funding: Government agency
sources.cited_for: glutathione-skin-iv and cautions: safety risks of injectable glutathione.

profiles.name: Iron
profiles.summary: Iron supplements reliably fix low iron and anaemia in people who are iron deficient, and may ease tiredness in people with low iron stores, but there is no good evidence they boost energy when your iron is already normal.
profiles.description: Iron is an essential mineral found in foods such as meat, seafood, beans and fortified cereals. Supplements usually contain iron salts such as ferrous sulfate, gluconate or fumarate. Iron is also in many multivitamins and prenatal vitamins.
profiles.biological_function: Iron is a core part of haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen around the body. When iron runs low, the body makes less haemoglobin, which can lead to iron-deficiency anaemia. According to NIH ODS, anaemia can affect thinking, immune function, exercise and work performance, and body temperature control.

formulations.name: Ferrous salts (sulfate, gluconate, fumarate)
formulations.notes: The most common forms. Ferrous iron is absorbed better than ferric iron because it is more soluble. They contain different amounts of actual (elemental) iron by weight: about 33% for ferrous fumarate, 20% for ferrous sulfate and 12% for ferrous gluconate (NIH ODS).

formulations.name: Ferric salts (ferric citrate, ferric sulfate)
formulations.notes: Also sold, but ferric iron is less soluble and less bioavailable than ferrous iron (NIH ODS).

formulations.name: Heme iron polypeptide, carbonyl iron, iron amino-acid chelates (e.g. bisglycinate), polysaccharide-iron complexes
formulations.notes: NIH ODS notes these may cause fewer stomach and gut side effects than iron salts. The trials cited in this profile mostly used ferrous sulfate.

claims.claim: Iron supplements correct anaemia and low iron stores in iron-deficient women
claims.popular_framing: Low iron? An iron supplement will fix your anaemia.
claims.question: Do iron supplements fix iron-deficiency anaemia?
claims.outcome: Anaemia, haemoglobin and iron stores
claims.population: Menstruating women (or women aged 12–50). The review's inclusion criteria did not require anaemia or iron deficiency at the start.
claims.bottom_line: Yes, in women who menstruate. Daily iron supplements lower the chance of being anaemic and raise haemoglobin and iron stores. The trade-off is more stomach and gut side effects.
claims.what_research_found: A Cochrane review of 67 trials with 8,506 women found that women given daily iron were much less likely to be anaemic at the end of the study (risk ratio 0.39, moderate-quality evidence) and had higher haemoglobin (51 studies, 6,861 women, high-quality evidence). Iron also reduced the risk of iron deficiency. Iron increased constipation and diarrhoea compared with control.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: The review could not establish whether iron improves thinking or memory, because results conflicted. No included study reported effects on death. These findings come from menstruating women and do not automatically apply to men, children or pregnant women.
claims.limitations: Only 10 of the 67 trials were at low overall risk of bias, and many trials gave too little detail about their quality. Doses and products varied between trials.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Daily oral iron (sometimes with folic acid or vitamin C) given at least five days a week, at any dose. The abstract does not give a single typical dose.

factors.study_quality: Most trials reported quality poorly; only 10 were rated low risk of bias. Haemoglobin evidence was still rated high quality.
factors.consistency: Anaemia, haemoglobin and iron-deficiency outcomes all pointed the same way.
factors.effect_size: Large: the risk of anaemia at the end of treatment was cut by about 60% (RR 0.39).
factors.clinical_significance: Correcting anaemia is clinically meaningful. NIH ODS lists effects of anaemia on cognition, immunity and work capacity.
factors.sample_size: Large: 67 trials and 8,506 women, with 6,861 analysed for haemoglobin.
factors.population: Menstruating women, a group NIH ODS lists as at higher risk of iron deficiency.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Independent Cochrane review. Authors declared no role for funders; some authors work for blood services or a micronutrient non-profit, which they disclosed.
factors.reproducibility: Many independent trials across different settings.
factors.formulation_dose: Oral iron of various forms and doses; findings are about iron supplementation in general rather than one product.

claims.claim: Iron supplements reduce tiredness in adults who have low iron stores but are not anaemic
claims.popular_framing: Always tired? Your iron might be low even if your blood count is normal — iron can help.
claims.question: Does iron help fatigue if my iron stores are low but I'm not anaemic?
claims.outcome: Self-reported fatigue
claims.population: Adults with low iron stores (low ferritin) and normal haemoglobin. The two individual trials read were in women aged 18–55.
claims.bottom_line: Possibly. In people with low iron stores but no anaemia, iron reduced self-reported tiredness in several trials. The effect was modest and based on only a few trials.
claims.what_research_found: A systematic review of non-anaemic, iron-deficient adults found iron was linked to less self-reported fatigue (4 trials, 714 participants; a small-to-moderate effect). In a French trial of 198 tired women with ferritin below 50 µg/L, fatigue scores fell 47.7% with 80 mg iron a day versus 28.8% with placebo over 12 weeks. A Swiss trial of 144 women also found less fatigue after four weeks of iron than placebo.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: Iron did not improve quality of life, depression or anxiety in the French trial. It is not established that iron helps tiredness that has another cause.
claims.limitations: Fatigue is self-reported and prone to placebo effects (fatigue also fell by about 29% on placebo). The French trial was observer-blinded but described as closed-label. Few trials contributed to the fatigue estimate.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Oral ferrous sulfate, 80 mg elemental iron daily, for 4 to 12 weeks in the individual trials. The review also included intramuscular and intravenous iron.

factors.study_quality: Randomised, placebo-controlled trials; the Swiss trial was double-blind. Risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane tool in the review.
factors.consistency: The fatigue trials pooled in the review agreed (I² 0%).
factors.effect_size: Small to moderate (standardised mean difference −0.38).
factors.clinical_significance: Likely noticeable for some people, but placebo groups also improved substantially.
factors.sample_size: Moderate: 714 participants for the pooled fatigue outcome.
factors.population: Mostly menstruating women with low ferritin; results may not apply to men or to people with normal iron stores.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: The review authors declared no competing interests. Funding was not stated in the trial abstracts we read.
factors.reproducibility: Independent trials in France and Switzerland, plus a pooled review, point the same way.
factors.formulation_dose: Mainly ferrous sulfate at 80 mg elemental iron daily, which is above the 45 mg/day adult upper limit; it was given in clinical trials with medical follow-up.

claims.claim: Iron supplements boost energy in people whose iron levels are already normal
claims.popular_framing: Take iron for more energy.
claims.question: Will iron give me more energy if my iron is normal?
claims.outcome: Energy and fatigue
claims.population: Adults with normal iron stores.
claims.bottom_line: There is no good evidence for this. In the trials we reviewed, the fatigue benefit appeared only in women with low or borderline iron stores.
claims.what_research_found: In a double-blind trial of 144 non-anaemic women with unexplained fatigue, a subgroup analysis found that only women with ferritin of 50 µg/L or lower improved with iron. The fatigue review covered only people who were iron deficient.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: We found no trial showing that iron improves energy in people with normal iron stores. This is a gap in evidence, not proof of no effect, because trials have focused on people with low iron.
claims.limitations: The key evidence is a subgroup analysis from one trial, which is weaker than a trial designed to answer this question.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Ferrous sulfate, 80 mg elemental iron daily for four weeks (Swiss trial).

factors.study_quality: The source trial was double-blind and placebo-controlled, but this finding comes from a subgroup analysis.
factors.consistency: The other trials and the review studied only iron-deficient or mostly low-ferritin people, so they do not test a benefit in people with normal iron.
factors.effect_size: No benefit was seen in women with ferritin above 50 µg/L; the abstract gives no size for that subgroup.
factors.clinical_significance: Taking iron without a need adds side-effect and overload risks (see safety) without a shown benefit.
factors.sample_size: Small for the subgroup in question.
factors.population: Women of reproductive age; no data we read on men with normal iron.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Not stated in the abstract.
factors.reproducibility: Not directly tested in a dedicated trial in the sources we read.
factors.formulation_dose: Ferrous sulfate 80 mg/day.

claims.claim: Iron supplements improve exercise capacity in iron-deficient adults who are not anaemic
claims.popular_framing: Athletes should take iron to boost endurance.
claims.question: Does iron improve fitness if I'm low in iron but not anaemic?
claims.outcome: Objective physical capacity (e.g. VO2max, timed exercise tests)
claims.population: Non-anaemic, iron-deficient adults.
claims.bottom_line: Not shown. In non-anaemic people with low iron, iron did not measurably improve fitness tests, although the studies were small.
claims.what_research_found: A systematic review found no association between iron and maximal oxygen uptake (9 trials, 235 participants) or timed exercise tests in non-anaemic, iron-deficient adults. Separately, a Cochrane review in menstruating women (not restricted to women without anaemia) reported that iron improved maximal and submaximal exercise performance.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: The small number of participants means a modest benefit cannot be ruled out. The evidence does not show iron improves performance in people with normal iron.
claims.limitations: Only 235 participants contributed to the VO2max analysis. The Cochrane review was not restricted to non-anaemic women, so it does not settle the question for the non-anaemic group.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Oral, intramuscular or intravenous iron at varied doses and durations.

factors.study_quality: Randomised trials assessed with the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool.
factors.consistency: No heterogeneity for VO2max (I² 0%), but results differ from the mixed-population Cochrane finding.
factors.effect_size: Close to zero (SMD 0.11, confidence interval crossing zero).
factors.clinical_significance: No meaningful performance gain shown in this group.
factors.sample_size: Small (235 participants for VO2max).
factors.population: Iron-deficient, non-anaemic adults; athletes were not analysed separately in the abstract.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Review authors declared no competing interests.
factors.reproducibility: Pooled from 9 trials.
factors.formulation_dose: Mixed routes and doses.

claims.claim: Drinking tea or coffee with a meal reduces how much iron you absorb from it
claims.popular_framing: Don't drink tea with your iron-rich meal; have vitamin C instead.
claims.question: Does tea or coffee block iron absorption?
claims.outcome: Non-heme iron absorption from a single meal
claims.population: Healthy adults in absorption studies.
claims.bottom_line: Yes, in absorption studies: polyphenol-rich drinks like black tea and coffee cut iron absorption from a bread meal considerably. Whether this changes long-term iron status for most people is less clear.
claims.what_research_found: In adults given a bread meal with labelled iron, black tea reduced iron absorption by 79–94%, and coffee, cocoa and herbal teas also reduced it. The more polyphenols a drink contained, the bigger the effect. Adding milk made little difference. NIH ODS says polyphenols and phytates reduce absorption of non-heme (plant) iron, vitamin C increases it, and calcium may reduce it, though the calcium effect is not definitively established.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: These were single-meal absorption measurements, not long-term studies of iron levels or anaemia. NIH ODS notes that in a typical mixed Western diet these effects matter little for most people.
claims.limitations: Short-term isotope studies in small groups; the abstract does not give participant numbers.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Beverages containing 20–400 mg of total polyphenols per serving, taken with a bread meal.

factors.study_quality: Controlled absorption measurements using radio-labelled iron; not randomised trials of health outcomes.
factors.consistency: All drinks tested inhibited absorption, in a dose-dependent way.
factors.effect_size: Large for single-meal absorption (47–94% reductions across the drinks tested; 79–94% for black tea).
factors.clinical_significance: Uncertain for people on mixed diets; may matter more for people at risk of deficiency or with mostly plant-based diets.
factors.sample_size: Not stated in the abstract.
factors.population: Adults eating a non-heme iron meal (bread). Heme iron from meat is affected less (NIH ODS).
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Not stated in the abstract.
factors.reproducibility: Consistent with the authoritative summary by NIH ODS on polyphenols.
factors.formulation_dose: Effect measured on food iron, not on iron supplement tablets.

claims.claim: Accidental overdose of iron supplements can be fatal for young children
claims.popular_framing: Iron is just a mineral, so it's harmless.
claims.question: Are iron supplements dangerous for children?
claims.outcome: Poisoning and death from accidental ingestion
claims.population: Children under 6 years.
claims.bottom_line: Yes. Iron supplements have been a leading cause of fatal poisoning in young children, and after unit-dose packaging was required in the US, deaths fell sharply.
claims.what_research_found: NIH ODS reports that at least 43 US children died from high-dose iron supplements between 1983 and 2000, and the FDA requires a warning that accidental iron overdose is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under 6. After the US required unit-dose packaging of iron supplements in 1997, iron-poisoning deaths in children under 6 fell from 29 in the 10 years before to 1 in the 5 years after.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: Packaging data cannot separate the effect of packaging from other changes over time.
claims.limitations: Evidence comes from poison-centre records and authoritative summaries; randomised trials are not possible for poisoning.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Large one-time overdoses; NIH ODS describes severe poisoning at around 60 mg/kg.

factors.study_quality: Before-and-after analysis of national poison-centre data plus regulatory warnings; this is the appropriate evidence type for accidental poisoning.
factors.consistency: Regulatory action, poison-centre data and NIH ODS all agree.
factors.effect_size: Severe: overdose can cause organ failure, coma, convulsions and death (NIH ODS).
factors.clinical_significance: Life-threatening.
factors.sample_size: National US poison-centre data over 15 years.
factors.population: Children under 6.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Not stated in the abstract.
factors.reproducibility: Consistent with the FDA warning requirement and NIH ODS.
factors.formulation_dose: Applies to iron-containing supplements and products kept in the home.

foods.food: Breakfast cereal, fortified with 100% DV iron
Oysters, eastern, cooked with moist heat

research_doses.note: Elemental iron per dose in the oral trials cited: 80 mg/day ferrous sulfate in the fatigue trials; 60 mg daily or on alternate days, and 120 mg single doses, in the absorption trial. The Cochrane review in menstruating women included many doses.

food_vs_supplement.comparison_note: Research doses (60–120 mg of elemental iron) are many times higher than what a serving of food provides (1–8 mg for most foods) and above the 45 mg/day adult upper limit. These doses were used to correct deficiency, not for everyday intake, so food and supplement amounts are not directly comparable.
food_vs_supplement.food_advantages: Meat, poultry and seafood provide heme iron, which is better absorbed than plant iron and less affected by other foods (NIH ODS). Foods also avoid the gut side effects seen with high-dose supplements.
food_vs_supplement.when_supplement_may_help: NIH ODS lists groups at higher risk of deficiency: pregnant women, infants and young children, teenage girls and premenopausal women, frequent blood donors, people with certain cancers, gut disorders or gut surgery, heart failure, and food insecurity. Research benefits were shown in people with confirmed low iron or anaemia; a clinician can check iron levels.

profiles.absorption: Heme iron from meat, poultry and seafood is absorbed better than non-heme iron from plants. NIH ODS estimates absorption at about 14–18% from mixed diets with meat and vitamin C, and 5–12% from vegetarian diets, which is why the RDA for vegetarians is 1.8 times higher. Vitamin C and meat increase non-heme iron absorption; phytates (grains, beans) and polyphenols reduce it, and calcium may reduce it (NIH ODS). In a single-meal study, black tea cut iron absorption from a bread meal by 79–94%. In iron-depleted women, a trial found that 60 mg of iron given on alternate days was absorbed better overall than the same dose on consecutive days (21.8% vs 16.3% cumulative fractional absorption), and splitting a dose into two daily doses did not improve absorption. Those results were in iron-depleted women (ferritin 25 µg/L or lower), and the authors said they need confirming in anaemic patients.
profiles.side_effects: Stomach upset, nausea and constipation, especially at 45 mg/day or more and on an empty stomach (NIH ODS). In a Cochrane review of menstruating women, iron roughly doubled the risk of constipation and of diarrhoea compared with control. Supplements with 25 mg or more of iron can reduce zinc absorption (NIH ODS).
profiles.interactions: Iron can reduce the absorption of levodopa (used for Parkinson's disease and restless legs) and can reduce the effect of levothyroxine (thyroid hormone); labels advise taking levothyroxine at least 4 hours apart from iron. Proton pump inhibitors (e.g. omeprazole) reduce stomach acid and lower non-heme iron absorption (NIH ODS).
profiles.cautions: Keep iron products away from children: accidental overdose is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under 6. People with hereditary haemochromatosis absorb too much iron and should generally avoid iron (and vitamin C) supplements (NIH ODS). Talk to a clinician before taking iron if you are pregnant, take thyroid or Parkinson's medication, or have a gut or blood disorder. Tiredness has many causes; a blood test can show whether iron is actually low.
profiles.upper_limit: 45 mg/day for adults 19+ and teens 14–18, including pregnancy and lactation; 40 mg/day for children under 14 (NIH ODS).
profiles.research_doses_summary: Doses used in research: in the fatigue trials, 80 mg of elemental iron a day as ferrous sulfate for 4–12 weeks in non-anaemic women with low iron stores. In an absorption trial in iron-depleted women, 60 mg on consecutive or alternate days and 120 mg single doses. These are research doses, not recommendations.

sources.title: Daily iron supplementation for improving anaemia, iron status and health in menstruating women.
sources.authors: Low MS, Speedy J, Styles CE, De-Regil LM, Pasricha SR.
sources.population: Menstruating women (or women aged 12–50).
sources.intervention: Daily oral iron, with or without folic acid or vitamin C, at least five days per week, any dose, versus control or placebo.
sources.findings: Iron reduced anaemia (RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.60; 10 studies, 3,273 women; moderate quality) and iron deficiency (RR 0.62), and raised haemoglobin (MD 5.30; 51 studies, 6,861 women; high quality). It improved maximal and submaximal exercise performance and appeared to reduce symptomatic fatigue. It increased gastrointestinal side effects (RR 1.99), diarrhoea (RR 2.13) and constipation (RR 2.07). Effects on cognition were uncertain.
sources.limitations: Only 10 studies at low overall risk of bias; most reported insufficient detail on quality.
sources.funding: Authors state funders had no role; some authors employed by the Australian Red Cross Blood Service or the Micronutrient Initiative (disclosed).
sources.cited_for: Iron corrects anaemia and low iron stores in menstruating women; GI side effects; exercise performance in a mixed population.

sources.title: Efficacy of iron supplementation on fatigue and physical capacity in non-anaemic iron-deficient adults: a systematic review of randomised controlled trials.
sources.authors: Houston BL, Hurrie D, Graham J, Perija B, Rimmer E, Rabbani R, Bernstein CN, Turgeon AF, Fergusson DA, Houston DS, Abou-Setta AM, Zarychanski R.
sources.population: Adults (18+) who were iron deficient but not anaemic.
sources.intervention: Oral, intramuscular or intravenous iron at any dose, frequency or duration, versus placebo or active therapy.
sources.findings: Iron was associated with less self-reported fatigue (SMD −0.38, 95% CI −0.52 to −0.23; I² 0%; 4 trials, 714 participants) but not with objective physical capacity, including VO2max (SMD 0.11, 95% CI −0.15 to 0.37; 9 trials, 235 participants) or timed exercise tests. Haemoglobin and ferritin rose.
sources.limitations: Few trials for the fatigue outcome; small numbers for physical capacity.
sources.funding: Competing interests: none declared. Funding not stated in abstract.
sources.cited_for: Fatigue reduction in non-anaemic iron-deficient adults; no improvement in objective physical capacity.

sources.title: Effect of iron supplementation on fatigue in nonanemic menstruating women with low ferritin: a randomized controlled trial.
sources.authors: Vaucher P, Druais PL, Waldvogel S, Favrat B.
sources.population: Women aged 18–53 with fatigue, ferritin below 50 µg/L and haemoglobin above 12.0 g/dL, recruited by 44 primary care physicians in France.
sources.intervention: Oral ferrous sulfate, 80 mg elemental iron daily, or placebo for 12 weeks.
sources.findings: Fatigue scores fell 47.7% with iron vs 28.8% with placebo (difference −18.9%, 95% CI −34.5 to −3.2; p=0.02). No significant effect on quality of life, depression or anxiety. Haemoglobin and ferritin rose with iron.
sources.limitations: Described as closed-label and observer-blinded; fatigue was self-reported.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract.
sources.cited_for: Fatigue reduction with iron in non-anaemic women with low ferritin; research dose of 80 mg/day.

sources.title: Iron supplementation for unexplained fatigue in non-anaemic women: double blind randomised placebo controlled trial.
sources.authors: Verdon F, Burnand B, Stubi CL, Bonard C, Graff M, Michaud A, Bischoff T, de Vevey M, Studer JP, Herzig L, Chapuis C, Tissot J, Pécoud A, Favrat B.
sources.population: Non-anaemic women aged 18–55 with unexplained fatigue in Swiss primary care.
sources.intervention: Oral ferrous sulphate, 80 mg elemental iron daily, or placebo for four weeks.
sources.findings: Fatigue decreased 29% with iron vs 13% with placebo (difference 0.95 points on a 10-point scale, 95% CI 0.32 to 1.62; P=0.004). Subgroup analysis showed only women with ferritin of 50 µg/L or lower improved.
sources.limitations: Short (four weeks); the ferritin finding is from a subgroup analysis.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract.
sources.cited_for: Fatigue benefit limited to women with low or borderline iron stores; no shown benefit with normal iron.

sources.title: Inhibition of non-haem iron absorption in man by polyphenolic-containing beverages.
sources.authors: Hurrell RF, Reddy M, Cook JD.
sources.population: Adult human subjects.
sources.intervention: Polyphenol-containing beverages (black tea, herb teas, coffee, cocoa) served with a bread meal, compared with water; absorption measured by radio-iron incorporation into red cells.
sources.findings: All beverages inhibited iron absorption in a dose-dependent way. Drinks with 20–50 mg polyphenols per serving cut absorption by 50–70%; those with 100–400 mg by 60–90%. Black tea inhibited absorption by 79–94%. Adding milk to tea and coffee had little or no influence.
sources.limitations: Single-meal absorption measurements; participant numbers not given in abstract; no DOI listed in the PubMed record.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract.
sources.cited_for: Tea and coffee reduce non-heme iron absorption from a meal.

sources.title: Iron absorption from oral iron supplements given on consecutive versus alternate days and as single morning doses versus twice-daily split dosing in iron-depleted women: two open-label, randomised controlled trials.
sources.authors: Stoffel NU, Cercamondi CI, Brittenham G, Zeder C, Geurts-Moespot AJ, Swinkels DW, Moretti D, Zimmermann MB.
sources.population: Iron-depleted women (ferritin ≤25 µg/L) aged 18–40 in Zurich.
sources.intervention: Isotope-labelled ferrous sulfate: 60 mg on consecutive days for 14 days vs alternate days for 28 days; 120 mg once daily vs 60 mg twice daily for 3 days.
sources.findings: Alternate-day dosing gave higher cumulative fractional absorption (21.8% vs 16.3%, p=0.0013) and total absorption (175.3 mg vs 131.0 mg). Split twice-daily dosing did not improve absorption and raised hepcidin. No grade 3 or 4 adverse events.
sources.limitations: Open-label, small, short-term absorption study; authors say findings need confirming in anaemic patients.
sources.funding: Swiss National Science Foundation.
sources.cited_for: Absorption section: alternate-day vs daily dosing; research doses.

sources.title: Unit-dose packaging of iron supplements and reduction of iron poisoning in young children.
sources.authors: Tenenbein M.
sources.sample_size: US poison control centre data, 10 years before vs 5 years after the 1997 rule
sources.population: Children younger than 6 years in the US.
sources.intervention: FDA-mandated unit-dose packaging of iron supplements (1997).
sources.findings: Iron ingestion calls fell from 2.99 to 1.91 per 1,000 calls about children under 6, and iron-poisoning deaths fell from 29 to 1. The author describes iron poisoning as a major cause of unintentional poisoning death in young children.
sources.limitations: Before-and-after design; cannot rule out other changes over time.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract.
sources.cited_for: Iron overdose risk in young children and effect of packaging.

sources.title: Iron: Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
sources.authors: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements
sources.population: General population; groups at risk of deficiency.
sources.findings: RDAs (8 mg men 19–50, 18 mg women 19–50, 27 mg pregnancy), ULs (45 mg adults; 40 mg under 14), food-content table, heme vs non-heme absorption and enhancers/inhibitors, supplement forms and elemental iron content, GI side effects, child poisoning (FDA warning; 43 US child deaths 1983–2000), haemochromatosis, and interactions with levodopa, levothyroxine and proton pump inhibitors.
sources.limitations: Summary document; last-updated date not recorded at time of reading.
sources.funding: US federal government (NIH).
sources.cited_for: Food table, RDA, upper limit, absorption factors (vitamin C, polyphenols, calcium), side effects, interactions, cautions, child poisoning.

profiles.name: L-theanine
profiles.summary: L-theanine, an amino acid from tea, may give a short-term boost to attention and may help sleep, but its reputation for reducing stress and anxiety rests on weak evidence, and much of the 'focus' effect of theanine-plus-caffeine may come from the caffeine.
profiles.description: L-theanine is an amino acid found in the leaves of the tea plant (Camellia sinensis). It is sold as a pure supplement and in combination products with caffeine.
profiles.biological_function: L-theanine is a non-protein amino acid, meaning the body does not use it to build proteins. Trials have measured its effects on attention, mood and sleep, and earlier calming effects and animal studies prompted the sleep research. How it works in people is not established by the sources reviewed here.

formulations.name: Pure L-theanine
formulations.notes: Most cited trials used 200 mg single doses or 200–400 mg/day; sleep trials ranged from 50 to 900 mg/day.

formulations.name: L-theanine with caffeine
formulations.notes: Combination studied for alertness and attention; effects tracked caffeine dose more than L-theanine dose.

claims.claim: L-theanine reduces stress and anxiety
claims.popular_framing: L-theanine gives you calm without drowsiness.
claims.question: Does L-theanine make you feel calmer or less anxious?
claims.outcome: Self-rated stress and anxiety
claims.population: Healthy adults and people under stress; some clinical groups.
claims.bottom_line: We don't know yet. The largest review found only a modest drop in acute stress, mostly driven by lower-quality studies, and no consistent effect on anxiety.
claims.what_research_found: A 2026 meta-analysis of 31 randomised trials (1,168 people) found a modest reduction in acute stress after a single dose (SMD 0.31), largely influenced by studies at high risk of bias. Anxiety effects were inconsistent and not significant overall. An earlier review of 9 studies suggested 200–400 mg/day may help people in stressful conditions, and in a small 4-week trial, trait anxiety scores fell after L-theanine (a before-and-after change; the abstract does not report a difference from placebo).
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It is not established that L-theanine reliably reduces stress or anxiety, or that it treats anxiety disorders.
claims.limitations: Small studies; stress findings depend on high-risk-of-bias trials; one cited trial was funded by, and used tablets supplied by, an L-theanine manufacturer.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Single 200 mg doses, or 200–400 mg/day over 4–8 weeks in the cited trials.

factors.study_quality: Many trials, but the stress effect depends on studies at high risk of bias.
factors.consistency: Inconsistent, especially for anxiety.
factors.effect_size: Modest (SMD 0.31) for acute stress.
factors.clinical_significance: Unclear whether people would notice.
factors.sample_size: 1,168 participants across 31 trials; numbers per outcome are not given in the abstract.
factors.population: Mostly healthy adults; matches the popular claim.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: One meta-analysis author founded a supplement company; a key trial was funded by, and used tablets from, an L-theanine manufacturer.
factors.reproducibility: Not consistently replicated.
factors.formulation_dose: Pure L-theanine at 200–400 mg.

claims.claim: L-theanine on its own improves focus and attention
claims.popular_framing: L-theanine sharpens your focus.
claims.question: Does L-theanine alone improve attention?
claims.outcome: Attention and reaction time on lab tests
claims.population: Healthy adults.
claims.bottom_line: Possibly, in the short term. A single 200 mg dose improved reaction time on attention tests in a 2026 meta-analysis, but that is a lab finding, not proof of better focus in daily life.
claims.what_research_found: A 2026 meta-analysis found a single 200 mg dose taken 30–60 minutes before testing improved choice reaction time (SMD 0.51), which the authors describe as a robust short-term benefit on attention in healthy adults.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: Real-world focus, work or study performance, and longer-term effects have not been shown.
claims.limitations: Short-term lab tasks only; one author has a supplement-company interest.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Single 200 mg dose, 30–60 minutes before testing.

factors.study_quality: Randomised placebo-controlled trials pooled in a meta-analysis.
factors.consistency: The authors call the attention effect robust.
factors.effect_size: Moderate (SMD 0.51).
factors.clinical_significance: Uncertain: faster reaction time on a lab task may not be noticeable in daily life.
factors.sample_size: Part of a 31-trial, 1,168-person meta-analysis; numbers for this outcome not given in the abstract.
factors.population: Healthy adults; matches the popular claim.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: One meta-analysis author founded a supplement company.
factors.reproducibility: Pooled across several trials (number not given in the abstract); one meta-analysis only.
factors.formulation_dose: 200 mg single dose.

claims.claim: L-theanine combined with caffeine improves alertness and attention
claims.popular_framing: Stack L-theanine with your coffee for smooth, jitter-free focus.
claims.question: Does L-theanine plus caffeine improve focus?
claims.outcome: Alertness and attention in the first hours after a dose
claims.population: Participants in short laboratory studies (the review abstract does not describe who was studied).
claims.bottom_line: The combination improved alertness and attention-switching in short lab studies, but the effect tracked the caffeine dose more than the L-theanine dose. Caffeine may be doing much of the work.
claims.what_research_found: A 2014 meta-analysis of 11 placebo-controlled studies found moderate effects favouring caffeine plus L-theanine within 2 hours on self-rated alertness and accuracy when switching attention, and smaller effects on some other attention tasks. Effect size changed more with caffeine dose than with L-theanine dose.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It is not shown that adding L-theanine to caffeine gives more benefit than caffeine alone, or that it prevents caffeine jitters.
claims.limitations: Few studies per outcome; acute lab testing only; review is from 2014.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Single combined doses of caffeine and L-theanine; doses varied across studies.

factors.study_quality: Randomised placebo-controlled acute studies.
factors.consistency: The abstract reports moderate pooled effects for alertness and attention switching but not how consistent individual studies were.
factors.effect_size: Moderate in the first 2 hours.
factors.clinical_significance: Possibly noticeable, but likely driven by caffeine.
factors.sample_size: 11 studies; participant numbers are not given in the abstract.
factors.population: Not described in the abstract; the popular claim targets healthy adults.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Not stated in abstract.
factors.reproducibility: Several studies, but the L-theanine-specific contribution is unclear.
factors.formulation_dose: Results depended more on caffeine dose.

claims.claim: L-theanine improves sleep
claims.popular_framing: L-theanine helps you wind down and sleep better.
claims.question: Does L-theanine improve sleep?
claims.outcome: Sleep quality and related measures
claims.population: Adults. The review calls for more trials in people with clinical insomnia.
