claims.bottom_line: Possibly. Small trials mostly report better sleep, but there is no pooled analysis, and the review's authors call for higher-quality trials with objective sleep measures.
claims.what_research_found: A 2026 systematic review of 13 trials (550 people; 11 randomised) concluded that 200–450 mg/day 'appears to be a safe and effective way to support healthy sleep in adults', with benefits reported for sleep latency, efficiency, satisfaction and feeling refreshed. In a 4-week crossover trial of 30 healthy adults, overall sleep quality scores fell (improved) after 200 mg/day (the abstract does not state a placebo comparison for this score), and the sleep latency, sleep disturbance and sleep medication subscales improved compared with placebo.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: Benefits for people with clinical insomnia, and the size of any effect, are not established.
claims.limitations: Small trials, a narrative review without pooled effects, two open-label trials included, and a key trial was funded by, and used tablets supplied by, an L-theanine manufacturer.
claims.formulation_and_dose: 50–900 mg/day across trials; the review's conclusion refers to 200–450 mg/day.

factors.study_quality: Mostly randomised trials, plus two open-label trials.
factors.consistency: Mostly positive in the review.
factors.effect_size: Not pooled; unknown.
factors.clinical_significance: Unknown.
factors.sample_size: 550 participants across 13 trials.
factors.population: Adults; few data in people with clinical insomnia, according to the review's call for such trials.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: One key trial was funded by the company supplying the L-theanine, and two of its authors were employees of that company.
factors.reproducibility: Several small trials, limited independent replication.
factors.formulation_dose: L-theanine alone, 50–900 mg/day across trials; the review highlights 200–450 mg/day.

foods.serving: Infusion from 1 g tea leaves (100 ml water)
Infusion from 1 g tea leaves (100 ml water)
Infusion from 1 g tea leaves (100 ml water)
Infusion from 1 g tea leaves (100 ml water)

research_doses.note: Cited trials used 200 mg single doses or 200–400 mg/day; sleep trials ranged 50–900 mg/day.

food_vs_supplement.comparison_note: Tea gives about 5–7 mg of L-theanine per gram of leaves with a 3-minute brew. Reaching a 200 mg research dose from tea would take roughly 30 grams of green tea leaves brewed this way, which would also bring a lot of caffeine (16–19 mg per gram in the same study). Theanine content varies widely between teas, and longer brewing extracts more.
food_vs_supplement.food_advantages: Tea also provides caffeine (16–19 mg per gram of tea in the same analysis) and other plant compounds. No verified research compares drinking tea with taking L-theanine supplements.
food_vs_supplement.when_supplement_may_help: Research doses (200–400 mg) are far above what tea provides, so trial results do not tell us what normal tea drinking does. None of the sources reviewed identifies a group for whom L-theanine supplementation is recommended.

profiles.absorption: Acute studies gave single doses 30–60 minutes before testing, with effects measured within 1–2 hours. The sources reviewed do not report absorption data.
profiles.side_effects: No serious adverse events were reported in a meta-analysis of 31 randomised trials, and a 2026 sleep review described 200–450 mg/day as appearing safe. Long-term safety data were not found in the sources reviewed.
profiles.interactions: No verified interaction data were found in the sources reviewed. Combination products also contain caffeine, which has its own effects and cautions.
profiles.cautions: Safety in pregnancy, breastfeeding, children and people taking medicines was not addressed by the sources reviewed; talk to a clinician first. Check labels of combination products for caffeine content.
profiles.research_doses_summary: Doses used in research: single 200 mg doses taken 30–60 minutes before testing; 200–400 mg/day for stress; 50–900 mg/day in sleep trials, with the sleep review's conclusion referring to 200–450 mg/day; repeated dosing for 4–8 weeks in the cited trials. These are not recommendations.

sources.title: Cognitive and affective effects of L-Theanine: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 31 randomized trials.
sources.authors: Gerolymos C, Saddier E, Boyer L, Fond G
sources.population: Healthy and clinical populations
sources.intervention: Oral L-theanine vs placebo, single doses (typically 200 mg) and repeated dosing.
sources.findings: A single 200 mg dose taken 30–60 minutes before testing improved choice reaction time (SMD 0.51, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.77), which the authors describe as a robust short-term benefit on attention in healthy adults. The reduction in acute stress was modest (SMD 0.31) and largely driven by studies at high risk of bias. Anxiety effects were inconsistent and non-significant (apart from one study in psychotic anxiety). No effect on fatigue. No serious adverse events were reported.
sources.limitations: Mixed healthy and clinical populations; stress findings depend on high-risk-of-bias studies.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract. One author founded a company selling dietary supplements.
sources.cited_for: l-theanine-focus (attention) and l-theanine-calm (stress and anxiety); safety.

sources.title: The Effects of Green Tea Amino Acid L-Theanine Consumption on the Ability to Manage Stress and Anxiety Levels: a Systematic Review.
sources.authors: Williams JL, Everett JM, D'Cunha NM, et al.
sources.population: People exposed to stressful conditions
sources.intervention: Pure L-theanine supplements vs control.
sources.findings: Supplementation of 200–400 mg/day may help reduce stress and anxiety in people exposed to stressful conditions. The authors say longer-term and larger studies are needed before L-theanine can be clinically justified for this purpose.
sources.limitations: Small number of studies; no pooled effect size in the abstract.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract.
sources.cited_for: l-theanine-calm: tentative support from a small set of trials.

sources.title: Effects of L-Theanine Administration on Stress-Related Symptoms and Cognitive Functions in Healthy Adults: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
sources.authors: Hidese S, Ogawa S, Ota M, Ishida I, Yasukawa Z, Ozeki M, Kunugi H
sources.population: Healthy adults (9 men, 21 women, mean age 48.3) without major psychiatric illness
sources.intervention: 200 mg/day L-theanine vs placebo for 4 weeks; double-blind crossover.
sources.findings: After L-theanine, depression, trait anxiety and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index scores decreased (p = 0.019, 0.006 and 0.013). Sleep latency, sleep disturbance and sleep medication subscales improved compared with placebo (all p < 0.05). Verbal fluency and executive function scores improved.
sources.limitations: Small trial; several outcomes; the abstract reports the depression, trait anxiety and overall sleep-quality score changes as changes after L-theanine, without a stated comparison with placebo.
sources.funding: Funded by Taiyo Kagaku Co., Ltd. (PubMed grant record), which also supplied the L-theanine and placebo tablets; two authors are Taiyo Kagaku employees.
sources.cited_for: l-theanine-sleep and l-theanine-calm: example 4-week trial.

sources.title: Acute effects of tea constituents L-theanine, caffeine, and epigallocatechin gallate on cognitive function and mood: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.authors: Camfield DA, Stough C, Farrimond J, Scholey AB
sources.population: Human participants in acute dosing studies (the abstract does not describe the populations)
sources.intervention: Single doses of L-theanine or EGCG, alone or combined with caffeine.
sources.findings: Moderate effect sizes favoured combined caffeine and L-theanine in the first 2 hours after a dose for self-rated alertness and accuracy when switching attention, and to a lesser extent for some other attention tasks. Changes in effect size tracked caffeine dose more than L-theanine dose, especially in the first hour.
sources.limitations: Few studies per outcome; short-term lab tasks only.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract.
sources.cited_for: l-theanine-caffeine-focus: combined effect and the larger role of caffeine.

sources.title: Examining the effect of L-theanine on sleep: a systematic review of dietary supplementation trials.
sources.authors: Cotter J, Caddick CE, Harper JL, Ebajemito JK
sources.population: Adults
sources.intervention: L-theanine alone at 50–900 mg/day.
sources.findings: The authors conclude 200–450 mg/day 'appears to be a safe and effective way to support healthy sleep in adults', with benefits reported on objective and self-reported measures, including sleep latency, maintenance, efficiency, satisfaction and feeling refreshed. They call for higher-quality trials with objective measures and in people with clinical insomnia.
sources.limitations: Narrative review without pooled effect sizes; includes open-label trials; small total sample.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract.
sources.cited_for: l-theanine-sleep: overall picture of sleep trials.

sources.title: Theanine and Caffeine Content of Infusions Prepared from Commercial Tea Samples.
sources.authors: Boros K, Jedlinszki N, Csupor D
sources.population: Not a human study (laboratory analysis of tea)
sources.intervention: Infusions of 1 g tea in 100 ml water at 80°C for 3 minutes, analysed by HPLC.
sources.findings: Mean L-theanine extracted per gram of tea was 6.56 mg (green), 6.26 mg (white), 6.09 mg (oolong) and 5.13 mg (black); pu-erh had practically none. Caffeine was 16–19 mg per gram. A 3-minute brew did not fully extract theanine: a 90-minute extraction gave about twice as much. Theanine content varied widely within each tea type.
sources.limitations: Small set of products from shops in Hungary and Taiwan; values per gram of tea, not per standard cup. The abstract reports 37 samples while the methods and conclusion refer to 34.
sources.funding: European Union and the State of Hungary (European Social Fund, TÁMOP 'National Excellence Program'); authors declare no conflicts of interest.
sources.cited_for: food_vs_supplement: L-theanine content of tea infusions.
