profiles.name: Magnesium
profiles.summary: Magnesium is an essential mineral, but as a supplement its popular benefits are mostly unproven: evidence for sleep and anxiety is weak, it does not prevent ordinary night-time leg cramps in older adults, and it lowers blood pressure only slightly, mainly in people with high blood pressure or low magnesium.
profiles.description: Magnesium is an essential mineral found in nuts, seeds, beans, leafy greens and whole grains. Supplements come as different salts, such as oxide, citrate, glycinate (bisglycinate) and L-threonate. Some forms appear to be absorbed better than others, and labels list the elemental magnesium, not the weight of the whole compound.
profiles.biological_function: Magnesium is an essential mineral. In healthy people, the kidneys remove extra magnesium from food in urine. When magnesium runs low, symptoms can include muscle contractions and cramps. Low magnesium is more common in people with gut diseases, type 2 diabetes or alcohol dependence, and in older adults.

formulations.name: Magnesium oxide and sulfate
formulations.notes: Appear less well absorbed than more soluble forms, based on small studies (NIH ODS). Oxide is among the forms most often linked to diarrhoea at high doses.

formulations.name: Magnesium citrate, aspartate, lactate and chloride
formulations.notes: Appear more bioavailable than oxide and sulfate, based on small studies (NIH ODS).

formulations.name: Magnesium bisglycinate (glycinate)
formulations.notes: Tested for sleep in one pre-registered trial at 250 mg elemental magnesium daily, with a small benefit. We found no verified source comparing its absorption with other forms.

formulations.name: Magnesium L-threonate
formulations.notes: Marketed for brain effects. Tested for sleep in one 21-day, industry-funded trial at 1 g/day of the compound (about 75 mg elemental magnesium, per the trial's full text).

claims.claim: Magnesium supplements improve sleep in adults
claims.popular_framing: Take magnesium before bed for deeper, better sleep.
claims.question: Does magnesium improve sleep?
claims.outcome: Sleep quality and insomnia symptoms
claims.population: Adults with poor sleep or insomnia symptoms.
claims.bottom_line: We don't know yet. Trials are mixed, and the most recent review rates the evidence low to very low certainty. Where benefits appear, they are small.
claims.what_research_found: A 2026 systematic review of 12 randomised trials found inconsistent results across self-reported sleep, EEG and wearable measures. It concluded magnesium is not supported as a routine insomnia treatment, though some adults may get modest benefits on some self-reported measures. One of the larger recent trials (155 adults, magnesium bisglycinate) found a statistically significant but small drop in insomnia severity after 4 weeks (effect size d = 0.2).
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It has not been shown that magnesium reliably helps people with normal magnesium intake sleep better. It is also unclear which form or dose, if any, works best.
claims.limitations: Trials are mostly small and vary widely in magnesium form, dose, duration and outcome measures. Many rely on self-reported sleep.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Forms and doses varied. Examples: 250 mg elemental magnesium as bisglycinate daily for 4 weeks; 500 mg magnesium daily for 8 weeks in older adults.

factors.study_quality: Randomised, placebo-controlled trials exist, but the 2026 review rated certainty low to very low.
factors.consistency: Inconsistent: some trials and measures show benefit, others do not.
factors.effect_size: Small where present (e.g. d = 0.2 for insomnia severity in the bisglycinate trial).
factors.clinical_significance: The extra improvement over placebo was 1.6 Insomnia Severity Index points, which the authors call modest.
factors.sample_size: Twelve trials in the main review, most of them small.
factors.population: Mostly adults with poor sleep. The bisglycinate trial's authors call for better assessment of baseline magnesium intake and status in future trials.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: One author of the bisglycinate trial runs a contract research organisation funded by nutraceutical companies; not the main limitation.
factors.reproducibility: Results have not replicated consistently across groups.
factors.formulation_dose: Different salts and elemental doses make results hard to compare with any one product.

claims.claim: Magnesium helps older adults with insomnia fall asleep faster
claims.popular_framing: Magnesium is a natural sleep aid for older people.
claims.question: Does magnesium help older adults with insomnia fall asleep?
claims.outcome: Time to fall asleep (sleep onset latency)
claims.population: Older adults with insomnia.
claims.bottom_line: Possibly, but the evidence is weak. Three small trials pooled together showed people fell asleep about 17 minutes faster, but the studies had a high risk of bias.
claims.what_research_found: A 2021 meta-analysis of 3 trials (151 older adults) found people fell asleep 17.4 minutes faster on magnesium than placebo. Total sleep time rose by about 16 minutes, but this was not statistically significant. A 2012 trial in 46 older adults (500 mg daily for 8 weeks) also reported better insomnia severity scores and sleep efficiency.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It is not established that these results hold in larger, well-run trials, or that magnesium works for younger adults.
claims.limitations: All three trials were at moderate-to-high risk of bias and the evidence was rated low to very low quality. Older adults are a group at higher risk of low magnesium (NIH ODS), so results may not apply to people with normal levels.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Oral magnesium; one included trial used 500 mg daily for 8 weeks. The review describes doses under 1 g up to three times a day.

factors.study_quality: Randomised trials, but at moderate-to-high risk of bias.
factors.consistency: The pooled result points one way, but the broader 2026 review finds results inconsistent overall.
factors.effect_size: About 17 minutes faster sleep onset, with a wide confidence interval (7 to 27 minutes).
factors.clinical_significance: Could be noticeable if real, but uncertain.
factors.sample_size: Only 151 participants in total.
factors.population: Older adults with insomnia only; a group NIH ODS lists as at higher risk of low magnesium.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Conflicts declared as none in the meta-analysis and the Abbasi trial.
factors.reproducibility: Few independent trials.
factors.formulation_dose: Salts and doses differ between trials.

claims.claim: Magnesium L-threonate improves deep sleep
claims.popular_framing: Magnesium L-threonate is the 'brain' magnesium that boosts deep sleep.
claims.question: Does magnesium L-threonate improve deep sleep?
claims.outcome: Sleep stages (deep and REM sleep) and daytime functioning
claims.population: Adults aged 35–55 with self-reported sleep problems.
claims.bottom_line: Not established. One 3-week trial reported better wearable-measured deep and REM sleep scores, but a single small trial using a consumer device can't settle it.
claims.what_research_found: In one trial of 80 adults, 1 g/day of magnesium L-threonate for 21 days improved Oura ring deep sleep and REM sleep scores and several self-rated daytime measures (energy, mood, alertness) compared with placebo. The abstract reports statistical significance but no effect sizes.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It has not been shown with lab-grade sleep measurement (polysomnography) or replicated by other groups. There is no head-to-head evidence that this form beats other forms.
claims.limitations: Single short trial; sleep stages estimated by a consumer wearable; funded by AIDP, Inc., with AIDP-affiliated co-authors.
claims.formulation_and_dose: 1 g/day magnesium L-threonate (compound weight) for 21 days. The full text states the product used contains about 75 mg elemental magnesium per gram.

factors.study_quality: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled.
factors.consistency: Only one trial, so consistency cannot be judged.
factors.effect_size: Not reported in the abstract (p < 0.05 only).
factors.clinical_significance: Unclear; wearable 'scores' are not the same as clinically measured sleep.
factors.sample_size: 80 participants.
factors.population: Middle-aged adults with self-reported sleep problems.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Industry-funded: the full text states the study was funded by AIDP, Inc., and three of the six authors list AIDP affiliations.
factors.reproducibility: Not independently replicated.
factors.formulation_dose: A specific branded-type form; results may not apply to other magnesium forms.

claims.claim: Magnesium supplements prevent ordinary night-time leg cramps in older adults
claims.popular_framing: Get leg cramps? You need more magnesium.
claims.question: Does magnesium prevent ordinary night-time leg cramps in older adults?
claims.outcome: Frequency of muscle cramps
claims.population: Older adults with ordinary (idiopathic) leg cramps, presumed to be night-time cramps. Pregnancy and exercise cramps are not covered by this rating.
claims.bottom_line: No. For the common night-time leg cramps of older adults, good research has looked and found no meaningful benefit. This verdict does not cover pregnancy cramps (evidence conflicts) or exercise cramps (no trials).
claims.what_research_found: A 2020 Cochrane review of 11 trials (735 people) found that, in older adults with idiopathic cramps, magnesium did not reduce cramp frequency compared with placebo (-0.18 cramps per week; moderate-certainty evidence). The chance of a 25% or better reduction was the same as placebo (high-certainty evidence). Cramp intensity and duration also did not improve.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: For pregnancy-related leg cramps the evidence conflicts. No randomised trials have tested magnesium for exercise-associated cramps.
claims.limitations: The 'evidence against' applies to older adults with idiopathic cramps. Pregnancy trials were at high risk of bias, and athletes have not been studied.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Mostly oral magnesium in various forms; one trial used intravenous infusions.

factors.study_quality: Cochrane review; only one of the five idiopathic-cramp trials was rated at high risk of bias.
factors.consistency: Consistent: minimal heterogeneity (I² = 0% to 12%) for older adults.
factors.effect_size: Near zero (-0.18 cramps per week).
factors.clinical_significance: No meaningful benefit a person would notice.
factors.sample_size: Five trials, 307 participants for cramps per week; three trials, 177 participants for the primary endpoint.
factors.population: Older adults; does not cover exercise cramps or pregnancy.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: One review author wrote an included study; Cochrane methods; grant funding from CIHR (Canada).
factors.reproducibility: Several independent trials agree.
factors.formulation_dose: Mostly oral magnesium; forms are not detailed in the review abstract. No benefit found for this group.

claims.claim: Magnesium reduces anxiety and stress
claims.popular_framing: Magnesium is nature's chill pill for anxiety.
claims.question: Does magnesium reduce anxiety or stress?
claims.outcome: Self-reported anxiety and stress
claims.population: People vulnerable to anxiety: mildly anxious adults, premenstrual syndrome, postpartum, hypertension.
claims.bottom_line: We don't know yet. Small studies lean positive for anxiety, but the evidence is of poor quality. No study in the 2017 review used a validated measure of stress.
claims.what_research_found: A 2017 systematic review of 18 studies found positive effects on self-reported anxiety in about half of studies in vulnerable groups (4 of 8 in anxious samples, 4 of 7 in premenstrual syndrome). A 2024 review found 5 of 7 anxiety studies reported improvement; its authors judged magnesium likely useful for mild anxiety, especially in people with low magnesium, but said larger randomised trials are needed. Both reviews describe small, varied studies.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: No study in the 2017 review used a validated measure of stress. It is not shown that magnesium helps people without low magnesium or without a specific vulnerability.
claims.limitations: Poor-quality, small studies; some products contained other active ingredients; no pooled effect size.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Doses, forms and durations varied widely across studies.

factors.study_quality: The 2017 review rates the evidence as poor quality; the 2024 review notes small samples and mixed designs.
factors.consistency: Mixed: roughly half to most studies positive, some negative. The two reviews differ in how confident they are.
factors.effect_size: Not pooled; unknown.
factors.clinical_significance: Unknown.
factors.sample_size: Mostly small studies.
factors.population: Selected vulnerable groups, not the general public.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Not the main concern; one review author has an industry advisory role.
factors.reproducibility: Limited.
factors.formulation_dose: Various forms and combination products.

claims.claim: Magnesium supplements lower blood pressure
claims.popular_framing: Magnesium is good for your blood pressure.
claims.question: Does magnesium lower blood pressure?
claims.outcome: Systolic and diastolic blood pressure
claims.population: Adults with and without high blood pressure; clearer effect in people with hypertension or low blood magnesium.
claims.bottom_line: Slightly, on average, mainly in people who already have high blood pressure or low magnesium. In people with normal blood pressure, trials did not find a significant effect.
claims.what_research_found: A 2025 meta-analysis of 38 trials (2,709 people) found magnesium lowered blood pressure by about 2.8/2.1 mmHg compared with placebo. Larger falls were seen in people with hypertension taking blood pressure medicine (systolic about 7.7 mmHg) and in people with low blood magnesium (about 6.0 mmHg). In people with normal blood pressure the change was not statistically significant. The NIH Office of Dietary Supplements describes the effect as marginal.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: No dose-response relationship was found, so higher doses were not shown to work better. The larger effect in treated hypertension was seen with magnesium taken alongside blood pressure medicine, not instead of it.
claims.limitations: High heterogeneity between studies; the authors advise interpreting results with caution.
claims.formulation_and_dose: 82.3–637 mg elemental magnesium daily (median 365 mg) for at least 4 weeks (median 12 weeks).

factors.study_quality: Randomised controlled trials, pooled.
factors.consistency: High heterogeneity between studies.
factors.effect_size: Small on average (about 2–3 mmHg).
factors.clinical_significance: Small for most people; larger only in specific groups.
factors.sample_size: 38 trials, 2,709 participants.
factors.population: Effect mainly in hypertension or low magnesium, not normal blood pressure.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: One meta-analysis author reports industry honoraria; not a major concern.
factors.reproducibility: Pattern also reported in earlier reviews summarised by NIH ODS.
factors.formulation_dose: Wide range of doses; no dose-response found.

research_doses.note: Daily doses in the sleep trials cited above: 250 mg elemental magnesium (bisglycinate) and 500 mg magnesium (older adults). Blood pressure trials used 82.3–637 mg elemental magnesium.

food_vs_supplement.comparison_note: An ounce (28 g) of pumpkin seeds (156 mg) plus a portion of beans or spinach supplies roughly as much magnesium as the lower doses used in sleep trials. Food and supplement amounts are not directly equivalent, because absorption differs between foods and supplement forms.
food_vs_supplement.food_advantages: Magnesium from food does not count towards the supplement upper limit, and food does not cause the diarrhoea linked to high supplement doses. Magnesium-rich foods also supply fibre and other nutrients.
food_vs_supplement.when_supplement_may_help: Research points to larger effects in people with low magnesium: blood pressure fell more in people with low blood magnesium, and a sleep trial hinted at more benefit in people with low dietary intake. Groups at higher risk of low magnesium include people with gut diseases, type 2 diabetes, alcohol dependence, older adults, and long-term users of some diuretics or proton pump inhibitors.

profiles.absorption: Forms that dissolve well in liquid are generally absorbed more completely. Aspartate, citrate, lactate and chloride forms appear more bioavailable than oxide and sulfate, based on small studies. Supplement labels list elemental magnesium, not the weight of the whole compound. Very high zinc intakes (142 mg/day) interfered with magnesium absorption in one study.
profiles.side_effects: High supplement doses often cause diarrhoea, nausea and stomach cramps; carbonate, chloride, gluconate and oxide forms are most often implicated. In the Cochrane cramp review, gastrointestinal side effects affected 11% to 37% of magnesium users vs 10% to 14% on control. Very large doses (over 5,000 mg/day, usually from laxatives or antacids) can cause toxicity, including low blood pressure, irregular heartbeat and, rarely, death.
profiles.interactions: Magnesium can reduce absorption of bisphosphonates and of tetracycline and quinolone antibiotics; NIH ODS says to separate bisphosphonates from magnesium by at least 2 hours, and to take these antibiotics at least 2 hours before or 4–6 hours after magnesium. Loop and thiazide diuretics increase magnesium loss; potassium-sparing diuretics reduce it. Long-term proton pump inhibitor use can cause low magnesium. Source: NIH ODS.
profiles.cautions: People with impaired kidney function are at higher risk of magnesium toxicity and should talk to a clinician first. Anyone taking the medicines listed under interactions should discuss magnesium with their prescriber.
profiles.upper_limit: 350 mg/day from supplements and medications for adults, including during pregnancy and breastfeeding. This limit does not include magnesium from food (NIH ODS).
profiles.research_doses_summary: Doses used in research: 250 mg elemental magnesium daily (bisglycinate, 4 weeks) and 500 mg daily (older adults, 8 weeks) in sleep trials; 1 g/day magnesium L-threonate compound (about 75 mg elemental magnesium) for 21 days; 82.3–637 mg elemental magnesium daily (median 365 mg) in blood pressure trials. Several of these exceed the 350 mg supplement upper limit. These are not recommendations.

sources.title: Oral magnesium supplementation for insomnia in older adults: a Systematic Review & Meta-Analysis.
sources.authors: Mah J, Pitre T
sources.population: Older adults with insomnia, in three countries
sources.intervention: Oral magnesium vs placebo (doses under 1 g, up to three times a day, per the authors' conclusion).
sources.findings: Pooled, people fell asleep 17.36 minutes faster after magnesium than placebo (95% CI -27.27 to -7.44). Total sleep time was 16.06 minutes longer but not statistically significant. All trials were at moderate-to-high risk of bias and evidence quality was low to very low. The authors say the literature is substandard for well-informed recommendations.
sources.limitations: Only three small trials; moderate-to-high risk of bias; low to very low quality evidence. An erratum was published in 2024.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract. Conflict statement: none declared.
sources.cited_for: magnesium-sleep-older-adults: pooled sleep-onset result and its low certainty.

sources.title: Magnesium Supplementation for Sleep in Adults: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials.
sources.authors: Lopresti AL, Smith SJ, Drummond PD
sources.sample_size: 12 RCTs on sleep, insomnia or poor sleep, plus 3 on movement- or cramp-related sleep disturbance (analysed separately)
sources.population: Adults
sources.intervention: Oral magnesium used alone (various forms and doses).
sources.findings: Twelve RCTs on sleep, insomnia or poor sleep were included in the main synthesis. Populations, forms, elemental doses, durations and outcome measures varied substantially, so results were combined narratively rather than pooled. Findings were inconsistent across self-reported outcomes, EEG, actigraphy, consumer wearables and physiological markers. Certainty of evidence was low to very low. The authors conclude current evidence does not support oral magnesium as a routine insomnia treatment; it may give modest benefits for some self-reported outcomes in some adults.
sources.limitations: Narrative synthesis (no pooled effect) because trials were too different; low to very low certainty (GRADE).
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: magnesium-sleep and magnesium-sleep-older-adults: the most recent overall review finds inconsistent, low-certainty evidence.

sources.title: Magnesium Bisglycinate Supplementation in Healthy Adults Reporting Poor Sleep: A Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Trial.
sources.authors: Schuster J, Cycelskij I, Lopresti A, Hahn A
sources.population: Adults aged 18–65 reporting poor sleep
sources.intervention: 250 mg elemental magnesium daily as magnesium bisglycinate vs placebo; outcome assessed at week 4.
sources.findings: Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) fell by 3.9 points with magnesium vs 2.3 points with placebo from baseline to week 4 (p = 0.049). The effect size was small (Cohen's d = 0.2). Exploratory analyses suggested greater improvements in people with lower dietary magnesium intake at baseline. No significant differences in other psychological outcomes. Pre-registered (DRKS00031494).
sources.limitations: Four-week primary comparison; self-reported sleep only; low-intake subgroup finding was exploratory.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract. Conflict statement: one author (Lopresti) directs a contract research organisation that receives funding from nutraceutical companies; others declare none.
sources.cited_for: magnesium-sleep: small effect of bisglycinate on insomnia severity; possible larger effect with low dietary intake.

sources.title: The effect of magnesium supplementation on primary insomnia in elderly: A double-blind placebo-controlled clinical trial.
sources.authors: Abbasi B, Kimiagar M, Sadeghniiat K, Shirazi MM, Hedayati M, Rashidkhani B
sources.population: Older adults with primary insomnia
sources.intervention: 500 mg magnesium daily vs placebo for 8 weeks.
sources.findings: Compared with placebo, magnesium improved Insomnia Severity Index score (P = 0.006), sleep time (P = 0.002), sleep efficiency (P = 0.03) and sleep onset latency (P = 0.02). Total sleep time did not differ significantly (P = 0.37). Serum melatonin and renin rose and serum cortisol fell.
sources.limitations: Small single trial; mostly self-reported sleep measures; the abstract does not specify the magnesium salt.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract. Conflict statement: none declared.
sources.cited_for: magnesium-sleep-older-adults: example of a small positive trial in older adults.

sources.title: Magnesium-L-threonate improves sleep quality and daytime functioning in adults with self-reported sleep problems: A randomized controlled trial.
sources.authors: Hausenblas HA, Lynch T, Hooper S, Shrestha A, Rosendale D, Gu J
sources.population: Adults aged 35–55 with self-reported sleep problems
sources.intervention: 1 g/day magnesium L-threonate (Magtein; about 75 mg elemental magnesium per gram, per the full text) vs placebo for 21 days; double-blind, parallel-arm.
sources.findings: The magnesium L-threonate group kept good sleep quality and daytime functioning while the placebo group declined. On Oura ring measures, deep sleep score, REM sleep score and several activity and readiness scores improved vs placebo (p < 0.05). Self-rated behaviour on waking, energy, productivity, mood and mental alertness also improved (p < 0.05). No effect sizes reported in the abstract. Reported as safe and well tolerated.
sources.limitations: Single short trial; industry-funded; sleep stages estimated by a consumer wearable, not polysomnography; no effect sizes in the abstract. An erratum has been published (PMID 40567408).
sources.funding: Funded by AIDP, Inc. (funding statement in the PMC full text); three of six authors list AIDP affiliations. The competing-interest statement is ambiguous. The test product was supplied by Threotech LLC.
sources.cited_for: magnesium-threonate-sleep: only trial found for this form.

verification.via: PubMed E-utilities; funding, competing-interest and methods sections checked in the PMC full text (PMC11381753) during the findings check

sources.title: Examining the Effects of Supplemental Magnesium on Self-Reported Anxiety and Sleep Quality: A Systematic Review.
sources.authors: Rawji A, Peltier MR, Mourtzanakis K, Awan S, Rana J, Pothen NJ, Afzal S
sources.sample_size: 15 studies (the abstract reports 8 on sleep, 7 on anxiety and 1 on both)
sources.population: Interventional trials in anxiety and sleep disorders
sources.intervention: Varied magnesium doses (at least 50 mg), forms and durations; some studies included other active ingredients.
sources.findings: Five of eight sleep studies reported improvements, two found none and one was mixed. Five of seven anxiety studies reported improvements in self-reported anxiety. Firm conclusions were limited by heterogeneity, small samples and differing doses, forms and durations. The authors call for larger randomised trials and suggest benefits may be most likely in people with low magnesium status.
sources.limitations: PubMed-only search; vote-counting without pooled effect sizes; small studies; some combination products.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract. Conflict statement: none declared.
sources.cited_for: magnesium-sleep and magnesium-anxiety: mixed, small studies.

sources.title: The Effects of Magnesium Supplementation on Subjective Anxiety and Stress-A Systematic Review.
sources.authors: Boyle NB, Lawton C, Dye L
sources.population: Samples with existing vulnerability to anxiety: mildly anxious, premenstrual syndrome, postpartum, hypertension
sources.intervention: Magnesium alone or with up to 5 other ingredients.
sources.findings: Four of eight studies in anxious samples, four of seven in premenstrual syndrome samples and one of two in hypertensive samples reported positive effects on subjective anxiety. No effect on postpartum anxiety. No study used a validated measure of stress. The authors describe the evidence as suggestive but of poor quality.
sources.limitations: Poor-quality evidence; combination products included; no validated stress outcome.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract. One author sits on a Sanofi Consumer Healthcare advisory board (Sanofi had no role in the review).
sources.cited_for: magnesium-anxiety: suggestive but poor-quality evidence; no stress data.

sources.title: Magnesium for skeletal muscle cramps.
sources.authors: Garrison SR, Korownyk CS, Kolber MR, Allan GM, Musini VM, Sekhon RK, Dugré N
sources.population: Idiopathic cramps (mostly older adults, mean age 61.6–69.3), pregnancy-associated leg cramps, liver cirrhosis
sources.intervention: Magnesium in any form, mostly oral; compared with placebo, no treatment or other therapies.
sources.findings: For idiopathic cramps in older adults, magnesium did not meaningfully reduce cramp frequency vs placebo: -0.18 cramps/week (95% CI -0.84 to 0.49; 5 studies, 307 participants; moderate certainty). The share of people with a 25% or better reduction did not differ (RR 1.04; high certainty). No difference in cramp intensity or duration. For pregnancy-associated cramps results conflicted. No trials were found for exercise-associated cramps. Gastrointestinal side effects such as diarrhoea affected 11% to 37% of magnesium users (vs 10% to 14% on control).
sources.limitations: Few trials outside older adults; pregnancy trials at high risk of bias.
sources.funding: Cochrane review; PubMed lists a grant from CIHR (Canada). Conflict statement: one author wrote an included study.
sources.cited_for: magnesium-cramps: evidence against for older adults; no trials for exercise cramps; side-effect rates.

sources.title: Magnesium Supplementation and Blood Pressure: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
sources.authors: Argeros Z, Xu X, Bhandari B, Harris K, Touyz RM, Schutte AE
sources.population: Hypertensive and normotensive adults
sources.intervention: Elemental magnesium 82.3–637 mg/day (median 365 mg) for at least 4 weeks (median 12 weeks).
sources.findings: Magnesium lowered systolic blood pressure by 2.81 mmHg (95% CI -4.32 to -1.29) and diastolic by 2.05 mmHg (95% CI -3.23 to -0.88) vs placebo. Reductions were larger in people with hypertension on blood pressure medication (systolic -7.68 mmHg) and in people with low blood magnesium (systolic -5.97 mmHg). In people with normal blood pressure the effect was not statistically significant. No dose-response relationship was found. Heterogeneity was high.
sources.limitations: High heterogeneity between studies; authors advise caution.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract. One author reports industry speaker honoraria and advisory roles; others none.
sources.cited_for: magnesium-blood-pressure: size of effect, who benefits, and no effect in normal blood pressure.

sources.title: Magnesium: Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
sources.authors: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements
sources.findings: Gives RDAs (adult men 400–420 mg, women 310–320 mg), a food-content table, and a Tolerable Upper Intake Level of 350 mg/day for magnesium from supplements and medications only (not food). Says aspartate, citrate, lactate and chloride forms appear more bioavailable than oxide and sulfate, based on small studies. High supplement doses often cause diarrhoea, nausea and cramping; toxicity risk rises with impaired kidney function. Lists interactions with bisphosphonates, tetracycline and quinolone antibiotics, diuretics and proton pump inhibitors. Describes the blood pressure effect of supplements as marginal (a Cochrane review found a 2.2 mmHg diastolic reduction; a meta-analysis found 3–4 mmHg systolic and 2–3 mmHg diastolic). Lists groups at risk of low magnesium: gastrointestinal disease, type 2 diabetes, alcohol dependence and older adults. Does not discuss sleep.
sources.limitations: Authoritative summary, not a primary study.
sources.funding: US government (NIH)
sources.cited_for: Food content, RDA, upper limit, forms, safety, interactions, at-risk groups, blood pressure context.

profiles.name: Melatonin
profiles.summary: Melatonin helps reduce jet lag when timed well and may shift sleep earlier in people with a diagnosed late body clock, but for everyday insomnia it helps people fall asleep only a few minutes faster at best, and it has not been shown to be an effective treatment for chronic insomnia.
profiles.description: Melatonin is a hormone the brain makes in response to darkness. Most supplements are synthetic. In the US it is sold as a dietary supplement; in several other countries it is prescription-only.
profiles.biological_function: Melatonin helps set the body's circadian rhythm, the internal clock that tells the body when it is night. Taken as a supplement, it has been used to re-align the body clock with local time. In jet lag research, timing mattered: taken early in the day it caused sleepiness and delayed adjustment, while doses from 0.5 to 5 mg worked similarly. Its other roles in the body are not fully understood.

formulations.name: Immediate-release melatonin
formulations.notes: Used in most jet lag trials at 0.5–5 mg. The Cochrane review suggests a short-lived higher peak works better for jet lag than slow release.

formulations.name: Prolonged-release melatonin
formulations.notes: Most tested in adult insomnia trials, with small effects. A 2 mg slow-release form was relatively ineffective for jet lag.

formulations.name: Gummies
formulations.notes: In a 2023 study summarised by NIH NCCIH, 22 of 25 gummy products were inaccurately labelled.

claims.claim: Melatonin helps people with sleep problems fall asleep faster
claims.popular_framing: Take melatonin and you'll be asleep in no time.
claims.question: Does melatonin help you fall asleep faster?
claims.outcome: Time to fall asleep (sleep onset latency)
claims.population: Adults (and in some reviews, children) with insomnia or primary sleep disorders.
claims.bottom_line: Slightly. On average, melatonin helped people fall asleep about 5 to 7 minutes faster than a placebo. That is far less than its reputation suggests.
claims.what_research_found: A 2013 meta-analysis of 19 studies (1,683 people) found melatonin cut the time to fall asleep by about 7 minutes and added about 8 minutes of sleep. A 2023 meta-analysis in adults with insomnia found prolonged-release melatonin shortened time to fall asleep by about 5 to 6 minutes. Higher doses and longer use showed somewhat larger effects in the 2013 review.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It is not shown that melatonin produces a large or reliably noticeable change in how fast most people fall asleep. A 2022 review found no significant effect on sleep onset in adults with chronic insomnia.
claims.limitations: Effects are measured in minutes. Reviews mix ages, doses and release types, and disagree on whether the small effect in adults is statistically significant.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Various doses; the 2023 adult review mostly tested prolonged-release melatonin.

factors.study_quality: Many randomised, placebo-controlled trials.
factors.consistency: Direction mostly consistent, but one review found no significant effect in adults.
factors.effect_size: Small: about 5–7 minutes.
factors.clinical_significance: Low. A few minutes faster is unlikely to feel meaningful; this kept the rating below Level 4.
factors.sample_size: Thousands of participants across reviews.
factors.population: Mostly people with diagnosed sleep problems; little data in healthy good sleepers.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: One review was partly funded by Eli Lilly-sponsored fellowships (alongside NIH grants); not a major concern.
factors.reproducibility: Two of three reviews found a small, statistically significant effect; one found no significant effect in adults.
factors.formulation_dose: Immediate- and prolonged-release forms at various doses; results may differ by product.

claims.claim: Melatonin is an effective treatment for chronic insomnia in adults
claims.popular_framing: Melatonin is a natural sleeping pill for insomnia.
claims.question: Does melatonin work as a treatment for chronic insomnia?
claims.outcome: Overall insomnia improvement and self-rated sleep quality
claims.population: Adults with chronic insomnia disorder.
claims.bottom_line: Not shown in any meaningful way. Reviews disagree: some find small benefits of a few minutes, mainly with prolonged-release melatonin, while others find no significant effect, and US sleep and physician bodies found the evidence insufficient to recommend it for chronic insomnia.
claims.what_research_found: A 2022 network meta-analysis of 154 double-blind trials (44,089 people, all drugs combined) concluded melatonin 'did not show overall material benefits' for adult insomnia. A 2022 review of 24 trials found no significant improvement in sleep onset, total sleep time or sleep efficiency in adults with chronic insomnia. In contrast, a 2023 meta-analysis found prolonged-release melatonin shortened time to fall asleep by about 5 to 6 minutes and slightly improved sleep efficiency (by about 2 to 3 percentage points), with a larger effect on sleep efficiency where the average age was 55 or over. NIH's NCCIH reports that the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the American College of Physicians found insufficient evidence to recommend it, and that the College recommends cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia first.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It has not been shown that melatonin works as an effective treatment for chronic insomnia. The small effects some reviews report (a few minutes faster to fall asleep, slightly better sleep efficiency) are too small to count as an effective treatment, but the evidence does not show that melatonin has no effect at all.
claims.limitations: Many trials tested prolonged-release melatonin; results for other products and doses may differ. Reviews differ on whether the small effects reach statistical significance.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Mostly prolonged-release melatonin at various doses in adult insomnia trials.

factors.study_quality: Large body of double-blind randomised trials.
factors.consistency: Inconsistent: one meta-analysis finds small significant effects of prolonged-release melatonin, another finds no significant effect in adults, and the network meta-analysis finds no material benefit.
factors.effect_size: Small to none: a few minutes for sleep onset; about 2 to 3 percentage points for sleep efficiency.
factors.clinical_significance: Not clinically meaningful as an insomnia treatment.
factors.sample_size: The network meta-analysis included 44,089 participants across all drugs (the abstract does not give the melatonin share); the 2023 review included 925 people given melatonin.
factors.population: Adults with insomnia disorder; children may respond differently.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: The network meta-analysis was publicly funded (UK NIHR); some of its authors report industry fees or employment.
factors.reproducibility: Reviews disagree on whether any effect is real; guideline bodies found the evidence insufficient to recommend melatonin.
factors.formulation_dose: Mostly prolonged-release products.

claims.claim: Melatonin reduces jet lag
claims.popular_framing: Pop a melatonin on a long-haul flight to beat jet lag.
claims.question: Does melatonin help with jet lag?
claims.outcome: Jet lag symptoms after crossing time zones
claims.population: Air travellers, airline staff and military personnel crossing several time zones.
claims.bottom_line: Yes, for many travellers, when taken at the right time. Trials found it reduced jet lag after crossing five or more time zones, especially flying east.
claims.what_research_found: A Cochrane review found 9 of 10 trials showed melatonin taken close to bedtime at the destination (10pm to midnight) reduced jet lag after flights crossing five or more time zones. The number needed to treat was 2: for every two travellers who took it, one more had relief than would have with placebo. Doses of 0.5 to 5 mg worked similarly, though 5 mg helped people fall asleep faster. Doses above 5 mg were no more effective.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: Benefits for shorter trips (2–4 time zones) and westward flights are less clear. Long-term safety of repeated use is not established.
claims.limitations: The Cochrane review dates from 2002, and its abstract does not report trial sizes; the later studies NCCIH cites are small (142 travellers for eastward and 90 for westward flights). Timing matters: taken early in the day, melatonin can cause sleepiness and delay adjustment.
claims.formulation_and_dose: 0.5–5 mg taken close to target bedtime at the destination. A 2 mg slow-release form was relatively ineffective.

factors.study_quality: Randomised placebo-controlled trials; 9 of 10 judged adequate quality.
factors.consistency: Consistent: 9 of 10 trials positive.
factors.effect_size: Large for a supplement (number needed to treat 2).
factors.clinical_significance: Noticeable reduction in jet lag symptoms.
factors.sample_size: Ten trials; NCCIH cites 142 travellers for eastward and 90 for westward flights in later reviews.
factors.population: Travellers crossing many time zones; matches the popular claim.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Not stated in abstract.
factors.reproducibility: Multiple independent trials; also summarised positively by NIH NCCIH.
factors.formulation_dose: Immediate-release 0.5–5 mg; slow-release 2 mg worked less well.

claims.claim: Melatonin shifts sleep earlier in people with delayed sleep phase
claims.popular_framing: Night owl? Melatonin can reset your body clock.
claims.question: Can melatonin shift a late body clock earlier?
claims.outcome: Timing of sleep onset and body-clock (melatonin) rhythm
claims.population: People diagnosed with delayed sleep phase disorder (adults and children).
claims.bottom_line: In people diagnosed with delayed sleep phase disorder, melatonin moved sleep earlier by about 40 minutes and helped them fall asleep faster. It has not been shown to do this for ordinary night owls.
claims.what_research_found: A 2010 meta-analysis (5 trials in 91 adults, 4 trials in 226 children) found melatonin moved sleep onset 0.67 hours earlier and cut time to fall asleep by about 23 minutes. Wake-up time and total sleep did not change significantly. NCCIH reports a 2018 trial of 307 people in which people fell asleep about 34 minutes earlier on average.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: Benefits for people without a diagnosed circadian rhythm disorder are not established. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine's recommendation for this use is weak.
claims.limitations: Few and small adult trials; wide confidence interval for time to fall asleep (about 5 to 42 minutes).
claims.formulation_and_dose: Melatonin vs placebo; doses and timing varied across trials.

factors.study_quality: Randomised placebo-controlled trials.
factors.consistency: Pooled results point the same way for sleep timing; the abstract does not report how much individual trials differed.
factors.effect_size: Moderate: sleep onset about 40 minutes earlier.
factors.clinical_significance: Likely noticeable for people with this disorder.
factors.sample_size: Only 91 adults in the meta-analysis; one larger trial reported by NCCIH.
factors.population: Diagnosed delayed sleep phase disorder only.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Not stated in abstract.
factors.reproducibility: Supported by a later trial summarised by NCCIH.
factors.formulation_dose: Doses and timing differ between trials.

profiles.absorption: For jet lag, doses of 0.5 to 5 mg worked similarly, and doses above 5 mg were no more effective. A 2 mg slow-release product worked relatively poorly for jet lag, suggesting a short, higher peak works better for shifting the body clock. Product content is unreliable: one analysis of 31 supplements found melatonin ranged from 83% below to 478% above the label, and a 2023 study of gummies found 74% to 347% of the stated amount.
profiles.side_effects: Short-term use appears safe for most adults. Reported side effects are usually mild: headache, dizziness, nausea and sleepiness. Taken at the wrong time of day, melatonin can cause daytime sleepiness and delay adjustment to a new time zone. Long-term safety information is lacking.
profiles.interactions: Case reports suggest people taking warfarin (a blood thinner) may come to harm, and NIH NCCIH advises medical supervision for people taking blood thinners. Anyone on regular medicines should check with a clinician first.
profiles.cautions: People with epilepsy, people taking blood thinners, pregnant or breastfeeding women (safety research is lacking), and older adults with dementia (a 2015 American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline recommends against use) should talk to a clinician first. Children: NIH NCCIH reports rising poison-centre calls and emergency visits from accidental ingestion by young children; keep products out of reach. Some products contain serotonin or far more melatonin than labelled.
profiles.research_doses_summary: Doses used in research: 0.5–5 mg taken close to target bedtime at the destination for jet lag (doses above 5 mg were no more effective); various doses, mostly prolonged-release, in adult insomnia trials. These are not recommendations.

sources.title: Melatonin for the prevention and treatment of jet lag.
sources.authors: Herxheimer A, Petrie KJ
sources.population: Airline passengers, airline staff and military personnel
sources.intervention: Oral melatonin 0.5–5 mg (some higher) taken close to target bedtime at the destination vs placebo; one trial also vs zolpidem.
sources.findings: Nine of ten trials found melatonin taken close to target bedtime at the destination (10pm to midnight) reduced jet lag after flights crossing five or more time zones. Doses of 0.5–5 mg were similarly effective, though people fell asleep faster and slept better after 5 mg than 0.5 mg; doses above 5 mg appeared no more effective. 2 mg slow-release melatonin was relatively ineffective. Number needed to treat was 2. Benefit is likely greater with more time zones and less for westward flights. Taken at the wrong time (early in the day), it can cause sleepiness and delay adaptation. Other side effects were uncommon; case reports suggest people with epilepsy and those taking warfarin may come to harm.
sources.limitations: Review is from 2002; the abstract does not report trial sizes; no newer Cochrane update was found.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract.
sources.cited_for: melatonin-jet-lag: effect, timing, dose range; safety notes on epilepsy and warfarin.

sources.title: Meta-analysis: melatonin for the treatment of primary sleep disorders.
sources.authors: Ferracioli-Oda E, Qawasmi A, Bloch MH
sources.population: Adults and children with primary sleep disorders
sources.intervention: Melatonin vs placebo; various doses and durations.
sources.findings: Melatonin reduced time to fall asleep by 7.06 minutes (95% CI 4.37 to 9.75) and increased total sleep time by 8.25 minutes (95% CI 1.74 to 14.75). Overall sleep quality improved slightly (standardised mean difference 0.22). Longer trials and higher doses showed greater effects on sleep onset and total sleep time. The authors call the effects modest and smaller than other insomnia medicines, but note they did not fade with continued use.
sources.limitations: PubMed-only search; mixes adults and children.
sources.funding: Partly funded by Eli Lilly-sponsored research fellowships to one author (competing-interest statement); PubMed also lists NIH grants (NIMH, NCRR).
sources.cited_for: melatonin-sleep-onset: size of the effect on falling asleep.

sources.title: Efficacy of melatonin and ramelteon for the acute and long-term management of insomnia disorder in adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.authors: Maruani J, Reynaud E, Chambe J, Palagini L, Bourgin P, Geoffroy PA
sources.population: Adults with insomnia disorder
sources.intervention: Mostly prolonged-release melatonin vs placebo; also ramelteon (a prescription melatonin-receptor drug).
sources.findings: Prolonged-release melatonin shortened self-reported time to fall asleep by 6.30 minutes and objectively measured time by 5.05 minutes, and raised objective sleep efficiency by 1.91%, described as small to medium effects. In trials where the mean age was 55 or over, the effect on sleep efficiency was larger (2.95%).
sources.limitations: Most studies tested short-term prolonged-release melatonin; effects measured in minutes.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract.
sources.cited_for: melatonin-sleep-onset and melatonin-insomnia: small effects of prolonged-release melatonin in adults with insomnia.

sources.title: Efficacy of melatonin for chronic insomnia: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses.
sources.authors: Choi K, Lee YJ, Park S, Je NK, Suh HS
sources.population: People with chronic insomnia (adults, children and adolescents); 4 studies of comorbid insomnia
sources.intervention: Melatonin vs placebo.
sources.findings: In adults with chronic insomnia (without other conditions), melatonin did not significantly improve sleep onset latency, total sleep time or sleep efficiency. It was effective for sleep onset and total sleep time in children and adolescents. The authors conclude melatonin did not appear effective in adults with chronic insomnia.
sources.limitations: High heterogeneity led to subgroup analyses by age.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract. Conflict statement: none.
sources.cited_for: melatonin-insomnia: no significant benefit in adults with chronic insomnia.

sources.title: Comparative effects of pharmacological interventions for the acute and long-term management of insomnia disorder in adults: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
sources.authors: De Crescenzo F, D'Alò GL, Ostinelli EG, et al.
sources.sample_size: 170 trials, 47,950 participants (154 trials, 44,089 participants in the network analysis)
sources.population: Adults with insomnia disorder
sources.intervention: 36 drug treatments, including melatonin, compared with placebo and each other.
sources.findings: Several prescription drugs (e.g. eszopiclone, zolpidem, benzodiazepines) improved self-rated sleep quality more than melatonin. The authors conclude that melatonin, ramelteon and non-licensed drugs 'did not show overall material benefits'.
sources.limitations: Network meta-analysis; certainty for many comparisons ranged from high to very low, and the abstract gives no melatonin-versus-placebo estimate.
sources.funding: UK National Institute for Health Research Oxford Health Biomedical Research Centre. Some authors report industry fees or employment.
sources.cited_for: melatonin-insomnia: no material benefit as an insomnia treatment in adults.

sources.title: The use of exogenous melatonin in delayed sleep phase disorder: a meta-analysis.
sources.authors: van Geijlswijk IM, Korzilius HP, Smits MG
sources.sample_size: 9 RCTs: 5 trials with 91 adults and 4 trials with 226 children
sources.population: People diagnosed with delayed sleep phase disorder
sources.intervention: Melatonin vs placebo.
sources.findings: Melatonin moved the body's own melatonin onset 1.18 hours earlier and clock time of sleep onset 0.67 hours earlier. Time to fall asleep fell by 23.27 minutes (95% CI 4.83 to 41.72). Wake-up time and total sleep time did not change significantly.
sources.limitations: Small trials, especially in adults; wide confidence interval.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract.
sources.cited_for: melatonin-delayed-sleep-phase: shifting sleep timing earlier.

sources.title: Melatonin Natural Health Products and Supplements: Presence of Serotonin and Significant Variability of Melatonin Content.
sources.authors: Erland LA, Saxena PK
sources.population: Commercial melatonin supplements of different brands and forms
sources.intervention: Laboratory analysis of product content.
sources.findings: Melatonin content ranged from 83% less to 478% more than the label. Lot-to-lot variation within a product reached 465%. More than 71% of products were not within 10% of their label claim, and 8 products contained serotonin.
sources.limitations: Product testing, not a health outcome study; products from one market and time.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract.
sources.cited_for: Product quality and label accuracy (cautions).

sources.title: Melatonin: What You Need To Know
sources.authors: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health
sources.journal: NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health
sources.findings: Summarises research: melatonin may reduce jet lag (4 studies, 142 travellers, eastward; 2 studies, 90 travellers, westward). For delayed sleep-wake phase disorder, a 2018 trial of 307 people found people fell asleep about 34 minutes earlier on average; the American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2015 recommendation was weak. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (2017) and American College of Physicians (2016) found insufficient strong evidence to recommend melatonin for chronic insomnia. Short-term use appears safe for most people, with mild side effects (headache, dizziness, nausea, sleepiness); long-term safety information is lacking. Research on pregnancy and breastfeeding is lacking. People with epilepsy or taking blood thinners need medical supervision. A 2017 study found most of 31 supplements did not match their label; a 2023 study found 22 of 25 gummy products inaccurately labelled (74% to 347% of the stated amount, one with none). In the US melatonin is a dietary supplement; in several other countries it is prescription-only. Page last updated May 2024.
sources.limitations: Authoritative summary, not a primary study.
sources.funding: US government (NIH)
sources.cited_for: Jet lag summary, delayed sleep phase trial, insomnia guideline positions, safety, interactions, label accuracy, regulatory status.

profiles.name: Protein powder (whey & plant)
profiles.summary: Protein powder modestly helps training gains when total protein is low, soy works about as well as whey, and you don't need powder at all if food gets you enough protein.
profiles.description: Protein powders are concentrated protein from milk (whey, casein) or plants (soy, pea, rice and others). They are a convenient way to add protein to the diet. Most powders on the market contain whey (NIH ODS).
profiles.biological_function: Protein supplies amino acids that muscles use to build and repair tissue. Resistance exercise and protein intake both stimulate muscle protein synthesis, and they work together when protein is eaten around training (ISSN). Leucine and other essential amino acids are key triggers.

formulations.name: Whey (concentrate, isolate)
formulations.notes: A complete milk protein that is quickly digested and higher in leucine than casein or soy (NIH ODS).

formulations.name: Casein
formulations.notes: The main milk protein; digests more slowly than whey (NIH ODS).

formulations.name: Soy protein
formulations.notes: Long-term trials show similar muscle and strength gains to whey; a larger serving may be needed to match whey's leucine.

formulations.name: Other plant proteins (pea, rice, oat, potato) and blends
formulations.notes: Few trials. Non-soy single plant proteins have limited evidence; a soy-pea blend matched whey in one trial. Many products combine sources to cover all essential amino acids (NIH ODS).

claims.claim: Protein supplements add to muscle and strength gains from resistance training in healthy adults
claims.popular_framing: Protein shakes help you build more muscle from your workouts.
claims.question: Does protein powder help you gain more muscle and strength when you train?
claims.outcome: Strength (1RM), fat-free mass, muscle size
claims.population: Healthy adults doing resistance training for 6 weeks or more.
claims.bottom_line: Yes, modestly. Protein supplements taken during training added a little more strength and muscle on average. Extra muscle gain levelled off once total daily protein reached about 1.6 g per kg of body weight.
claims.what_research_found: A meta-analysis of 49 trials (1,863 people) found protein supplements added about 2.5 kg to 1RM strength and 0.3 kg to fat-free mass, with larger muscle fibre size. The benefit was bigger in trained people and smaller in older people. Fat-free mass gains stopped increasing above a total protein intake of about 1.62 g/kg/day.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It did not show a large effect: on average the extra gain is small. A 2026 meta-analysis in 18–30-year-olds (12 trials, 261 people) found no significant effect on lean mass, though whey improved strength.
claims.limitations: Effects are modest and vary between studies. One author of the main meta-analysis has dairy-industry funding ties. Benefits depend on total daily protein, not on the powder itself.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Dietary protein supplements during at least 6 weeks of resistance training; the meta-analysis abstract does not list protein types or serving sizes. Fat-free mass gains levelled off at a total intake of about 1.6 g/kg/day.

factors.study_quality: Randomised controlled trials pooled in a large meta-analysis with meta-regression.
factors.consistency: Generally positive, but a smaller 2026 meta-analysis in young adults found no significant lean-mass effect.
factors.effect_size: Modest: about 2.5 kg strength and 0.3 kg fat-free mass on average.
factors.clinical_significance: Small but real for people training regularly; less for older adults.
factors.sample_size: 1,863 participants in 49 trials.
factors.population: Healthy adults; larger effect in trained people, smaller with age.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Main meta-analysis has an author with US National Dairy Council support.
factors.reproducibility: Based on 49 trials pooled in one large meta-analysis; a smaller 2026 meta-analysis agreed on strength (whey) but not on lean mass.
factors.formulation_dose: The meta-analysis abstract does not give protein types or doses, so how closely they match common powders cannot be confirmed from what was read.

claims.claim: Protein powder builds more muscle than getting the same amount of protein from food
claims.popular_framing: If you're not drinking protein shakes, you won't build muscle.
claims.question: Do you need protein powder to build muscle, or does protein from food work just as well?
claims.outcome: Muscle gain with resistance training: protein powder vs the same amount of protein from food
claims.population: Healthy, exercising adults.
claims.bottom_line: There is no evidence that powder works better than food. No trial we read compared protein powder with the same amount of protein from ordinary food. The research we did read points to total daily protein and training as what matters, and NIH ODS says athletes can usually meet their protein needs through food.
claims.what_research_found: No study read compared powder with an equal amount of protein from whole food. Indirect evidence: in the largest meta-analysis (49 trials), extra fat-free mass from protein supplements levelled off once total daily intake reached about 1.6 g/kg, which points to total intake rather than the form it comes in. NIH ODS states athletes can usually meet protein needs through food, and that eating more than recommended gives no added benefit. The ISSN position stand says active people can get their daily protein from whole foods, while noting supplements are a practical way to get enough protein while limiting calories.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: No trial has directly compared powder with the same amount of protein from food, so whether powder is better, worse or the same has not been tested directly. Nothing in the sources read suggests powder is required to build muscle.
claims.limitations: This rating reflects a gap in direct trials, not evidence that powder is needed. The indirect evidence (the total-intake plateau, and NIH ODS and ISSN statements) consistently points to total protein, not powder, as what matters. The ISSN notes supplements can be a practical way to reach a protein target.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Total daily protein figures given by NIH ODS (about 1.2–2.0 g/kg for athletes) and the ISSN (1.4–2.0 g/kg), from food, supplements or both.

factors.study_quality: No head-to-head trials. Indirect evidence from a large meta-analysis of RCTs (supplement vs no supplement), plus NIH ODS and ISSN statements.
factors.consistency: The indirect sources agree that food can meet protein needs.
factors.effect_size: Not measured for powder vs food. The supplement benefit for fat-free mass levelled off above about 1.6 g/kg/day total intake.
factors.clinical_significance: The sources read point to adequate total protein, from any source, as what matters.
factors.sample_size: No direct trials; 1,863 participants in the indirect meta-analysis.
factors.population: Healthy exercising adults.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Several ISSN position-stand authors are affiliated with companies, including a supplement maker; one meta-analysis author has US National Dairy Council support; NIH ODS is a government source.
factors.reproducibility: Not applicable: no direct trials to replicate.
factors.formulation_dose: Concerns total protein regardless of form.

claims.claim: Soy protein (alone or blended with pea) supports muscle and strength gains as well as whey or other animal protein
claims.popular_framing: Plant protein is inferior to whey for building muscle.
claims.question: Is soy or a soy-based plant blend as good as whey?
claims.outcome: Lean mass, muscle size and strength with resistance training
claims.population: Adults; the individual trials were in untrained young adults doing resistance training.
claims.bottom_line: Yes, for soy. Long-term trials find soy, and a soy-pea blend, produce similar muscle and strength gains to whey.
claims.what_research_found: A 2025 meta-analysis found no difference between soy and milk protein for muscle mass (17 trials). A 2018 meta-analysis of 9 studies found soy produced similar strength and lean mass gains to whey and other animal proteins. In a 12-week trial, leucine-matched soy (26 g) and whey (19 g) gave similar gains in lean mass and leg strength, with no significant differences. A 2025 trial found a soy-pea blend matched whey at 45 g/day.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: Short-term lab studies show whey stimulates muscle protein synthesis more than soy, likely because of its leucine content; long-term trials did not find that this changed outcomes.
claims.limitations: The two individual trials were 12 weeks long in untrained young people; the meta-analysis abstracts give few details on duration, training status or doses, and the 2025 meta-analysis abstract does not say whether its trials included resistance training. Some trials matched leucine by giving more soy protein than whey.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Soy isolate about 26 g (matched to 19 g whey for 2 g leucine); soy-pea blend 15 g three times daily; with training 3 times a week for about 12 weeks.

factors.study_quality: Randomised trials and two meta-analyses.
factors.consistency: Consistent: no meaningful difference in long-term outcomes.
factors.effect_size: Differences near zero (SMD −0.02 soy vs milk).
factors.clinical_significance: Soy users can expect similar results to whey users.
factors.sample_size: 17 RCTs in the 2025 soy-milk comparison; 266 participants in the 2018 meta-analysis.
factors.population: Adults; the individual trials were in untrained young people.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: The blend trial was funded by a plant-based food company (no role in analysis); others declared none or not stated.
factors.reproducibility: Seen in two meta-analyses from different groups and in two trials; two authors of the 2018 meta-analysis also ran the 2020 leucine-matched trial.
factors.formulation_dose: Doses comparable to a typical scoop; leucine matching may need a larger soy serving.

claims.claim: Non-soy single plant proteins (such as rice, oat or potato) build muscle as well as animal protein
claims.popular_framing: Any plant protein powder works just as well as whey.
claims.question: Are rice, oat or potato proteins as good as whey?
claims.outcome: Muscle mass
claims.population: Adults in randomised trials comparing protein sources.
claims.bottom_line: Not shown. The few trials available favour animal protein over non-soy plant proteins for muscle mass, but there are too few studies to be sure.
claims.what_research_found: A 2025 meta-analysis found animal protein produced more muscle mass than non-soy plant proteins such as rice, chia, oat and potato (SMD −0.58), based on only 5 trials. Across all plant proteins, there was no difference for strength. NIH ODS notes many products combine protein sources to cover all essential amino acids.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It is not established that these proteins are inferior in all situations, or how blends of them compare.
claims.limitations: Only 5 trials; wide confidence interval; varied protein types.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Rice, chia, oat and potato proteins compared with animal protein; doses varied (not detailed in the abstract).

factors.study_quality: Randomised trials within a registered meta-analysis.
factors.consistency: Few trials; direction favours animal protein for muscle mass but not strength.
factors.effect_size: Moderate (SMD −0.58) but uncertain.
factors.clinical_significance: Unclear in practice.
factors.sample_size: Only 5 trials.
factors.population: Mixed adult populations.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Authors declare none.
factors.reproducibility: Not yet well replicated.
factors.formulation_dose: Single-source plant powders; blends may differ.

foods.food: Tuna, white, canned in oil, drained

research_doses.note: Per serving in trials and position stands: 15 g three times daily (soy-pea vs whey trial), 19 g whey or 26 g soy (leucine-matched trial), 20–40 g or 0.25 g/kg per serving and 1.4–2.0 g/kg a day in total (ISSN position-stand figures, not trial doses); benefit plateaued at about 1.6 g/kg/day.

food_vs_supplement.comparison_note: A 3-oz serving of meat or fish provides about 22–26 g of protein, similar to a typical research serving of powder (15–40 g). NIH ODS gives athletes' needs as about 1.2–2.0 g/kg a day (about 75–135 g for a 150-lb person), which food alone can usually supply.
food_vs_supplement.food_advantages: Whole foods provide protein along with other nutrients. NIH ODS notes athletes can usually meet protein needs through food, and eating a variety of plant foods is one way to get all essential amino acids.
food_vs_supplement.when_supplement_may_help: Research benefits were seen in people doing resistance training, and extra protein stopped adding fat-free mass above a total intake of about 1.6 g/kg/day. The ISSN notes supplements are a practical way to get enough protein while limiting calories.

profiles.absorption: Whey is digested quickly and is high in leucine; casein digests more slowly (NIH ODS). Acute studies show whey stimulates muscle protein synthesis more than soy or casein, likely due to leucine, but long-term trials show similar gains with soy. The ISSN notes rapidly digested proteins high in essential amino acids and leucine best stimulate muscle protein synthesis, with servings spread every 3–4 hours.
profiles.side_effects: NIH ODS notes that high-protein diets (two to three times the RDA) do not appear to harm kidneys or bones in healthy people, though long-term data are limited, and that high protein intakes appear quite safe but eating more than recommended gives no added benefit.
profiles.interactions: No specific drug interactions were described in the sources read for this profile.
profiles.cautions: NIH ODS notes high-protein diets do not appear to harm kidneys or bones in healthy people, but long-term data are limited; people with kidney disease should speak to a clinician. Whey and casein come from milk, so people with milk allergy should check the source.
profiles.upper_limit: No Tolerable Upper Intake Level set for protein (NIH ODS).
profiles.research_doses_summary: Doses used in research: protein servings of about 15–40 g, often taken around training, with total daily intakes of about 1.2–2.0 g/kg. In a large meta-analysis, extra protein stopped adding muscle above a total intake of about 1.6 g/kg/day.

sources.title: A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults.
sources.authors: Morton RW, Murphy KT, McKellar SR, Schoenfeld BJ, Henselmans M, Helms E, Aragon AA, Devries MC, Banfield L, Krieger JW, Phillips SM.
sources.population: Healthy adults doing resistance training for at least 6 weeks
sources.intervention: Dietary protein supplementation vs control during resistance training
sources.findings: Protein supplementation increased gains in 1RM strength (2.49 kg, 95% CI 0.64–4.33), fat-free mass (0.30 kg, 95% CI 0.09–0.52) and muscle fibre and mid-femur cross-sectional area. The effect on fat-free mass fell with increasing age and was larger in resistance-trained people (0.75 kg). Beyond a total protein intake of 1.62 g/kg/day, there were no further gains in fat-free mass.
sources.limitations: Effects are modest; an erratum was published in 2020.
sources.funding: One author (Phillips) has received grants, travel and honoraria from the US National Dairy Council, which supported some included trials.
sources.cited_for: protein-training-gains and protein-powder-necessary: size of benefit and the ~1.6 g/kg/day plateau.

sources.title: The Impact of Whey and Soy Protein Supplementation on Resistance Training in Young Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
sources.authors: Davis BE, Young I, Giglotti JC, Yao J, Tou JC.
sources.population: Trained or untrained young adults aged 18–30 doing resistance training
sources.intervention: Whey or soy protein (concentrate or isolate)
sources.findings: No significant effect of either whey or soy on lean body mass. Whey significantly improved bench press (MD 8.87) and squat (MD 9.60; units not given in the abstract). Authors call for larger, high-quality RCTs.
sources.limitations: Small total sample.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: protein-training-gains: mixed evidence on lean mass in young adults.

sources.title: Effect of Plant Versus Animal Protein on Muscle Mass, Strength, Physical Performance, and Sarcopenia: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
sources.authors: Reid-McCann RJ, Brennan SF, Ward NA, Logan D, McKinley MC, McEvoy CT.
sources.population: Adults (subgroups under and over 60)
sources.intervention: Plant vs animal protein (supplements and diets)
sources.findings: Overall, plant protein gave slightly lower muscle mass than animal protein (SMD −0.20), mainly in adults under 60. No difference between soy and milk protein (SMD −0.02; 17 RCTs). Animal protein beat non-soy plant proteins such as rice, chia, oat and potato (SMD −0.58; 5 RCTs) and plant-based diets (SMD −0.51; 7 RCTs). No difference for muscle strength (14 RCTs) or physical performance (5 RCTs).
sources.limitations: Few trials of non-soy plant proteins.
sources.funding: Authors declare none.
sources.cited_for: protein-soy-vs-whey and protein-other-plant: comparison of protein sources.

sources.title: No Difference Between the Effects of Supplementing With Soy Protein Versus Animal Protein on Gains in Muscle Mass and Strength in Response to Resistance Exercise.
sources.authors: Messina M, Lynch H, Dickinson JM, Reed KE.
sources.journal: Int J Sport Nutr Exerc Metab
sources.population: Adults doing resistance training for 6 weeks or more
sources.intervention: Soy protein vs whey or other animal proteins (beef, milk, dairy)
sources.findings: Soy and whey both increased strength, with no difference between them. In the 5 whey-vs-soy studies, neither had a significant effect on lean mass, and there was no difference between them. Strength and lean mass rose with soy and with other proteins, with no between-group differences. Notes acute studies show whey stimulates muscle protein synthesis more than soy or casein, likely due to leucine.
sources.limitations: Small number of studies.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract (first author affiliated with Nutrition Matters, Inc.).
sources.cited_for: protein-soy-vs-whey: soy matches animal protein for long-term gains.

sources.title: No Significant Differences in Muscle Growth and Strength Development When Consuming Soy and Whey Protein Supplements Matched for Leucine Following a 12 Week Resistance Training Program in Men and Women: A Randomized Trial.
sources.authors: Lynch HM, Buman MP, Dickinson JM, Ransdell LB, Johnston CS, Wharton CM.
sources.journal: Int J Environ Res Public Health
sources.population: Untrained young men and women aged 18–35
sources.intervention: 19 g whey isolate or 26 g soy isolate (both 2 g leucine) with supervised resistance training 3 times a week for 12 weeks
sources.findings: Both groups increased lean body mass (1.54 kg) and leg strength, with no differences between soy and whey.
sources.limitations: Untrained participants; modest sample.
sources.funding: Authors declare no conflict of interest.
sources.cited_for: protein-soy-vs-whey: leucine-matched soy equals whey.

sources.title: Similar effects between animal-based and plant-based protein blend as complementary dietary protein on muscle adaptations to resistance training: findings from a randomized clinical trial.
sources.authors: Santini MH, Erwig Leitão A, Mazzolani BC, Smaira FI, de Souza MSC, Santamaria A, Gualano B, Roschel H.
sources.sample_size: 44 men recruited (number completing not stated in the abstract)
sources.population: Untrained young men
sources.intervention: Three 15 g doses a day (45 g/day) of a soy-and-pea blend or whey, with supervised resistance training 3 times a week for 12 weeks
sources.findings: Both groups gained whole-body lean mass (about 2.4–2.5 kg), muscle cross-sectional area and leg-press strength (about 63–64 kg), with no between-group differences.
sources.limitations: Men only; untrained.
sources.funding: Funded by NotCo (a plant-based food company), which had no role in design, analysis or writing.
sources.cited_for: protein-soy-vs-whey: soy-pea blend matched whey.

sources.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition Position Stand: protein and exercise.
sources.authors: Jäger R, Kerksick CM, Campbell BI, Cribb PJ, Wells SD, Skwiat TM, Purpura M, Ziegenfuss TN, Ferrando AA, Arent SM, Smith-Ryan AE, Stout JR, Arciero PJ, Ormsbee MJ, Taylor LW, Wilborn CD, Kalman DS, Kreider RB, Willoughby DS, Hoffman JR, Krzykowski JL, Antonio J.
sources.population: Healthy, exercising individuals

Physically active people can meet requirements from whole foods; supplements are a practical way to ensure quality and quantity while limiting calories. Rapidly digested proteins high in essential amino acids and leucine best stimulate muscle protein synthesis.

sources.authors: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements
sources.population: Athletes and exercisers
sources.intervention: Protein 1.2–2.0 g/kg/day for athletes
sources.findings: Protein builds, maintains and repairs muscle; athletes' needs about 1.2–2.0 g/kg/day. No Tolerable Upper Intake Level set for protein. High-protein diets (two to three times the RDA) do not appear to harm kidneys or bones, but long-term data are limited. Most protein powders contain whey, a complete milk protein; casein digests more slowly; whey has more leucine than casein or soy. Many products combine protein sources to cover all essential amino acids.
