profiles.name: Turkesterone
profiles.summary: There is no human evidence that turkesterone builds muscle; research on the related compound ecdysterone is mixed, and lab tests show many of these products contain far less than their labels claim.
profiles.description: Turkesterone is a plant steroid (a phytoecdysteroid) found in Ajuga turkestanica. It is related to ecdysterone (20-hydroxyecdysone), which occurs in plants such as Rhaponticum carthamoides, spinach and quinoa. These compounds are sold as 'natural anabolic' supplements, but they are not the same as anabolic steroids.
profiles.biological_function: Ecdysteroids are steroid compounds made by some plants. Earlier research cited by human-study authors suggests ecdysterone's muscle effects in animals and cells may work through estrogen receptor binding, not the androgen pathway used by anabolic steroids. Human evidence is very limited, and almost none exists for turkesterone specifically.

formulations.name: Turkesterone / Ajuga turkestanica extract
formulations.notes: Only one small human study (single doses). Turkesterone content varies between products sold as standardised extracts.

formulations.name: Ecdysterone (20-hydroxyecdysone) extracts
formulations.notes: A few small human training trials with mixed results. Lab tests often find far less than labelled.

formulations.name: BIO101 (pharmaceutical 20-hydroxyecdysone)
formulations.notes: An investigational drug tested in older adults with sarcopenia; not a dietary supplement.

claims.claim: Turkesterone increases muscle growth in humans
claims.popular_framing: Turkesterone is a natural steroid alternative that builds muscle.
claims.question: Does turkesterone build muscle?
claims.outcome: Muscle growth (and anabolic markers such as IGF-1)
claims.population: Only one human study: 11 healthy, recreationally active young men.
claims.bottom_line: There's no human evidence that turkesterone builds muscle. The only human study we found tested single doses and found no significant effect on IGF-1 or metabolism.
claims.what_research_found: In a 2024 crossover study, 11 young men took single doses of 1,000 mg and 2,000 mg of turkesterone or placebo. There were no significant changes in IGF-1 (a growth-related hormone) or resting metabolic rate compared with placebo. The authors said the data fail to fully support turkesterone as a potent anabolic supplement.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: No trial has tested turkesterone over weeks of training or measured muscle size or strength in people. Claims rely on animal and lab research and on studies of a different compound (ecdysterone).
claims.limitations: One tiny, short, single-blind study with no training and no muscle measurements. This is a gap in research, not evidence that it fails.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Single oral doses of 1,000 mg and 2,000 mg of a commercial turkesterone product.

factors.study_quality: One small randomised, single-blind crossover trial.
factors.consistency: Cannot be judged with a single study.
factors.effect_size: No significant effects.
factors.clinical_significance: No meaningful outcome (muscle or strength) was measured.
factors.sample_size: 11 participants.
factors.population: Young active men only.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Academic funding; authors declare no conflicts.
factors.reproducibility: Not replicated.
factors.formulation_dose: Single doses, unlike the daily use promoted by sellers; product content was not reported as verified in the abstract.

claims.claim: Ecdysterone (20-hydroxyecdysone), a related ecdysteroid, increases muscle mass and strength with resistance training
claims.popular_framing: Ecdysteroids like turkesterone and ecdysterone are proven muscle builders.
claims.question: Does the related compound ecdysterone build muscle?
claims.outcome: Muscle mass and strength with training
claims.population: Young men doing resistance training.
claims.bottom_line: The evidence is mixed. One study funded by the World Anti-Doping Agency found gains, but a randomised trial found none, and a third trial used a product that barely contained ecdysterone. These findings do not transfer to turkesterone.
claims.what_research_found: In a 10-week study of 46 young men, those given ecdysterone had larger gains in muscle mass and bench press. In a randomised double-blind trial of 45 trained men split across four groups (about 11 per group), 200 mg of 20-hydroxyecdysone for 8 weeks made no significant difference to fat-free mass, strength or sprint power compared with the other groups, including placebo. In a 2025 trial of 24 trained men, a commercial product made no difference, but it contained less than 1% of the labelled 20-hydroxyecdysone.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It has not been established that ecdysterone reliably adds muscle in people, or what dose would do so. A drug-grade version (BIO101) is being tested for age-related muscle loss, but that trial measured walking speed in older adults, not muscle growth in young people.
claims.limitations: Few, small studies. The positive study's abstract does not state whether it was randomised or placebo-controlled, nor the doses. Supplement content is unreliable.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Ecdysterone-containing supplements at varying doses over 10 weeks; 200 mg 20-hydroxyecdysone for 8 weeks; a 20-hydroxyecdysone and diosgenin product three times daily for 12 weeks.

factors.study_quality: Mixed: one randomised double-blind trial (null), one study with unclear design (positive), one randomised trial with an under-dosed product (null).
factors.consistency: Conflicting results.
factors.effect_size: Not quantified in the positive study's abstract.
factors.clinical_significance: Unclear.
factors.sample_size: Small: 46, 45 (about 11 on ecdysterone) and 24 participants.
factors.population: Young men only.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: The positive study was funded by the World Anti-Doping Agency (per publisher funder data); several BIO101 trial authors are employees or advisors of its developer, Biophytis.
factors.reproducibility: The positive finding has not been replicated.
factors.formulation_dose: Products often contain far less than labelled, so trials may not have tested what they intended.

claims.claim: Turkesterone and related ecdysteroids raise anabolic hormones such as IGF-1 or testosterone
claims.popular_framing: Turkesterone boosts your hormones naturally.
claims.question: Does turkesterone raise testosterone or IGF-1?
claims.outcome: Blood IGF-1 and testosterone
claims.population: Young men.
claims.bottom_line: No study has shown it. Two small human studies found no significant hormone changes.
claims.what_research_found: Single doses of turkesterone (1,000–2,000 mg) did not significantly change IGF-1 compared with placebo in 11 men. Eight weeks of 200 mg 20-hydroxyecdysone did not change active or free testosterone or cortisol in trained men.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: No study has tested long-term turkesterone use on testosterone.
claims.limitations: Very small studies, one with single doses only.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Turkesterone 1,000 mg and 2,000 mg single doses; 20-hydroxyecdysone 200 mg for 8 weeks.

factors.study_quality: Two small placebo-controlled trials.
factors.consistency: Both null.
factors.effect_size: No significant changes.
factors.clinical_significance: No meaningful hormone change found.
factors.sample_size: 11 and about 11 per group.
factors.population: Young men only.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Academic studies; no conflicts declared or not stated.
factors.reproducibility: Not replicated with turkesterone over time.
factors.formulation_dose: Short or single-dose exposure.

claims.claim: Turkesterone and ecdysterone supplements reliably contain the amount stated on the label
claims.popular_framing: A standardised 95% extract gives you a precise dose.
claims.question: Do these products contain what they claim?
claims.outcome: Measured vs labelled ecdysteroid content
claims.population: Commercial supplements (laboratory analysis).
claims.bottom_line: Often not. Independent lab tests have found many ecdysteroid products contain much less than the label says, and turkesterone content varies between products.
claims.what_research_found: Testing of 12 ecdysterone supplements found actual content generally much lower than labelled. A 2026 analysis of 13 products found several 'standardised' 80–95% products contained substantially less than declared, and turkesterone content varied among products. In a 2025 training trial, the product contained less than 1% of its labelled 20-hydroxyecdysone.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: These studies do not show that every product is mislabelled; some contained moderate to high amounts.
claims.limitations: A limited number of products and brands were tested, and markets change over time.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Products labelled as ecdysterone, turkesterone, Ajuga turkestanica, Rhaponticum or Cyanotis extracts.

factors.study_quality: Validated laboratory methods.
factors.consistency: Under-dosing found in all three analyses; two of them share a senior author (Parr), so they are not fully independent.
factors.effect_size: Large gaps: one trial product had less than 1% of its labelled 20-hydroxyecdysone, and some products had none detectable.
factors.clinical_significance: Buyers may not get the dose they pay for.
factors.sample_size: 12 + 13 products plus one trial product.
factors.population: Commercial supplements on the market.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Authors declare no conflicts or not stated.
factors.reproducibility: Found by research groups in Germany/Italy and in Bulgaria.
factors.formulation_dose: Directly concerns the products sold.

profiles.absorption: No human absorption data for turkesterone were found in the sources read. Ecdysteroid supplements vary widely in actual content, which makes the dose a person receives uncertain.
profiles.side_effects: Short-term data only. Single doses of 1,000–2,000 mg turkesterone did not significantly change heart rate, blood pressure or gut symptoms in 11 men. A 10-week ecdysterone study found no rise in liver or kidney toxicity markers. In a 6–9 month drug trial of pharmaceutical 20-hydroxyecdysone in older adults, treatment-related side effects were similar to placebo.
profiles.interactions: No interaction data were found in the sources read.
profiles.cautions: Long-term safety is unknown. Pregnant or breastfeeding people and anyone on medication should speak to a clinician first. Competitive athletes should note that anti-doping researchers have recommended adding ecdysterone to the WADA prohibited list; check current anti-doping rules, as its status was not verified here. Product labels are often inaccurate.
profiles.research_doses_summary: Doses used in research: turkesterone 1,000 mg and 2,000 mg as single doses; 20-hydroxyecdysone 200 mg for 8 weeks; drug-grade 20-hydroxyecdysone 175–350 mg twice daily for 6–9 months in older adults. There is no established effective dose.

sources.title: The Effects of Multiple Acute Turkesterone Doses on Indirect Measures of Hypertrophy and Metabolic Measures: A Preliminary Investigation.
sources.authors: Harris DR, Chapman-Lopez T, Machek SB, Forsse JS, Sulak T, Funderburk LK.
sources.population: Healthy, recreationally active men (mean age about 23)
sources.intervention: Single doses of turkesterone (1,000 mg and 2,000 mg) vs cellulose placebo, randomised, single-blind crossover; blood at baseline, 3 h and 24 h
sources.findings: No significant condition, time or interaction effects on serum IGF-1, resting metabolic rate, or fat and carbohydrate metabolism. IGF-1 rose non-significantly with both turkesterone doses. Neither dose significantly changed heart rate, blood pressure or gut symptoms (full text). Authors say the data fail to fully support turkesterone as a potent anabolic supplement.
sources.limitations: Very small, single doses only, no training and no direct muscle measures; single-blind.
sources.funding: Baylor University master's thesis research grant and Texas Chapter of ACSM student research award (PMC full text); authors declare no conflicts.
sources.cited_for: turkesterone-muscle-growth and ecdysteroid-hormones: the only human turkesterone trial found.

verification.via: PubMed E-utilities (abstract) and PMC full text (PMC12121319) for doses, design and funding

sources.title: Ecdysterone and Turkesterone-Compounds with Prominent Potential in Sport and Healthy Nutrition.
sources.authors: Todorova V, Ivanova S, Chakarov D, Kraev K, Ivanov K.
sources.intervention: Narrative review of ecdysterone and turkesterone
sources.findings: Describes ecdysterone and turkesterone as naturally occurring plant compounds found in Rhaponticum carthamoides, spinach, quinoa and Ajuga turkestanica, and reviews possible benefits for health and athletic performance. The abstract does not report human trial results for turkesterone.
sources.limitations: Narrative review; the abstract gives no quantitative human evidence.
sources.funding: Authors declare no conflicts of interest.
sources.cited_for: Background on what turkesterone is and its plant sources.

sources.title: Ecdysteroids as non-conventional anabolic agent: performance enhancement by ecdysterone supplementation in humans.
sources.authors: Isenmann E, Ambrosio G, Joseph JF, Mazzarino M, de la Torre X, Zimmer P, Kazlauskas R, Goebel C, Botrè F, Diel P, Parr MK.
sources.population: Young men doing a 10-week strength training programme
sources.intervention: Different doses of ecdysterone-containing supplements (doses not given in the abstract); supplement tested for steroid contamination
sources.findings: Participants given ecdysterone had significantly larger increases in muscle mass and one-repetition bench press. No increase in liver or kidney toxicity biomarkers. Authors recommend adding ecdysterone to the WADA prohibited list (class S1.2).
sources.limitations: The abstract does not state whether the study was randomised or placebo-controlled, or give doses or effect sizes.
sources.funding: World Anti-Doping Agency (award 15C18MP, per publisher funder metadata in Crossref). No conflict-of-interest statement in the PubMed record.
sources.cited_for: ecdysterone-muscle: the main positive human study of ecdysterone.

sources.title: Effects of methoxyisoflavone, ecdysterone, and sulfo-polysaccharide supplementation on training adaptations in resistance-trained males.
sources.authors: Wilborn CD, Taylor LW, Campbell BI, Kerksick C, Rasmussen CJ, Greenwood M, Kreider RB.
sources.population: Resistance-trained men, about 20 years old
sources.intervention: Double-blind: placebo, methoxyisoflavone 800 mg/day, 20-hydroxyecdysone (ecdysterone) 200 mg, or sulfo-polysaccharide 1,000 mg/day, for 8 weeks of training
sources.findings: No significant differences between groups in fat-free mass, body fat, bench press or leg press 1RM, or sprint power. No differences in active or free testosterone, cortisol, or kidney markers (urea nitrogen, creatinine).
sources.limitations: Small groups (about 11 per arm); 8 weeks.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: ecdysterone-muscle and ecdysteroid-hormones: null randomised trial.

sources.title: How reliable is the labeling of a commercial phytosteroid product? A 12-week randomized double-blind training study.
sources.authors: Dissemond J, Havers T, Held S, Geisler S, Kostov T, Diel P, Türschmann S, Parr MK, Isenmann E.
sources.population: Resistance-trained young men
sources.intervention: Commercial 20-hydroxyecdysone + diosgenin product taken three times a day as labelled, vs placebo, with free-weight training 3 times a week for 12 weeks
sources.findings: Strength, fat-free mass, muscle mass and muscle thickness improved over time in both groups with no group differences. Lab analysis found less than 1% of the claimed 20-hydroxyecdysone and 10.4% of the claimed diosgenin in the capsules, and no biological activity in muscle cells.
sources.limitations: Small; the product barely contained the active compound, so it cannot test ecdysterone itself.
sources.funding: Authors report no conflicts.
sources.cited_for: ecdysterone-muscle and ecdysteroid-labels: null training trial and severe under-dosing.

sources.title: How reliable is dietary supplement labelling?-Experiences from the analysis of ecdysterone supplements.
sources.authors: Ambrosio G, Wirth D, Joseph JF, Mazzarino M, de la Torre X, Botrè F, Parr MK.
sources.population: Commercial dietary supplements (not a human study)
sources.intervention: Validated UHPLC-MS/MS analysis of products labelled to contain ecdysterone
sources.findings: Applied to 12 supplements labelled as containing ecdysterone, the method found actual content generally much lower than labelled.
sources.limitations: Product analysis only; small number of products.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: ecdysteroid-labels: label accuracy.

sources.title: Simultaneous LC-MS Profiling of Bioactive Ecdysteroids in Nutrient-Dense Plant Sources and Dietary Supplements.
sources.authors: Todorova V, Ivanova S, Ardasheva R, Ivanov K.
sources.population: Commercial supplements and foods (not a human study)
sources.intervention: LC-MS quantification of 20-hydroxyecdysone, turkesterone and ponasterone
sources.findings: Confirmed kaniwa, spinach, quinoa and asparagus as natural sources of phytoecdysteroids. Of 13 supplements labelled as containing Rhaponticum, Cyanotis, Ajuga turkestanica or ecdysteroid extracts, several products standardised to 80–95% ecdysterone contained substantially less than declared (from below detection to about 50 mg per capsule). Turkesterone content varied among products marketed as standardised extracts.
sources.limitations: Product analysis only; amounts in foods not given in the abstract.
sources.funding: Authors declare no conflicts of interest.
sources.cited_for: ecdysteroid-labels: label accuracy and turkesterone variability; food sources.

sources.title: BIO101 in Sarcopenic Seniors at Risk of Mobility Disability: Results of a Double-Blind Randomised Interventional Phase 2b Trial.
sources.authors: Fielding RA, Dao MM, Cannon K, Desvarieux M, Miller SS, Gimness MP, Brandon DM, Villareal DT, Bruyere O, Bautmans I, et al.
sources.population: Adults aged 65+ with sarcopenia (mean age 75.5; 54% female)
sources.intervention: BIO101 (pharmaceutical-grade 20-hydroxyecdysone) 175 mg or 350 mg twice daily vs placebo for 6–9 months
sources.findings: The 350 mg twice-daily dose improved 400-m walking speed by 0.07 m/s vs placebo in the full analysis (not significant) and 0.09 m/s in the per-protocol group (significant). Treatment-related adverse events were similar to placebo (16.0% placebo, 13.3% and 13.5% on BIO101). COVID-19 disrupted 55% of end-of-treatment assessments.
sources.limitations: Investigational drug, not a supplement; older sarcopenic population; power reduced by the pandemic.
sources.funding: Several authors are employees, former employees or advisors of Biophytis SA, the drug's developer, which holds joint copyright; other authors report various industry ties.

profiles.name: Vitamin B12
profiles.summary: Vitamin B12 supplements raise B12 levels in people who are low, vegans who take them have better B12 status, and long-term metformin use can lower B12; but there is no good evidence that B12 boosts energy, memory or mood in people who are not deficient.
profiles.description: Vitamin B12 is a water-soluble vitamin found naturally only in animal foods such as meat, fish, eggs and dairy, and added to some fortified foods like nutritional yeast and breakfast cereals. Supplements most often contain cyanocobalamin; methylcobalamin, adenosylcobalamin and hydroxocobalamin are also used.
profiles.biological_function: B12 is needed to make red blood cells, DNA and healthy nerves. Deficiency can cause a type of anaemia (megaloblastic anaemia), tiredness, weakness, pale skin, palpitations, and numbness or tingling in the hands and feet, sometimes without anaemia (NIH ODS). Absorbing B12 from food depends on stomach acid and a protein called intrinsic factor.

formulations.name: Cyanocobalamin
formulations.notes: The most common form in supplements; converted in the body to the active forms (NIH ODS).

formulations.name: Methylcobalamin and adenosylcobalamin
formulations.notes: The forms the body actually uses. NIH ODS states that no evidence indicates absorption from supplements varies by form.

formulations.name: Hydroxocobalamin
formulations.notes: Used mainly in injections; converted to active forms in the body (NIH ODS).

claims.claim: Vitamin B12 supplements boost energy and reduce tiredness in people who are not deficient
claims.popular_framing: B12 shots and gummies for an instant energy boost.
claims.question: Will B12 give me more energy if my levels are normal?
claims.outcome: Energy, fatigue and physical performance
claims.population: People without B12 deficiency.
claims.bottom_line: There is no good evidence that extra B12 gives you more energy if your levels are already adequate. Tiredness from B12 deficiency is a different situation.
claims.what_research_found: A 2021 systematic review of 16 randomised trials (6,276 participants without advanced neurological disorders or overt B12 deficiency) found only one study that measured unexplained fatigue, so no pooled analysis was possible. NIH ODS states that B12 supplementation appears to have no beneficial effect on performance in the absence of a nutritional deficit.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: There are not enough trials on fatigue in non-deficient people to say whether there is a small effect. This is a lack of evidence, not proof that it does nothing.
claims.limitations: Very few trials measure energy or fatigue as an outcome in non-deficient people.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Not specified for fatigue in the sources read.

factors.study_quality: Systematic review of RCTs, but only one trial addressed fatigue.
factors.consistency: Cannot be judged with a single study.
factors.effect_size: Not estimable.
factors.clinical_significance: No meaningful benefit shown.
factors.sample_size: Very limited for this outcome.
factors.population: People without overt deficiency or advanced neurological disorders.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Review authors declare none.
factors.reproducibility: No replicated positive findings in the sources read.
factors.formulation_dose: Not applicable.

claims.claim: Oral vitamin B12 supplements raise B12 levels in people who are deficient or at risk
claims.popular_framing: If you're low in B12, you need injections.
claims.question: Do B12 tablets fix low B12?
claims.outcome: Blood B12 levels and B12 status markers
claims.population: People with B12 deficiency (Cochrane review: mean ages 38.6–72); adult vegans; people after gastric bypass surgery.
claims.bottom_line: Yes. In small trials, high-dose oral B12 (1,000–2,000 mcg/day) raised blood levels about as well as injections, and vegans who use B12 supplements have better B12 status than those who don't.
claims.what_research_found: A 2018 Cochrane review of 3 trials (153 people) found that 1,000 mcg/day oral B12 gave no clinically relevant difference in blood B12 compared with injections, and in one trial 2,000 mcg/day oral B12 gave higher levels than injections (mean difference 680 pg/mL). Oral treatment cost less. A 2024 meta-analysis found adult vegans had lower B12 and higher homocysteine than omnivores, and vegans taking B12 supplements had significantly better levels on all markers than those who did not. NIH ODS reports that 1,000 mcg/day oral methylcobalamin appeared as effective as hydroxocobalamin injections after gastric bypass.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: The Cochrane trials did not report on symptoms such as tiredness or nerve problems, or quality of life. Some people, such as those with pernicious anaemia, have conditions that affect absorption and need clinician-directed treatment.
claims.limitations: Cochrane rated the evidence as low quality because of few trials and participants. The vegan evidence is observational.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Oral B12 1,000 or 2,000 mcg/day for 3–4 months versus intramuscular injections (Cochrane); 1,000 mcg/day methylcobalamin after gastric bypass (NIH ODS).

factors.study_quality: Cochrane review of RCTs (low quality); observational meta-analysis in vegans; authoritative summary.
factors.consistency: Consistent: all sources show improved B12 status with supplementation.
factors.effect_size: Blood levels comparable to or higher than injections.
factors.clinical_significance: Correcting deficiency matters because untreated deficiency can cause anaemia and nerve damage (NIH ODS).
factors.sample_size: Small for the oral-vs-injection comparison (153 people).
factors.population: Deficient or at-risk groups only.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Cochrane authors declare none known.
factors.reproducibility: Supported by independent sources (Cochrane, NIH ODS, vegan meta-analysis).
factors.formulation_dose: High oral doses (1,000–2,000 mcg) were used, well above the 2.4 mcg RDA, because only a small fraction is absorbed at high doses (NIH ODS).

claims.claim: Long-term metformin use lowers vitamin B12 levels
claims.popular_framing: Diabetes medication can drain your B12.
claims.question: Does metformin cause low B12?
claims.outcome: Blood B12 levels and B12 deficiency
claims.population: People with type 2 diabetes on insulin (Dutch RCT); adults with prediabetes and overweight (DPP/DPPOS).
claims.bottom_line: Yes. In randomised trials, people taking metformin for years were more likely to develop low B12 than people on placebo. Researchers suggest regular B12 testing during long-term metformin use.
claims.what_research_found: In a randomised placebo-controlled trial of 390 people with type 2 diabetes, metformin for 4.3 years lowered B12 by 19% compared with placebo, and raised the absolute risk of B12 deficiency by 7.2 percentage points. In the Diabetes Prevention Program, low or borderline-low B12 was more common with metformin at 5 years (19.1% vs 9.5%) and 13 years (20.3% vs 15.6%), and each year of metformin use was associated with 13% higher odds of deficiency (OR 1.13 per year). Clearly low B12 (≤203 pg/mL) was more common with metformin at 5 years (4.3% vs 2.3%) but not significantly at 13 years (7.4% vs 5.4%). NIH ODS also notes metformin may reduce B12 absorption.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: These studies show that metformin lowers B12; they do not test whether routine supplements prevent symptoms. Nobody should stop or change metformin because of this.
claims.limitations: In the DPP, metformin was open-label after the first 3.2 years. The Dutch trial was funded by a drug manufacturer.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Metformin 850 mg three times daily for 4.3 years (Dutch RCT); 850 mg twice daily (DPP).

factors.study_quality: Randomised placebo-controlled trial plus long-term follow-up of a randomised trial.
factors.consistency: Both studies agree.
factors.effect_size: About 19% lower B12; number needed to harm 13.8 over 4.3 years for deficiency.
factors.clinical_significance: Meaningful: in DPPOS, neuropathy was more common in metformin users with low B12.
factors.sample_size: 390 (Dutch RCT); over 1,500 with B12 measured at each DPP time point.
factors.population: People with diabetes or prediabetes on metformin.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Dutch trial funded by Merck Sharp & Dohme.
factors.reproducibility: Independent groups in different countries.
factors.formulation_dose: Typical metformin doses.

claims.claim: Methylcobalamin is better absorbed or more effective than cyanocobalamin
claims.popular_framing: Avoid cyanocobalamin; methyl B12 is the 'active' form your body needs.
claims.question: Is methylcobalamin better than cyanocobalamin?
claims.outcome: Absorption and effectiveness
claims.population: General supplement users.
claims.bottom_line: There is no evidence that one form is absorbed better than the other. NIH ODS states that absorption from supplements does not appear to vary by form, and cyanocobalamin is converted in the body into the active forms.
claims.what_research_found: NIH ODS states that methylcobalamin and adenosylcobalamin are the active forms, that cyanocobalamin is converted into them, and that no evidence indicates absorption from supplements varies by form.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: No head-to-head trial was read for this profile showing a clinical advantage for either form.
claims.limitations: Based on an authoritative summary; no comparative trials were identified in this review.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Not applicable.

factors.study_quality: No comparative trials identified.
factors.consistency: Not applicable.
factors.effect_size: Not applicable.
factors.clinical_significance: No evidence of a practical difference.
factors.sample_size: Not applicable.
factors.population: General supplement users.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Not applicable: no comparative studies identified.
factors.reproducibility: Not applicable.
factors.formulation_dose: Both forms are sold at similar doses.

claims.claim: Vitamin B12 supplements improve memory and mood in people without deficiency
claims.popular_framing: B12 for brain power and a better mood.
claims.question: Does B12 improve memory or mood if you're not deficient?
claims.outcome: Cognitive function and depressive symptoms
claims.population: People without advanced neurological disorders or overt B12 deficiency (16 RCTs); the abstract does not report participants' ages.
claims.bottom_line: No. Across 16 randomised trials, B12 alone or with other B vitamins did not improve memory or thinking, and did not improve depressive symptoms overall.
claims.what_research_found: A 2021 meta-analysis of 16 RCTs (6,276 participants) found no effect of B12 alone or B complex on any area of cognitive function, and no overall effect on depression measures. Meta-regression found no factor that predicted a benefit. NIH ODS also states that RCTs show B12 does not improve cognitive function in older adults, even though it lowers homocysteine.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: This does not apply to people with real deficiency, where low B12 can itself cause neurological and mood symptoms (NIH ODS).
claims.limitations: Effect sizes and participant ages are not given in the abstract, so it is unclear how well the results apply to young adults.
claims.formulation_and_dose: B12 alone or with folic acid with or without B6; doses not stated in the abstract.

factors.study_quality: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs.
factors.consistency: Consistent null results; no predictors of benefit on meta-regression.
factors.effect_size: No detectable effect.
factors.clinical_significance: No meaningful benefit.
factors.sample_size: 6,276 participants in 16 RCTs.
factors.population: People without overt deficiency; ages not reported in the abstract (NIH ODS describes the cognition trials it summarises as in older adults).
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Authors declare none.
factors.reproducibility: Agrees with the NIH ODS summary of RCTs.
factors.formulation_dose: B12 alone and B complex both tested.

research_doses.note: Oral doses used to treat deficiency in the Cochrane review trials. Nutritional yeast ranges from 8.3 to 24 mcg per serving depending on the product.

reference_intake.label: RDA, adults 19+ (2.6 mcg pregnancy, 2.8 mcg lactation)

food_vs_supplement.comparison_note: A 3 oz serving of salmon or ground beef roughly meets the 2.4 mcg RDA. Treatment doses (1,000–2,000 mcg) are hundreds of times higher, partly because absorption falls sharply at high doses: about 50% at 1–2 mcg but about 1.3% at 1,000 mcg (NIH ODS). Plant foods contain no B12 unless fortified.
food_vs_supplement.food_advantages: Animal foods provide protein, iron and other nutrients alongside B12. Fortified foods offer B12 for people who eat few animal products.
food_vs_supplement.when_supplement_may_help: NIH ODS lists older adults (especially with atrophic gastritis), people with pernicious anaemia, people who have had stomach or weight-loss surgery, vegans and vegetarians, and breastfed infants of vegan mothers as at higher risk of deficiency. Long-term metformin and acid-reducing medicines can also lower B12. A clinician can test B12 status.

profiles.absorption: NIH ODS: about 50% of B12 is absorbed at doses below 1–2 mcg, but only about 2% at 500 mcg and 1.3% at 1,000 mcg, because intrinsic factor becomes saturated. No evidence indicates that absorption varies by supplement form.
profiles.side_effects: NIH ODS states that even at large doses, B12 is generally considered safe. In the Cochrane review, one trial reported no treatment-related adverse events and another reported 2 of 30 participants leaving the oral group because of adverse events.
profiles.interactions: Metformin may reduce B12 absorption and blood levels. Proton pump inhibitors (such as omeprazole and lansoprazole) and H2 blockers (such as cimetidine) can reduce B12 absorption from food by lowering stomach acid (NIH ODS).
profiles.cautions: Tiredness has many causes; talk to a clinician rather than assuming it is low B12. People on long-term metformin or acid-reducing medicines, older adults, vegans, pregnant or breastfeeding people on plant-based diets, and anyone who has had stomach surgery should discuss B12 testing with a clinician. Do not stop or change prescribed medicines because of B12 concerns.
profiles.upper_limit: No upper limit set; the Food and Nutrition Board cites a low potential for toxicity (NIH ODS).
profiles.research_doses_summary: Doses used in research cited here: oral B12 1,000–2,000 mcg/day for 3–4 months in people with deficiency; 1,000 mcg/day methylcobalamin after gastric bypass. These describe research only and are not recommendations.

sources.title: Vitamin B12: Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
sources.authors: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements
sources.population: General population and at-risk groups
sources.findings: RDA 2.4 mcg adults. Food table. No UL. Forms: no evidence absorption varies by form. Absorption ~50% at <1–2 mcg, ~2% at 500 mcg, 1.3% at 1,000 mcg. At-risk groups: older adults, pernicious anaemia, GI surgery, vegans/vegetarians, infants of vegan mothers. No performance benefit without a deficit. Does not reduce CVD risk; RCTs show no cognitive benefit in older adults. Metformin, PPIs and H2 blockers interactions. Generally safe at large doses.
sources.limitations: Summary document; last updated 26 March 2024.
sources.funding: US government (NIH)
sources.cited_for: Food amounts, RDA, UL, absorption, forms, risk groups, interactions; context for energy, cognition and form claims.

sources.title: Effects of Vitamin B12 Supplementation on Cognitive Function, Depressive Symptoms, and Fatigue: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Meta-Regression.
sources.authors: Markun S, Gravestock I, Jäger L, et al.
sources.population: People without advanced neurological disorders or overt B12 deficiency
sources.intervention: B12 alone or B complex (B12 + folic acid ± B6)
sources.findings: No effect on any cognitive subdomain; no overall effect on depression measures; only one study on idiopathic fatigue, so no analysis possible. Meta-regression found no predictors of effect. B12 likely ineffective for cognition and depressive symptoms in people without advanced neurological disorders.
sources.limitations: Effect sizes not reported in abstract.
sources.funding: Authors declare no conflict of interest
sources.cited_for: Energy/fatigue claim (lack of evidence) and memory/mood claim (evidence against).

verification.via: Europe PMC; abstract re-read via PubMed E-utilities

sources.title: Oral vitamin B(12) versus intramuscular vitamin B(12) for vitamin B(12) deficiency.
sources.authors: Wang H, Li L, Qin LL, et al.
sources.population: People with B12 deficiency; mean ages 38.6–72 years
sources.intervention: Oral B12 (1,000 or 2,000 mcg/day) vs intramuscular B12, 3–4 months
sources.findings: 1,000 mcg/day oral: no clinically relevant difference in serum B12 vs IM (2 trials). 2,000 mcg/day oral: mean difference 680 pg/mL (95% CI 392.7–967.3) in favour of oral. Low-quality evidence of similar effects; oral cheaper; very low-quality evidence oral is as safe.
sources.limitations: Few trials and participants; no trial reported symptoms or quality of life.
sources.funding: Authors report no known conflicts
sources.cited_for: Correcting deficiency claim; research doses.

sources.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of functional vitamin B12 status among adult vegans.
sources.authors: Niklewicz A, Hannibal L, Warren M, Ahmadi KR
sources.population: Adult vegans vs vegetarians and omnivores
sources.intervention: Observational comparison; subgroup by B12 supplement use
sources.findings: Vegans had lower serum B12 and higher homocysteine than omnivores, indicating functional deficiency. Vegans using B12 supplements had significantly better levels of all biomarkers than unsupplemented vegans.
sources.limitations: Observational studies.
sources.funding: Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (UK) grant listed in the PubMed record; not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: Correcting deficiency claim (vegans); at-risk groups.

sources.title: Long term treatment with metformin in patients with type 2 diabetes and risk of vitamin B-12 deficiency: randomised placebo controlled trial.
sources.authors: de Jager J, Kooy A, Lehert P, et al.
sources.population: People with type 2 diabetes on insulin, Netherlands
sources.intervention: Metformin 850 mg three times daily vs placebo for 4.3 years
sources.findings: B12 fell 19% (95% CI −24% to −14%) vs placebo. Absolute risk of deficiency (<150 pmol/L) 7.2 percentage points higher (95% CI 2.3–12.1); number needed to harm 13.8 over 4.3 years. Low B12 (150–220 pmol/L) 11.2 points higher. Authors suggest regular B12 measurement during long-term metformin treatment.
sources.limitations: Insulin-treated patients only.
sources.funding: Merck Sharp & Dohme
sources.cited_for: Metformin claim.

sources.title: Long-term Metformin Use and Vitamin B12 Deficiency in the Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study.
sources.authors: Aroda VR, Edelstein SL, Goldberg RB, et al.
sources.sample_size: 2,155 randomised (1,082 placebo; 1,073 metformin); B12 measured in ~1,500–1,700 at each time point
sources.population: US adults with elevated glucose and overweight/obesity
sources.intervention: Metformin 850 mg twice daily vs placebo for 3.2 years, then open-label metformin for ~9 more years
sources.findings: Low B12 (≤203 pg/mL) 4.3% vs 2.3% at 5 years but not significantly different at 13 years (7.4% vs 5.4%, P = .12); low or borderline (≤298 pg/mL) 19.1% vs 9.5% at 5 years and 20.3% vs 15.6% at 13 years. OR 1.13 (95% CI 1.06–1.20) per year of metformin. Neuropathy more common in metformin users with low B12.
sources.limitations: Secondary analysis; open-label phase.
sources.funding: NIH (NIDDK) grants listed in the PubMed record; not stated in abstract
sources.cited_for: Metformin claim.

profiles.name: Vitamin D
profiles.summary: Vitamin D is essential for bones, but large trials show that taking it on its own does not prevent fractures, depression, cancer or heart disease in generally healthy adults; combined with calcium it modestly lowers fractures in older people, and its benefit for colds is unclear and at most small.
profiles.description: Vitamin D is a fat-soluble vitamin. The skin makes it when exposed to sunlight, and it is found in a few foods, such as oily fish, cod liver oil, egg yolk and fortified milk. Supplements come as vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) or vitamin D2 (ergocalciferol).
profiles.biological_function: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium, which bones need. Without enough of it, bones can become thin, brittle or misshapen; severe deficiency causes rickets in children. It also plays a role in immune function and inflammation. Doctors measure vitamin D status with a blood test for 25-hydroxyvitamin D, written 25(OH)D.

formulations.name: Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol)
formulations.notes: Made from 7-dehydrocholesterol (lanolin). The large trials cited here (VITAL) used vitamin D3 at 2,000 IU/day.

formulations.name: Vitamin D2 (ergocalciferol)
formulations.notes: Made from UV-irradiated yeast. NIH ODS states the two forms appear equivalent at nutritional doses, but D2 appears less potent at high doses, and firm conclusions about different effects cannot be drawn.

formulations.name: Combined vitamin D + K2 products
formulations.notes: One randomised trial in older men without known heart disease (vitamin K2 720 mcg/day plus vitamin D 25 mcg/day for 2 years) found no significant reduction in coronary calcification overall. See the Vitamin K profile.

claims.claim: Vitamin D supplements prevent fractures and falls in generally healthy adults
claims.popular_framing: Take vitamin D for strong bones.
claims.question: Does taking vitamin D prevent broken bones in healthy people?
claims.outcome: Fractures, falls and bone mineral density
claims.population: Community-dwelling adults not selected for vitamin D deficiency, low bone mass or osteoporosis (VITAL: men 50+ and women 55+).
claims.bottom_line: No. In large, well-run trials, vitamin D supplements did not reduce fractures or falls in adults who were not selected for vitamin D deficiency, and did not meaningfully change bone density.
claims.what_research_found: The VITAL trial gave 25,871 adults 2,000 IU/day of vitamin D3 or placebo for a median of 5.3 years. Fracture risk was almost identical: total fractures hazard ratio 0.98 (95% CI 0.89–1.08), hip fractures 1.01 (0.70–1.47). A 2018 meta-analysis of 81 trials (53,537 people) found no effect on total fracture (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.93–1.07), hip fracture (RR 1.11, 0.97–1.26) or falls (RR 0.97, 0.93–1.02), and no clinically relevant change in bone density. Higher and lower doses gave similar results.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: These findings are about people not selected for deficiency or osteoporosis. They do not tell us about people with very low vitamin D levels, or about vitamin D combined with calcium in frail older adults living in care homes (see the separate claim).
claims.limitations: VITAL participants were middle-aged and older; adults aged 18–40 were not studied. Participants were not recruited on the basis of low vitamin D, so the trial was not designed to test people who are deficient.
claims.formulation_and_dose: VITAL: vitamin D3 2,000 IU/day for a median 5.3 years. The meta-analysis pooled a range of doses, with subgroup analyses comparing doses above and below 800 IU/day.

factors.study_quality: Large randomised placebo-controlled trial (VITAL) plus a meta-analysis of 81 randomised trials.
factors.consistency: Consistent: both the trial and the meta-analysis found no benefit; treatment effects in VITAL did not differ across baseline subgroups.
factors.effect_size: Effect estimates were close to zero. The meta-analysis's trial sequential analysis gave reliable evidence that vitamin D does not reduce total fractures or falls by 7.5% or more (and total fractures by 5% or more).
factors.clinical_significance: No clinically meaningful benefit for fractures, falls or bone density.
factors.sample_size: Very large: 25,871 in VITAL; 53,537 in the meta-analysis.
factors.population: Generally healthy middle-aged and older adults; not selected for deficiency. Results may not apply to people who are deficient.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: VITAL was funded by the US National Institutes of Health. The meta-analysis was funded by the Health Research Council of New Zealand.
factors.reproducibility: Independent groups (VITAL investigators; New Zealand/UK meta-analysis team) reached the same conclusion.
factors.formulation_dose: Vitamin D3 at typical supplement doses, matching products on sale.

claims.claim: Vitamin D taken together with calcium modestly reduces fractures in older adults, especially those living in care institutions
claims.popular_framing: Older people should take calcium and vitamin D to protect their bones.
claims.question: Does vitamin D plus calcium help older people avoid fractures?
claims.outcome: Fractures
claims.population: Postmenopausal women and older men (Cochrane review); adults over 65 (2023 meta-analysis). The absolute benefit is largest in people living in institutions.
claims.bottom_line: Yes, but only for a narrower group than the popular claim implies. Vitamin D combined with calcium slightly lowers fracture risk in older people, with a meaningful absolute benefit mainly in high-risk people in care homes. Vitamin D on its own does not.
claims.what_research_found: A 2014 Cochrane review (53 trials, 91,791 participants) found high-quality evidence that vitamin D plus calcium gives a small reduction in hip fracture (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.74–0.96) and any fracture (RR 0.95, 0.90–0.99). That equals about 1 fewer hip fracture per 1,000 older adults per year in the community, and about 9 fewer per 1,000 per year in institutions. Vitamin D alone was unlikely to prevent hip fracture (RR 1.12, 0.98–1.29) or any new fracture (RR 1.03, 0.96–1.11). A 2023 meta-analysis of 7 trials in people over 65 (12,620 participants) found 800 IU vitamin D3 plus calcium lowered hip fracture (OR 0.75, 0.64–0.87).
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: This does not show a benefit for younger adults or for vitamin D taken without calcium. The 2023 meta-analysis found no effect on femoral neck bone density.
claims.limitations: Many trials in the Cochrane review had unclear risk of bias for randomisation and allocation. The review found a small increase in gastrointestinal symptoms with calcium plus vitamin D (RR 1.05), a significant increase in kidney disease (RR 1.16), and more, mostly mild, high blood calcium with vitamin D or its analogues (RR 2.28).
claims.formulation_and_dose: Vitamin D with calcium. In the 2023 meta-analysis, 800 IU/day vitamin D3 with 1,200 mg calcium showed a clearer effect (OR 0.69) than 800 IU with 1,000 mg calcium (OR 1.08, not significant).

factors.study_quality: Cochrane systematic review rating the main findings as high-quality evidence, though many individual trials had unclear risk of bias.
factors.consistency: Consistent that vitamin D alone does not work and that the combination has a small effect; benefit is inconsistent in community-dwelling people (NIH ODS).
factors.effect_size: Small relative effect (about 16% lower hip fracture risk in the Cochrane review).
factors.clinical_significance: Meaningful in high-risk care-home residents (about 9 fewer hip fractures per 1,000 per year); very small in the community (about 1 fewer per 1,000 per year).
factors.sample_size: Large: 49,853 participants in the vitamin D plus calcium hip-fracture analysis.
factors.population: Older adults, many aged 80+. Not relevant evidence for 18–40-year-olds.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: The Cochrane lead author ran one included trial and did not extract its data; the 2023 review declared no conflicts.
factors.reproducibility: Two independent reviews point in the same direction.
factors.formulation_dose: Combination with calcium; vitamin D alone did not reduce fractures.

claims.claim: Vitamin D supplements prevent colds and other acute respiratory infections
claims.popular_framing: Take vitamin D in winter to boost your immune system and avoid colds.
claims.question: Does vitamin D stop you catching colds?
claims.outcome: Acute respiratory infections (colds, flu-like illness, chest infections)
claims.population: Children and adults in 40 randomised trials, across ages and baseline vitamin D levels.
claims.bottom_line: Not clearly. The latest pooled analysis of 40 trials found no statistically significant protection. If there is a benefit, it appears small.
claims.what_research_found: A 2025 meta-analysis pooled 40 randomised trials with 61,589 participants. Vitamin D compared with placebo gave an odds ratio of 0.94 (95% CI 0.88–1.00, p = 0.057), which is not statistically significant. An earlier 2021 version (37 trials) had found a small protective effect (OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.86–0.99). No subgroup (by age, starting vitamin D level, dose size or dosing frequency) showed a clearly different effect.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: The research does not show a reliable benefit, and it cannot fully rule out a small one. It does not show that vitamin D treats infections once you have them.
claims.limitations: Trials differed in populations, doses and how infections were defined. The 2025 analysis found funnel-plot asymmetry, which can signal small-study effects.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Various doses and schedules of vitamin D (daily, weekly and less frequent) across trials.

factors.study_quality: Meta-analysis of randomised placebo-controlled trials.
factors.consistency: Low between-trial heterogeneity (I² 26.4%), but the overall result moved from just significant (2021) to not significant (2025).
factors.effect_size: Small at best: point estimate a 6% lower odds of infection.
factors.clinical_significance: Any benefit would be modest for an individual.
factors.sample_size: Large: 61,589 participants.
factors.population: Broad range of ages and settings.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: The abstract states no funding; the PubMed record lists an NIH grant. The senior author reports grants from supplement companies (including Pharma Nord and DSM Nutritional Products) outside the submitted work.
factors.reproducibility: Updated analysis by the same group; earlier and later estimates are similar in size but differ in statistical significance.
factors.formulation_dose: Mixed doses; no clear dose effect found.

claims.claim: Vitamin D supplements prevent depression and improve mood in adults without depression
claims.popular_framing: Low mood? Vitamin D is the 'sunshine vitamin' that lifts your mood.
claims.question: Does vitamin D prevent depression or improve mood?
claims.outcome: New or recurrent depression; mood scores
claims.population: Adults aged 50 and over without clinically relevant depressive symptoms at the start (VITAL-DEP).
claims.bottom_line: No, for preventing depression. A large five-year trial found vitamin D did not lower the risk of depression or change mood scores compared with placebo.
claims.what_research_found: VITAL-DEP randomised 18,353 adults aged 50+ to vitamin D3 2,000 IU/day or placebo for a median of 5.3 years. Depression or clinically relevant symptoms occurred at 12.9 vs 13.3 per 1,000 person-years (hazard ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.87–1.09). The difference in mood-score change was 0.01 points (95% CI −0.04 to 0.05), far below the 0.5 points considered clinically important.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: This trial was about prevention in people without depression. It did not test vitamin D as a treatment for people who already have depression, or in people with low vitamin D, or in adults under 50.
claims.limitations: Participants were aged 50+, so results may not fully apply to younger adults. One large trial carries most of this claim.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Vitamin D3 2,000 IU/day for a median 5.3 years.

factors.study_quality: Large, randomised, placebo-controlled trial (matching placebo) with high completion (90.5%).
factors.consistency: Both depression risk and mood scores showed no effect.
factors.effect_size: Essentially zero; confidence intervals exclude a clinically important mood effect.
factors.clinical_significance: No meaningful benefit for preventing depression.
factors.sample_size: Very large: 18,353 participants.
factors.population: Adults 50+; not selected for low vitamin D or depression.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Funded by the US National Institutes of Health.
factors.reproducibility: Single large trial; not replicated at this scale in younger adults.
factors.formulation_dose: Typical supplement dose of vitamin D3.

claims.claim: Vitamin D supplements reduce depressive symptoms in adults
claims.popular_framing: Vitamin D works like a natural antidepressant.
claims.question: Can vitamin D ease symptoms of depression?
claims.outcome: Depressive symptom scores
claims.population: Adults from general and clinical populations, including people with other (systemic) illnesses (41 trials).
claims.bottom_line: Unclear. A pooled analysis found lower depressive symptoms with vitamin D, but the authors rated the certainty of that evidence as very low, and results varied widely between trials.
claims.what_research_found: A 2022 meta-analysis of 41 placebo-controlled trials (53,235 participants) found a small-to-moderate reduction in depressive symptoms (Hedges' g −0.317, 95% CI −0.405 to −0.230). The authors suggested doses of 2,000 IU/day or more appeared to reduce symptoms.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: Because certainty was very low and heterogeneity very high, it is not established that vitamin D treats depression. It has not been shown to replace standard depression treatment.
claims.limitations: Very high heterogeneity (I² 88%), risk-of-bias concerns in most studies, and GRADE certainty rated very low by the authors themselves.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Various doses of vitamin D across 41 trials; the authors highlight 2,000 IU/day or more.

factors.study_quality: Meta-analysis of RCTs, but risk of bias was concerning in most included studies.
factors.consistency: Poor: I² 88% indicates trials disagree substantially.
factors.effect_size: Small to moderate pooled effect (g −0.32), of uncertain reliability.
factors.clinical_significance: Unclear given the very low certainty.
factors.sample_size: Large overall (53,235 participants across 41 trials); the abstract does not give individual trial sizes.
factors.population: Mixed general and clinical populations.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Funded by Finnish foundations (Finnish Medical Foundation, Juho Vainio Foundation).
factors.reproducibility: Meta-analyses on this question have been inconsistent, as the authors note.
factors.formulation_dose: Mixed doses and schedules.

claims.claim: Vitamin D supplements prevent cancer and heart disease
claims.popular_framing: Vitamin D protects against cancer and heart attacks.
claims.question: Does taking vitamin D lower your risk of cancer or heart disease?
claims.outcome: Invasive cancer and major cardiovascular events
claims.population: Generally healthy US adults (men 50+, women 55+) in VITAL.
claims.bottom_line: No. In a large trial of nearly 26,000 adults, vitamin D did not lower the number of people who developed invasive cancer or had major heart events over about five years.
claims.what_research_found: VITAL randomised 25,871 adults to vitamin D3 2,000 IU/day or placebo for a median of 5.3 years. Invasive cancer was diagnosed in 793 people on vitamin D vs 824 on placebo (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.88–1.06). Major cardiovascular events occurred in 396 vs 409 (HR 0.97, 0.85–1.12). There was no excess risk of high blood calcium or other adverse events. NIH ODS also concludes that studies do not support a role for vitamin D, with or without calcium, in reducing cancer risk.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: The trial does not tell us about people with very low vitamin D, about younger adults, or about effects over much longer periods.
claims.limitations: Most evidence here comes from one very large trial in middle-aged and older adults.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Vitamin D3 2,000 IU/day for a median 5.3 years.

factors.study_quality: Large, randomised, placebo-controlled trial.
factors.consistency: Agrees with the NIH ODS summary for cancer.
factors.effect_size: Hazard ratios close to 1 for both primary outcomes.
factors.clinical_significance: No meaningful benefit shown for disease prevention.
factors.sample_size: Very large: 25,871 participants.
factors.population: Generally healthy older adults, not selected for deficiency.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Funded mainly by the US National Institutes of Health.
factors.reproducibility: NIH ODS reports earlier trials (e.g. the Women's Health Initiative) also showing no colorectal cancer benefit.
factors.formulation_dose: Typical supplement dose of vitamin D3.

foods.food: Milk, fortified (nonfat, reduced fat or whole)
Egg, large (vitamin D is in the yolk)

research_doses.note: VITAL used 2,000 IU/day of vitamin D3; the 2018 meta-analysis compared trials above and below 800 IU/day. Other trials in the respiratory-infection meta-analysis used a range of doses and schedules.

reference_intake.label: RDA, adults 19–70 (15 mcg); 800 IU (20 mcg) over 70

food_vs_supplement.comparison_note: Few foods are rich in vitamin D. A 3 oz serving of sockeye salmon gives about 447 IU, close to the 600 IU RDA, while a cup of fortified milk gives about 115 IU. The 2,000 IU/day used in VITAL is hard to reach from food alone. Sunlight is also a major source, which food tables do not capture.
food_vs_supplement.food_advantages: Oily fish also provide protein and omega-3 fats; fortified dairy provides calcium. Food sources carry no realistic risk of vitamin D toxicity.
food_vs_supplement.when_supplement_may_help: NIH ODS lists groups at higher risk of inadequacy: breastfed infants, older adults, people with limited sun exposure, people with dark skin, people with fat-malabsorption conditions (such as Crohn's disease, celiac disease or cystic fibrosis), people with obesity or after gastric bypass, and people with milk allergy, lactose intolerance or a vegan diet. A clinician can check vitamin D status with a blood test.

profiles.absorption: Vitamin D is fat-soluble. NIH ODS reports that D2 and D3 both raise blood 25(OH)D and appear equivalent at nutritional doses, but D2 appears less potent at high doses. Conditions that reduce fat absorption (such as Crohn's disease, celiac disease, cystic fibrosis and some liver diseases) and gastric bypass can lower vitamin D absorption.
profiles.side_effects: At typical doses, VITAL found no excess risk of high blood calcium or other adverse events with 2,000 IU/day. Too much vitamin D can cause loss of appetite, weight loss, frequent urination and heart rhythm problems; very high blood calcium can calcify blood vessels and damage the heart and kidneys (NIH ODS). In the Women's Health Initiative, women taking calcium plus vitamin D had a 17% higher risk of kidney stones over 7 years (NIH ODS). Sun exposure does not cause vitamin D toxicity.
profiles.interactions: NIH ODS lists: corticosteroids such as prednisone (reduce calcium absorption and impair vitamin D metabolism); orlistat and cholestyramine (reduce absorption of fat-soluble vitamins); and the anticonvulsants phenobarbital and phenytoin (speed up vitamin D breakdown and reduce calcium absorption).
profiles.cautions: Talk to a clinician before taking vitamin D if you take any of the medicines above, have kidney disease or kidney stones, have a condition affecting calcium levels, or are pregnant or breastfeeding. More is not better: blood levels above about 125–150 nmol/L (50–60 ng/mL) are advised against by the Food and Nutrition Board (NIH ODS).
profiles.upper_limit: 4,000 IU (100 mcg) per day for adults aged 9 and over, including during pregnancy and breastfeeding (NIH ODS).
profiles.research_doses_summary: Doses used in the research cited here: vitamin D3 2,000 IU/day for about 5 years (VITAL); 800 IU/day vitamin D3 with 1,000–1,200 mg calcium in older adults (fracture meta-analysis); a range of daily, weekly and less frequent doses in respiratory-infection and depression meta-analyses. These describe research only and are not recommendations.

sources.title: Vitamin D: Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
sources.authors: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements
sources.population: General population; groups at risk of inadequacy
sources.findings: RDA 600 IU (15 mcg) for adults 19–70 and 800 IU (20 mcg) over 70; UL 4,000 IU (100 mcg) for ages 9+. Food content table (IU per serving). D2 and D3 equivalent at nutritional doses; D2 less potent at high doses. Vitamin D plus calcium gives small BMD gains and reduces fractures in institutionalised older adults, with inconsistent benefit in community-dwelling people; vitamin D alone does not reduce fractures or falls in older adults. Studies do not support a role in reducing cancer risk. Toxicity signs, kidney-stone finding in WHI, and drug interactions (corticosteroids, orlistat, cholestyramine, phenobarbital, phenytoin).
sources.limitations: The version of the page served during this session displayed 'Reviewed: June 24, 2011' and did not mention the VITAL trial, so it may not be the most current version; the reviewer should re-check the live page and update food values if they differ.
sources.funding: US government (NIH)
sources.cited_for: Food amounts, RDA, upper limit, forms, risk groups, toxicity, interactions; fracture summary for institutionalised older adults; cancer summary.

sources.title: Supplemental Vitamin D and Incident Fractures in Midlife and Older Adults.
sources.authors: LeBoff MS, Chou SH, Ratliff KA, et al.
sources.population: Generally healthy men aged 50+ and women aged 55+ in the US (VITAL ancillary study), not selected for deficiency, low bone mass or osteoporosis
sources.intervention: Vitamin D3 2,000 IU/day vs placebo; median follow-up 5.3 years
sources.findings: 1,991 fractures in 1,551 participants. Total fractures 769/12,927 (vitamin D) vs 782/12,944 (placebo): HR 0.98 (95% CI 0.89–1.08). Nonvertebral fractures HR 0.97 (0.87–1.07). Hip fractures HR 1.01 (0.70–1.47). Effects consistent across subgroups.
sources.limitations: Population not selected for deficiency; middle-aged and older adults only.
sources.funding: US National Institutes of Health grants (NCI, NCCIH, NIAMS, NIA) listed
sources.cited_for: Fracture claim in generally healthy adults (evidence against).

verification.via: Europe PMC; abstract re-read via PubMed E-utilities

sources.title: Effects of vitamin D supplementation on musculoskeletal health: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and trial sequential analysis.
sources.authors: Bolland MJ, Grey A, Avenell A
sources.population: Adults in randomised trials of vitamin D supplementation
sources.intervention: Vitamin D supplementation at various doses (subgroups above vs below 800 IU/day)
sources.findings: Total fracture RR 1.00 (95% CI 0.93–1.07; 36 trials); hip fracture RR 1.11 (0.97–1.26; 20 trials); falls RR 0.97 (0.93–1.02; 37 trials). Bone density differences −0.16% to 0.76%, not clinically relevant. High and low doses similar. Trial sequential analysis: reliable evidence that vitamin D does not reduce total fracture or falls by 7.5% or more (total fracture also by 5%); for hip fracture, reliable evidence of no 15% reduction, with uncertainty about a possible increase.
sources.limitations: Pools heterogeneous trials and populations.
sources.funding: Health Research Council of New Zealand (abstract); Chief Scientist Office grant listed in record
sources.cited_for: Fracture/falls/bone density claim in generally healthy adults.

verification.via: Europe PMC; abstract re-read via PubMed E-utilities

sources.title: Vitamin D supplementation to prevent acute respiratory infections: systematic review and meta-analysis of stratified aggregate data.
sources.authors: Jolliffe DA, Camargo CA Jr, Sluyter JD, et al.
sources.population: Children and adults in randomised placebo-controlled trials
sources.intervention: Vitamin D (various doses and dosing frequencies) vs placebo
sources.findings: Odds of at least one acute respiratory infection: OR 0.94 (95% CI 0.88–1.00; p = 0.057; I² 26.4%), no longer statistically significant. The 2021 version (37 RCTs) had found OR 0.92 (0.86–0.99). No effect modification by age, baseline 25(OH)D, dose size or frequency. Serious adverse events OR 0.96 (0.90–1.04). Funnel-plot asymmetry (Egger p = 0.0020).
sources.limitations: Funnel-plot asymmetry; heterogeneous trials.
sources.funding: Abstract states 'FUNDING: None'. Senior author reports grants from supplement companies (including Pharma Nord and DSM Nutritional Products) outside the submitted work.
sources.cited_for: Colds/respiratory infection claim.

sources.title: Effect of Long-term Vitamin D3 Supplementation vs Placebo on Risk of Depression or Clinically Relevant Depressive Symptoms and on Change in Mood Scores: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
sources.authors: Okereke OI, Reynolds CF, Mischoulon D, et al.
sources.population: Adults aged 50+ (mean 67.5 years; 49.2% women) without clinically relevant depressive symptoms at baseline (VITAL-DEP)
sources.intervention: Vitamin D3 2,000 IU/day vs placebo; median 5.3 years
sources.findings: Depression or clinically relevant symptoms: 609 events (12.9 per 1,000 person-years) vs 625 (13.3); HR 0.97 (95% CI 0.87–1.09). Mood score (PHQ-8) change difference 0.01 points (−0.04 to 0.05), below the 0.5-point minimal clinically important difference. Authors conclude results do not support vitamin D3 for preventing depression.

sources.title: Vitamin D Supplements and Prevention of Cancer and Cardiovascular Disease.
sources.authors: Manson JE, Cook NR, Lee IM, et al.
sources.population: Generally healthy US men aged 50+ and women aged 55+
sources.intervention: Vitamin D3 2,000 IU/day (and omega-3, 2x2 factorial) vs placebo; median 5.3 years
sources.findings: Invasive cancer: 793 (vitamin D) vs 824 (placebo), HR 0.96 (95% CI 0.88–1.06). Major cardiovascular events: 396 vs 409, HR 0.97 (0.85–1.12). Death from cancer HR 0.83 (0.67–1.02); all-cause death HR 0.99 (0.87–1.12). No excess hypercalcaemia or other adverse events.

sources.funding: US National Institutes of Health (NCI, NHLBI, NIMH, NIAMS) and others

sources.title: Vitamin D and vitamin D analogues for preventing fractures in post-menopausal women and older men.
sources.authors: Avenell A, Mak JC, O'Connell D
sources.population: Postmenopausal women and older men in community, nursing home or hospital settings
sources.intervention: Vitamin D (or analogues), alone or with calcium, vs placebo, no treatment or calcium
sources.findings: High-quality evidence: vitamin D alone unlikely to prevent hip fracture (RR 1.12, 0.98–1.29) or any fracture (RR 1.03, 0.96–1.11). Vitamin D plus calcium: hip fracture RR 0.84 (0.74–0.96), about 1 fewer per 1,000/year in community and 9 fewer per 1,000/year in institutions; any fracture RR 0.95 (0.90–0.99). Hypercalcaemia RR 2.28 (1.57–3.31); GI symptoms RR 1.04 (1.00–1.08), RR 1.05 (1.01–1.09) for calcium plus vitamin D; renal disease RR 1.16 (1.02–1.33); no effect on mortality.
sources.limitations: Many trials at unclear risk of bias for randomisation and allocation concealment.
sources.funding: Lead author participated in included trials (did not extract their data); others nothing to declare
sources.cited_for: Vitamin D plus calcium fracture claim; vitamin D alone not effective; adverse effects.

sources.title: What is the impact of daily oral supplementation of vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) plus calcium on the incidence of hip fracture in older people? A systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.authors: Manoj P, Derwin R, George S
sources.population: Adults over 65
sources.intervention: Daily oral vitamin D3 plus calcium
sources.findings: Hip fracture OR 0.75 (0.64–0.87). 800 IU D3 + 1,200 mg calcium: OR 0.69 (0.58–0.82); 800 IU + 1,000 mg calcium: OR 1.08 (0.74–1.56). Non-vertebral fracture OR 0.80 (0.72–0.89). Femoral neck BMD: no significant effect.
sources.limitations: Fixed-effect model; small number of trials.
sources.funding: Authors declare no conflict of interest
sources.cited_for: Vitamin D plus calcium fracture claim in older adults; dose used.

sources.title: The effect of vitamin D supplementation on depressive symptoms in adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
sources.authors: Mikola T, Marx W, Lane MM, et al.
sources.population: Adults in general and clinical populations
sources.intervention: Vitamin D vs placebo (various doses)
sources.findings: Reduction in depressive symptoms: Hedges' g −0.317 (95% CI −0.405 to −0.230), I² 88.16%, GRADE very low certainty. Risk of bias concerning in most studies. Doses of 2,000 IU/day or more appeared to reduce symptoms.

sources.funding: Finnish Medical Foundation; Juho Vainio Foundation
sources.cited_for: Depressive symptoms claim.

sources.title: Effects of Vitamin K2 and D Supplementation on Coronary Artery Disease in Men: A RCT.
sources.authors: Hasific S, Oevrehus KA, Lindholt JS, et al.
sources.sample_size: 389 randomised; 304 without ischemic heart disease analysed
sources.population: Men, mean age 71, no prior ischemic heart disease
sources.intervention: Vitamin K2 720 mcg/day plus vitamin D 25 mcg/day vs placebo for 24 months
sources.findings: No significant difference in mean coronary calcium score progression (Δ203 vs Δ254 AU, P = 0.089). Lower progression in those with CAC ≥400 AU (Δ288 vs Δ380, P = 0.047); safety events 1.9% vs 6.7% (P = 0.048), described as hypothesis-generating.
