profiles.name: Vitamin K
profiles.summary: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone proteins; pooled trials suggest vitamin K may slightly slow calcium build-up in arteries (a marker, not a heart outcome), but it has not been shown to prevent heart attacks, and anyone taking warfarin needs to keep vitamin K intake steady.
profiles.description: Vitamin K is a family of fat-soluble compounds. Vitamin K1 (phylloquinone) comes mainly from leafy green vegetables. Vitamin K2 (menaquinones, such as MK-4 and MK-7) is found in fermented foods like natto and in smaller amounts in meat, dairy and eggs.
profiles.biological_function: Vitamin K helps the body make proteins needed for blood clotting. It also activates proteins involved in bone, such as osteocalcin, and matrix Gla protein (MGP), which helps stop calcium building up in blood vessel walls. The idea that more vitamin K means less arterial calcification comes largely from animal studies (NIH ODS).

formulations.name: Vitamin K1 (phylloquinone / phytonadione)
formulations.notes: The main dietary form. NIH ODS reports free phylloquinone is absorbed at about 80%, but the body absorbs only 4% to 17% as much from spinach as from a tablet; eating vegetables with some fat helps.

formulations.name: Vitamin K2 as MK-7
formulations.notes: Found in natto. NIH ODS reports that data are limited, but MK-7 appears well absorbed and has a longer half-life than K1. The heart trials cited here used 360–720 mcg/day.

formulations.name: Vitamin K2 as MK-4
formulations.notes: Older fracture trials summarised by NIH ODS used very high doses (15 or 45 mg/day), far above dietary amounts.

claims.claim: Vitamin K supplements (especially K2) slow calcium build-up in the arteries
claims.popular_framing: Vitamin K2 directs calcium into your bones and out of your arteries.
claims.question: Does vitamin K2 keep calcium out of your arteries?
claims.outcome: Progression of vascular and coronary artery calcification (an imaging marker, not heart attacks)
claims.population: Adults in calcification trials. The individual trials read include people with symptomatic coronary artery disease and older men without known ischemic heart disease; the meta-analysis abstracts do not report how many participants had kidney disease, diabetes or heart disease.
claims.bottom_line: Possibly a small effect. Pooled trials show slightly slower artery calcification with vitamin K, but results are inconsistent, and calcification scores are a marker, not a heart outcome.
claims.what_research_found: A 2019 meta-analysis of 13 controlled trials (2,162 people) found vitamin K reduced vascular calcification by 9.1% (95% CI −17.7% to −0.5%) compared with control, with no significant effect on artery stiffness. A 2023 meta-analysis of 14 RCTs (1,533 patients) found slower coronary calcium score progression (mean difference −17.37, 95% CI −34.18 to −0.56). A 2026 trial in 180 people with symptomatic coronary artery disease found 360 mcg/day MK-7 for 2 years slowed calcium score increases versus placebo (P = .02). But a 2023 trial of K2 (720 mcg/day) plus vitamin D in 304 older men without known ischemic heart disease found no significant reduction in mean progression.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: None of these show that vitamin K prevents heart attacks, strokes or deaths. A 2020 systematic review of 9 RCTs concluded vitamin K does not consistently prevent progression of calcification, atherosclerosis or artery stiffness, though there may be some benefit in people with calcification at the start.
claims.limitations: Small numbers of trials, substantial heterogeneity, short follow-up, and mixed K1 and K2 forms. The pooled confidence intervals only just exclude no effect.
claims.formulation_and_dose: K1 and K2 (MK-4, MK-7) at varied doses; MK-7 360 mcg/day for 2 years (VitaK-CAC); K2 720 mcg/day plus vitamin D 25 mcg/day for 2 years (Danish trial). NIH ODS also describes a 3-year trial of 500 mcg/day phylloquinone with no overall difference in coronary calcification.

factors.study_quality: Meta-analyses of randomised trials plus individual placebo-controlled RCTs; underlying trials are mostly small.
factors.consistency: Mixed: two meta-analyses show a small significant effect; a systematic review and a neutral RCT find inconsistent benefit.
factors.effect_size: Small; confidence intervals close to zero.
factors.clinical_significance: Unknown: calcification is a surrogate marker, and the 2026 trial authors say the clinical significance remains to be determined.
factors.sample_size: Modest: about 1,500–2,200 people pooled.
factors.population: Includes people with symptomatic coronary artery disease and older men; the pooled analyses do not report the population mix. Little or no evidence in healthy young adults.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: In the 2026 MK-7 trial one author reported grants from Gnosis by Lesaffre outside the submitted work; the Danish trial received free tablets from Kappa Bioscience and Orkla Care.
factors.reproducibility: Independent groups report differing results.
factors.formulation_dose: Forms and doses vary widely across trials.

claims.claim: Vitamin K2 supplements prevent heart disease and heart attacks
claims.popular_framing: Take K2 to protect your heart.
claims.question: Does vitamin K2 lower your risk of heart attack or heart disease?
claims.outcome: Heart attacks, cardiovascular disease and death
claims.population: Adults in general.
claims.bottom_line: Not shown. The link comes from observational studies and calcification markers. No trial read for this profile has shown that K2 supplements prevent heart attacks or heart disease.
claims.what_research_found: In a Dutch cohort of 4,807 adults aged 55+, higher dietary menaquinone (K2) intake was linked to lower coronary heart disease death, while phylloquinone (K1) intake was not (NIH ODS). A 2019 meta-analysis found that levels of inactive vitamin K-dependent proteins were associated with cardiovascular disease or death in longitudinal studies. In a Danish trial of K2 plus vitamin D, safety events (heart attack, revascularisation or death) were fewer with supplementation (1.9% vs 6.7%), but the authors called this hypothesis-generating, not proof.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: Observational links cannot show that supplements cause a benefit. No adequately powered trial in the sources read used heart attacks or deaths as its main outcome.
claims.limitations: Evidence is observational or based on surrogate markers and secondary outcomes from small trials.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Dietary menaquinone in the cohort; K2 720 mcg/day plus vitamin D 25 mcg/day in the Danish trial.

factors.study_quality: Observational cohort data and a secondary safety endpoint from one RCT.
factors.consistency: Not enough outcome trials to judge.
factors.effect_size: Not reliably estimated for clinical events.
factors.clinical_significance: Unknown.
factors.sample_size: Clinical-event data come from small numbers of events.
factors.population: Older adults; not studied in young adults.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Danish trial tablets were provided free of charge by Kappa Bioscience and Orkla Care; the funders had no role in design or analysis.
factors.reproducibility: Not replicated in outcome trials.
factors.formulation_dose: Dietary K2 is not the same as supplements.

claims.claim: Vitamin K supplements strengthen bones and reduce fractures
claims.popular_framing: Vitamin K is the missing piece for strong bones.
claims.question: Does vitamin K prevent fractures?
claims.outcome: Fractures and bone mineral density
claims.population: Mainly postmenopausal women, including women with osteoporosis.
claims.bottom_line: Maybe, in postmenopausal women, but the evidence is mixed. A meta-analysis found fewer fractures, while later trials found no benefit for bone density.
claims.what_research_found: A 2022 meta-analysis of randomised trials lasting at least 6 months found lower odds of vertebral fracture (OR 0.42, 95% CI 0.27–0.66) and clinical fracture (OR 0.44, 0.23–0.88) with vitamin K, mainly in postmenopausal and osteoporotic women, but no significant improvement in femoral bone density. NIH ODS describes an earlier meta-analysis in which MK-4 at 15 or 45 mg/day reduced hip, vertebral and non-vertebral fractures, a trial where MK-7 at 180 mcg/day for 3 years reduced vertebral height loss, and later trials in older adults finding no bone density benefit.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It is not established that typical-dose vitamin K supplements prevent fractures in younger adults or men. The authors say more studies are needed to establish vitamin K as an osteoporosis treatment.
claims.limitations: Many fracture data come from very high-dose MK-4 trials; results for bone density are inconsistent; co-administered calcium and vitamin D may partly explain mixed results (NIH ODS).
claims.formulation_and_dose: MK-4 15–45 mg/day; MK-7 180 mcg/day; phylloquinone in other trials; at least 6 months.

factors.study_quality: Meta-analysis of RCTs; quality of included trials not detailed in the abstract.
factors.consistency: Inconsistent between fracture and bone-density outcomes and across trials.
factors.effect_size: Large relative reduction in fracture odds in the pooled analysis; the abstract does not say which vitamin K forms or doses drove it.
factors.clinical_significance: Potentially meaningful for fracture-prone women if confirmed.
factors.sample_size: 20 citations reviewed; participant totals not given in the abstract.
factors.population: Postmenopausal and osteoporotic women, not the general public.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: 2022 meta-analysis authors declare none.
factors.reproducibility: Later trials did not reproduce bone-density gains.
factors.formulation_dose: MK-4 doses of 15–45 mg/day are far above typical supplement doses.

claims.claim: Changes in vitamin K intake change how well warfarin works
claims.popular_framing: If you're on blood thinners, avoid leafy greens.
claims.question: Does vitamin K interfere with warfarin?
claims.outcome: Blood clotting control (INR) in people taking warfarin
claims.population: People taking warfarin (Coumadin) or similar vitamin K antagonists.
claims.bottom_line: Yes. Warfarin works by blocking vitamin K, so sudden changes in vitamin K intake can make it work more or less strongly. NIH ODS advises consistent intake rather than avoidance.
claims.what_research_found: NIH ODS describes this as a serious and potentially dangerous interaction: warfarin blocks vitamin K's activity, and sudden changes in vitamin K intake can increase or decrease its anticoagulant effect. In a randomised crossover study of 12 stable patients, a vitamin K-depleted diet raised INR from 2.6 to 3.3, and a vitamin K-enriched diet lowered it from 3.1 to 2.8. The same paper's observational protocol in 39 outpatients linked vitamin K intake to both over- and under-anticoagulation.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: The research does not mean people on warfarin should avoid vitamin K foods; the key point in NIH ODS is keeping intake consistent. Any change should be managed by the prescribing clinician.
claims.limitations: The randomised dietary study was small and short (4-day interventions).
claims.formulation_and_dose: Dietary changes giving a 500% increase or an 80% decrease in vitamin K intake.

factors.study_quality: Small randomised crossover study plus authoritative summary; the mechanism is well understood.
factors.consistency: Consistent across observational and randomised data and the NIH ODS summary.
factors.effect_size: INR shifted by about 0.3–0.7 units within 4–7 days of diet changes; the observational data linked intake to both over- and under-anticoagulation.
factors.clinical_significance: High: over-anticoagulation raises bleeding risk and under-anticoagulation raises clot risk.
factors.sample_size: Small (12 in the randomised protocol; 39 observational).
factors.population: People on warfarin; not relevant to people not on these drugs.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Not stated in abstract.
factors.reproducibility: Consistent with the drug's known mechanism as summarised by NIH ODS.
factors.formulation_dose: Food-level changes in vitamin K, not just supplements.

research_doses.note: MK-7 180 mcg/day (bone trial, NIH ODS), 360 mcg/day (VitaK-CAC) and K2 720 mcg/day (Danish trial). Older fracture trials used MK-4 at 15–45 mg (15,000–45,000 mcg) per day, far outside this range.

reference_intake.label: Adequate Intake, men 19+ (90 mcg for women 19+)

food_vs_supplement.comparison_note: Leafy greens supply K1 at amounts similar to or above the Adequate Intake, but K1 from spinach is absorbed much less well than from a tablet. Natto is the only food in the NIH ODS table with large amounts of K2 (MK-7). Research doses of K2 (180–720 mcg) are not available from typical Western diets.
food_vs_supplement.food_advantages: Leafy greens provide fibre, folate and other nutrients. Eating them with some fat improves vitamin K1 absorption.
food_vs_supplement.when_supplement_may_help: NIH ODS lists newborns (given vitamin K at birth), people with malabsorption disorders such as cystic fibrosis, celiac disease and short bowel syndrome, and people who have had bariatric surgery as at risk of inadequacy. People on warfarin should not start or stop vitamin K supplements without their clinician.

profiles.absorption: NIH ODS: free phylloquinone (K1) is absorbed at about 80%, but only 4% to 17% as much is absorbed from spinach as from a tablet; fat in the meal helps. Data on MK-7 are limited, but it appears well absorbed with a longer half-life than K1. Menadione (K3) is no longer used in supplements because it damaged liver cells in lab studies.
profiles.side_effects: NIH ODS reports no adverse effects from vitamin K in food or supplements in humans or animals. One trial cited here (VitaK-CAC) reported no significant adverse effects from MK-7 at 360 mcg/day for 2 years.
profiles.interactions: Warfarin (Coumadin) and similar anticoagulants: serious interaction; sudden changes in vitamin K intake can raise or lower their effect (NIH ODS). Antibiotics, especially cephalosporins, may reduce gut bacterial vitamin K production. Bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colestipol) and orlistat can reduce vitamin K absorption; orlistat combined with warfarin may significantly raise prothrombin time (NIH ODS).
profiles.cautions: Anyone taking warfarin or another vitamin K antagonist should talk to their clinician before changing vitamin K intake from food or supplements. People with malabsorption conditions or after bariatric surgery should discuss vitamin K status with a clinician.
profiles.upper_limit: No upper limit set; the Food and Nutrition Board cites a low potential for toxicity (NIH ODS).
profiles.research_doses_summary: Doses used in research cited here: MK-7 180–720 mcg/day for 2–3 years; phylloquinone 500 mcg/day for 3 years; MK-4 15–45 mg/day in older fracture trials. These describe research only and are not recommendations.

sources.title: Vitamin K: Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
sources.authors: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements
sources.population: General population
sources.findings: AI 120 mcg/day men, 90 mcg/day women. Food table (natto 850 mcg, collards 530 mcg, etc.). No UL. K1 absorption and MK-7 half-life. Cardiovascular evidence: MGP hypothesis largely from animal data; menaquinone intake linked to lower CHD mortality in Dutch cohort (4,807 adults); 3-year 500 mcg K1 trial showed no overall difference in coronary calcification. Bone: Cockayne 2006 meta-analysis (MK-4 15/45 mg reduced fractures), MK-7 180 mcg trial, later null BMD trials. Warfarin interaction serious; keep intake consistent. Other drug interactions.
sources.limitations: Summary document.
sources.funding: US government (NIH)
sources.cited_for: Food amounts, AI, UL, forms, absorption, risk groups, warfarin and other interactions; context for heart and bone claims.

sources.title: Vitamin K status, supplementation and vascular disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
sources.authors: Lees JS, Chapman FA, Witham MD, et al.
sources.population: Adults in vitamin K trials and cohort studies
sources.intervention: Vitamin K supplementation vs control
sources.findings: Vitamin K reduced vascular calcification by 9.1% (95% CI −17.7 to −0.5; p=0.04) and dp-ucMGP by 44.7%; non-significant improvement in vascular stiffness. Inactive vitamin K-dependent protein levels associated with CVD or mortality in longitudinal studies (HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.07–0.83). Conclusions limited by small numbers of studies with substantial heterogeneity.
sources.limitations: Few studies; substantial heterogeneity.
sources.funding: Authors report British Heart Foundation and Kidney Research UK funding for related trials
sources.cited_for: Arterial calcification claim; observational link to CVD.

sources.title: Vitamin K supplementation and vascular calcification: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
sources.authors: Li T, Wang Y, Tu WP
sources.population: Patients in vascular calcification RCTs
sources.intervention: Vitamin K supplementation vs control
sources.findings: Slower coronary artery calcification progression (MD −17.37, 95% CI −34.18 to −0.56; p=0.04; I² 34%); lower dp-ucMGP; no difference in adverse events. More rigorous RCTs required.
sources.limitations: Mixed populations and forms.
sources.funding: Authors declare no commercial conflicts
sources.cited_for: Arterial calcification claim.

sources.title: Vitamin K Supplementation for the Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease: Where Is the Evidence? A Systematic Review of Controlled Trials.
sources.authors: Vlasschaert C, Goss CJ, Pilkey NG, et al.
sources.population: Adults in controlled trials of K1 or K2
sources.intervention: Vitamin K1 or K2 supplementation
sources.findings: Vitamin K does not consistently prevent progression of calcification, atherosclerosis or arterial stiffness; may be some benefit in people with calcification at entry. Role in mitigating vascular calcification uncertain.
sources.limitations: Heterogeneous studies, short follow-up, varied outcomes.
sources.funding: Authors declare no conflict of interest
sources.cited_for: Arterial calcification claim (inconsistency).

sources.title: Two Years of Menaquinone-7 Supplementation and Coronary Artery Calcification: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
sources.authors: Vossen LM, de Leeuw PW, Schurgers LJ, et al.
sources.sample_size: 180 randomised (90 per group); 85 received MK-7 and 82 placebo
sources.population: Symptomatic patients with coronary artery disease and CAC score 50–400 AU, Netherlands
sources.intervention: MK-7 360 mcg/day vs placebo for 2 years
sources.findings: CAC score rose from 145 to 214 AU (placebo) vs 135 to 184 AU (MK-7); group difference significant (P = .02); similar for calcium mass. No significant adverse effects. Clinical significance for plaque stability remains to be determined.
sources.limitations: Small; surrogate outcome; patients with existing disease.
sources.funding: One author reported grants from Gnosis by Lesaffre outside the submitted work
sources.cited_for: Arterial calcification claim; MK-7 dose.

sources.title: Effects of Vitamin K2 and D Supplementation on Coronary Artery Disease in Men: A RCT.
sources.authors: Hasific S, Oevrehus KA, Lindholt JS, et al.
sources.sample_size: 389 randomised; 304 without ischemic heart disease analysed
sources.population: Men, mean age 71, no prior ischemic heart disease
sources.intervention: Vitamin K2 720 mcg/day plus vitamin D 25 mcg/day vs placebo for 24 months
sources.findings: No significant difference in mean CAC progression (Δ203 vs Δ254 AU, P = 0.089). Lower progression in those with CAC ≥400 AU (Δ288 vs Δ380 AU, P = 0.047). No difference in noncalcified plaque volume. Safety events fewer with supplementation (1.9% vs 6.7%, P = 0.048); described as hypothesis-generating.
sources.limitations: Secondary analysis; older men only.
sources.funding: Danish Heart Foundation, Region of Southern Denmark, Novo Nordisk Foundation; tablets supplied free by Kappa Bioscience and Orkla Care (no role in design or analysis)
sources.cited_for: Arterial calcification and heart disease claims; research dose.

sources.title: Effect of Vitamin K on Bone Mineral Density and Fracture Risk in Adults: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
sources.authors: Salma, Ahmad SS, Karim S, et al.
sources.population: Adults, mainly postmenopausal and osteoporotic women
sources.intervention: Oral vitamin K for at least 6 months
sources.findings: Vertebral fracture OR 0.42 (95% CI 0.27–0.66); clinical fracture OR 0.44 (0.23–0.88). Non-significant effect on femoral BMD. Further studies needed to establish therapeutic value.
sources.limitations: Search to January 2020; included trial quality not reported in abstract.
sources.funding: Funded by the Deputyship for Research & Innovation, Saudi Ministry of Education, and King Abdulaziz University (PubMed record); authors declare no conflict of interest
sources.cited_for: Bone and fracture claim.

sources.title: Role of dietary vitamin K intake in chronic oral anticoagulation: prospective evidence from observational and randomized protocols.
sources.authors: Franco V, Polanczyk CA, Clausell N, Rohde LE
sources.population: Patients on chronic oral anticoagulation (coumarin)
sources.intervention: 4-day in-hospital diets with 500% higher or 80% lower vitamin K intake
sources.findings: Vitamin K intake independently associated with over- and under-anticoagulation. INR rose from 2.6 to 3.3 on a vitamin K-depleted diet and fell from 3.1 to 2.8 on a vitamin K-enriched diet.
sources.limitations: Small, short study.
sources.funding: Not stated in abstract

profiles.name: Zinc
profiles.summary: Zinc lozenges may shorten a cold by a day or two, but the evidence is low certainty and inconsistent; zinc does not appear to prevent colds, there is little evidence it 'boosts' immunity in people who already get enough, and high doses over time can cause copper deficiency.
profiles.description: Zinc is an essential mineral found in oysters, meat, shellfish, dairy, beans, nuts and whole grains. It is sold as tablets, capsules, lozenges and syrups, and is in many multivitamins and cold remedies.
profiles.biological_function: Zinc is needed for the activity of hundreds of enzymes. It plays a role in immune function, making proteins and DNA, and wound healing (NIH ODS). Zinc deficiency can affect the immune system.

formulations.name: Zinc gluconate, acetate and sulfate
formulations.notes: The most common supplement forms (NIH ODS). Lozenge trials have mostly used gluconate or acetate.

formulations.name: Zinc citrate and zinc oxide
formulations.notes: NIH ODS reports zinc citrate and gluconate are absorbed similarly (about 61% in young adults) and zinc oxide somewhat less (about 50%).

formulations.name: Zinc lozenges
formulations.notes: Dissolved slowly in the mouth. Cochrane reported gluconate lozenge doses of 45–276 mg/day for 4.5–21 days in cold trials. Labels list elemental zinc, not the weight of the whole compound.

claims.claim: Zinc lozenges or syrup taken at the start of a cold shorten how long it lasts
claims.popular_framing: Take zinc at the first sign of a cold and it'll be gone days sooner.
claims.question: Do zinc lozenges shorten colds?
claims.outcome: Duration of cold symptoms
claims.population: Adults and children with colds (Cochrane: 22 adult and 12 child studies across prevention and treatment).
claims.bottom_line: Maybe. Pooled trials suggest zinc can shorten a cold by about 2 days in adults, but the evidence is low certainty and individual trials disagree, including one recent double-blind trial that found no benefit.
claims.what_research_found: A 2024 Cochrane review found zinc taken to treat colds may shorten them by about 2.4 days (8 studies, 972 participants; low-certainty evidence). A 2012 meta-analysis of 17 trials found colds were about 1.65 days shorter overall, and about 2.6 days shorter in adults, but with no significant effect in children. A pooled analysis of three zinc acetate lozenge trials (199 patients) estimated colds were about 2.7–2.9 days shorter, against an average cold length of 7 days.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: It is not clear that zinc makes cold symptoms less severe; Cochrane found no clear effect on severity. A 2020 double-blind trial in Finland (87 people with colds) found a commercial zinc acetate lozenge (13 mg, six times a day for up to 5 days) did not speed recovery, and recovery was slower in the zinc group for 2 days after stopping. The best dose, form and timing are not established.
claims.limitations: Results vary enormously between trials (I² 95–97%), many trials have unclear or high risk of bias, and products, doses and outcomes differ. Zinc lozenges have a distinctive taste, which makes blinding hard.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Lozenges, syrups and tablets. Gluconate lozenges at 45–276 mg/day for 4.5–21 days in Cochrane-included trials; 13 mg zinc acetate lozenges six times a day (78 mg/day) for up to 5 days in the Finnish trial. NIH ODS notes an earlier review found benefit only at lozenge doses above 75 mg/day.

factors.study_quality: Randomised, placebo-controlled trials, but most were at unclear or high risk of bias in at least one domain (Cochrane).
factors.consistency: Poor. Heterogeneity was very high in both reviews, and a recent trial found no benefit.
factors.effect_size: About 1.5–3 days shorter on average when positive, with wide confidence intervals.
factors.clinical_significance: A 2-day shorter cold would be noticeable, if real.
factors.sample_size: Moderate: 972 participants in the Cochrane duration analysis; 2,121 across the 2012 review.
factors.population: Benefit appears in adults; the 2012 review found no significant effect in children.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Cochrane authors declared no relevant conflicts (one reports NIH funding to Cochrane Complementary Medicine, paid to her institution). Funding and conflicts of the individual-patient-data analysis are not stated in its abstract; its co-authors (Petrus, Prasad) appear to be investigators of the pooled trials, which a human reviewer should confirm.
factors.reproducibility: Mixed: several independent groups found benefit, others did not.
factors.formulation_dose: Effects may depend on form and dose; the evidence cannot say which product, if any, works best.

claims.claim: Taking zinc regularly prevents colds
claims.popular_framing: Take zinc daily through winter so you don't catch colds.
claims.question: Does taking zinc every day stop me catching colds?
claims.outcome: Risk of developing a cold
claims.population: Children and adults in prevention trials.
claims.bottom_line: Probably not. The best available review found zinc may make little or no difference to your chance of catching a cold, though the evidence is low certainty.
claims.what_research_found: Cochrane found little or no reduction in the risk of developing a cold with zinc compared with placebo (risk ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.01; 9 studies, 1,449 participants; low certainty), and little or no reduction in the number of colds over 5–18 months. NIH ODS also notes zinc did not prevent colds after deliberate rhinovirus exposure in a 2021 meta-analysis.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: The evidence is low certainty, so a small preventive effect cannot be fully ruled out. Results may differ in people who are zinc deficient.
claims.limitations: Few prevention trials, varied products and doses, and incomplete reporting. Some prevention trials looked at upper respiratory infections rather than colds specifically.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Various oral and other forms in 15 prevention trials; doses varied.

factors.study_quality: Randomised, placebo-controlled; certainty rated low by Cochrane.
factors.consistency: Low heterogeneity for risk of a cold (I² 20%).
factors.effect_size: Near zero (RR 0.93, confidence interval including no effect).
factors.clinical_significance: No meaningful preventive effect shown.
factors.sample_size: 1,449 participants for the main prevention outcome.
factors.population: Mixed children and adults; zinc status not stated in the abstract.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Cochrane review; authors declared no relevant conflicts.
factors.reproducibility: Pooled across 9 studies.
factors.formulation_dose: Varied.

claims.claim: Zinc supplements boost the immune system in people who already get enough zinc
claims.popular_framing: Zinc supercharges your immune system.
claims.question: Will zinc boost my immunity if I'm healthy?
claims.outcome: Immune markers and infection rates
claims.population: Healthy older adults (aged 55–87) in the trials we found; no trials we read in healthy younger adults.
claims.bottom_line: Not established. Zinc is needed for a working immune system, and deficiency harms it, but there is little evidence that extra zinc improves immunity in people who are not deficient.
claims.what_research_found: In a 6-month trial in healthy people aged 55–70, 15 or 30 mg/day of zinc produced only scattered changes in immune markers, and the authors concluded total intakes up to 40 mg/day had no significant long-term effect on immune status. A small 12-month trial (50 healthy people aged 55–87) found fewer infections with 45 mg/day of zinc than placebo, but these older participants had lower blood zinc than younger adults at the start. NIH ODS notes that zinc deficiency can affect the immune system.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: No trial we read tested whether zinc improves immunity or reduces infections in healthy young adults with adequate zinc. The positive infection trial was small and in a group with lower zinc levels.
claims.limitations: Small trials, older populations, and immune-marker outcomes that may not translate into fewer illnesses.
claims.formulation_and_dose: 15–30 mg/day for 6 months (ZENITH); zinc gluconate 45 mg/day for 12 months (Prasad 2007).

factors.study_quality: Randomised trials; the infection trial was double-blind and placebo-controlled.
factors.consistency: Inconsistent: one small trial found fewer infections, another found no meaningful long-term immune change.
factors.effect_size: Not quantified in the abstracts for infections.
factors.clinical_significance: Unclear for non-deficient people.
factors.sample_size: Small (50 participants in the infection trial).
factors.population: Older adults only; the positive trial's participants had lower baseline zinc.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: The infection trial was supported by NIH and non-US government funding (listed in PubMed); not otherwise stated.
factors.reproducibility: The infection result has not been replicated in the sources we read.
factors.formulation_dose: Doses of 15–45 mg/day; 45 mg exceeds the 40 mg/day adult upper limit.

claims.claim: Taking high-dose zinc for a long time can cause copper deficiency
claims.popular_framing: Zinc is harmless, so more is better.
claims.question: Can too much zinc cause problems?
claims.outcome: Copper deficiency, anaemia and low white blood cell counts
claims.population: People taking high-dose zinc supplements or using large amounts of zinc-containing denture creams.
claims.bottom_line: Yes. Zinc at 50 mg a day or more over weeks can interfere with copper absorption. In rare reported cases this has caused anaemia, low white blood cell counts and nerve problems. The blood problems mostly improved after stopping zinc, but nerve problems recovered more slowly and sometimes not fully.
claims.what_research_found: NIH ODS states that zinc doses of 50 mg or more over weeks can interfere with copper absorption, reduce immune function and lower HDL ('good') cholesterol, and that the adult upper limit of 40 mg/day is based on copper status. A 2026 systematic review of 37 published cases found zinc-induced copper deficiency from supplements, denture adhesive creams and swallowed coins, at roughly 50 mg to over 1,500 mg of zinc a day. Anaemia was present in nearly all cases and copper was low in all of them. Stopping zinc and giving copper usually reversed the blood problems within weeks to months, but nerve symptoms recovered more slowly and sometimes incompletely.
claims.what_research_did_not_establish: How often this happens at typical supplement doses is not known; case reports cannot give a rate.
claims.limitations: Evidence on clinical harm comes from case reports, which cannot show how common it is. The upper limit itself comes from an authoritative review summarised by NIH ODS.
claims.formulation_and_dose: Elemental zinc of about 50 mg/day or more for weeks or longer; denture creams containing up to 34 mg zinc per gram (NIH ODS).

factors.study_quality: Authoritative intake guidance plus descriptive case series; harm of this kind is not studied in randomised trials.
factors.consistency: Case reports and the basis for the official upper limit agree.
factors.effect_size: Can be serious: anaemia, neutropenia, pancytopenia and nerve damage in reported cases.
factors.clinical_significance: High for those affected; often initially misdiagnosed as a bone-marrow disorder.
factors.sample_size: 37 cases in the systematic review.
factors.population: People with high or prolonged zinc exposure.
factors.conflicts_of_interest: Review authors declared no competing interests.
factors.reproducibility: Reported repeatedly from 1972 to 2025.
factors.formulation_dose: Risk relates to total daily zinc dose and duration, not a particular form.

foods.food: Breakfast cereal, fortified with 25% DV zinc

research_doses.note: Daily zinc doses in the cited trials: 15–30 mg/day (immune markers, older adults), 45 mg/day (infections, older adults), about 78 mg/day as acetate lozenges (Finnish cold trial), and 45–276 mg/day as gluconate lozenges for short periods (cold trials in the Cochrane review).

food_vs_supplement.comparison_note: Apart from oysters, a serving of food gives about 1–4 mg of zinc. Cold-lozenge doses are many times higher and above the 40 mg/day adult upper limit, but they were used only for a few days. Long-term doses of 50 mg/day or more are linked to copper deficiency. NIH ODS notes food alone rarely reaches 50 mg, so food is unlikely to cause toxicity.
food_vs_supplement.food_advantages: Zinc from animal foods is absorbed better than from plant foods high in phytates (NIH ODS). Food is very unlikely to reach amounts that interfere with copper.
food_vs_supplement.when_supplement_may_help: NIH ODS lists groups at risk of low zinc: people with gut disorders such as inflammatory bowel disease or after some weight-loss surgery, vegetarians and vegans, pregnant or breastfeeding women, exclusively breastfed infants over 6 months, children with sickle cell disease, and people with alcohol use disorder.

profiles.absorption: Phytates in beans, nuts and whole grains bind zinc in the gut and reduce absorption. Absorption from food ranges from about 5% to over 50% depending on phytate content, and meals with only animal foods are absorbed better than mixed plant-and-animal meals (NIH ODS). In supplements, zinc citrate and gluconate are absorbed similarly (about 61% in young adults) and zinc oxide about 50%. Iron supplements of 25 mg or more taken with zinc reduce zinc absorption, though iron in fortified foods does not (NIH ODS).
profiles.side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, stomach upset, dizziness and headache at high doses (NIH ODS). In cold trials, zinc increased non-serious side effects (Cochrane RR 1.34), and a 2012 meta-analysis found more bad taste and nausea with zinc. In the Finnish lozenge trial, only 37% of the zinc group reported no adverse effects, versus 69% on placebo.
profiles.interactions: Zinc can reduce absorption of quinolone and tetracycline antibiotics; taking the antibiotic at least 2 hours before or 4–6 hours after zinc reduces this. Zinc can reduce absorption of penicillamine (space doses at least 1 hour apart). Thiazide diuretics increase zinc loss in urine (NIH ODS).
profiles.cautions: Long-term doses at or above 50 mg/day can cause copper deficiency. People using zinc-containing denture creams heavily should be aware these have been linked to copper deficiency. Talk to a clinician if you take antibiotics, penicillamine or diuretics, or have a gut disorder.
profiles.upper_limit: 40 mg/day for adults 19+, including pregnancy and lactation (NIH ODS). The UL is based on copper status and does not apply to people receiving zinc as medical treatment.
profiles.research_doses_summary: Doses used in research: zinc lozenges providing roughly 45–276 mg/day for a few days to three weeks in cold-treatment trials (13 mg acetate lozenges six times a day in one trial); 15–45 mg/day for 6–12 months in older adults in immune studies. These are research doses, not recommendations.

sources.title: Zinc for prevention and treatment of the common cold.
sources.authors: Nault D, Machingo TA, Shipper AG, Antiporta DA, Hamel C, Nourouzpour S, Konstantinidis M, Phillips E, Lipski EA, Wieland LS.
sources.population: Children (12 studies) and adults (22 studies).
sources.intervention: Zinc alone (lozenges, tablets, capsules, syrups, powders, intranasal) vs placebo; gluconate lozenges at 45–276 mg/day for 4.5–21 days.
sources.findings: Prevention: little or no reduction in risk of a cold (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.01; 9 studies, 1,449 participants; low certainty). Treatment: may shorten colds (MD −2.37 days, 95% CI −4.21 to −0.53; I² 97%; 8 studies, 972 participants; low certainty); uncertain effect on severity. Probably more non-serious adverse events in treatment (RR 1.34, 95% CI 1.15 to 1.55; moderate certainty).
sources.limitations: Most studies at unclear or high risk of bias; wide variation in interventions and outcomes; incomplete reporting.
sources.funding: Authors declared no conflicts; one author reports NIH NCCAM funding for Cochrane Complementary Medicine paid to institution.
sources.cited_for: Cold duration (treatment), cold prevention, side effects, dose ranges.

sources.title: Zinc for the treatment of the common cold: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
sources.authors: Science M, Johnstone J, Roth DE, Guyatt G, Loeb M.
sources.population: Children and adults with the common cold.
sources.intervention: Oral zinc vs placebo or no treatment.
sources.findings: Shorter cold symptoms with zinc (MD −1.65 days, 95% CI −2.50 to −0.81; I² 95%). Adults: −2.63 days; children: no significant effect (−0.26 days). More adverse events (RR 1.24), bad taste (RR 1.65) and nausea (RR 1.64) with zinc. Authors call for large high-quality trials.
sources.limitations: High heterogeneity in all subgroups.
sources.funding: Canadian Institutes of Health Research (grant listed in the PubMed record); not stated in abstract.
sources.cited_for: Cold duration in adults vs children; inconsistency; side effects.

sources.title: Zinc acetate lozenges for treating the common cold: an individual patient data meta-analysis.
sources.authors: Hemilä H, Petrus EJ, Fitzgerald JT, Prasad A.
sources.population: Common cold patients, mostly women, 80% aged 20–50.
sources.intervention: Zinc acetate lozenges vs placebo.
sources.findings: Colds were 2.73 days (one-stage; 95% CI 1.8 to 3.3) or 2.94 days (two-stage; 95% CI 2.1 to 3.8) shorter with zinc acetate, compared with an average cold length of 7 days. Effect not modified by allergy, smoking, baseline severity, age, sex or ethnicity.
sources.limitations: Only three trials; co-authors appear to include investigators of the pooled trials (author list only; not stated in abstract).
sources.funding: NIH (National Institute on Aging) grant listed in the PubMed record; not stated in abstract.
sources.cited_for: Zinc acetate lozenges and cold duration.

sources.title: Zinc acetate lozenges for the treatment of the common cold: a randomised controlled trial.
sources.authors: Hemilä H, Haukka J, Alho M, Vahtera J, Kivimäki M.
sources.population: Working adults in Finland who usually had at least one cold per winter.
sources.intervention: Zinc acetate lozenges (13 mg elemental zinc) six times a day for up to 5 days vs placebo.
sources.findings: No difference in recovery rate over 10 days (rate ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.08; p=0.10). For 2 days after stopping, the zinc group recovered more slowly (p=0.003). 37% of the zinc group reported no adverse effects vs 69% on placebo.
sources.limitations: Only 87 participants caught colds and were analysed.
sources.funding: Medical Research Council (UK) grant listed in the PubMed record; competing interests: none declared.
sources.cited_for: Inconsistency: a recent double-blind trial found a commercial zinc acetate lozenge ineffective.

sources.title: Effect of zinc supplementation on the immune status of healthy older individuals aged 55-70 years: the ZENITH Study.
sources.authors: Hodkinson CF, Kelly M, Alexander HD, Bradbury I, Robson PJ, Bonham MP, O'Connor JM, Coudray C, Strain JJ, Wallace JM.
sources.journal: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci
sources.population: Apparently healthy adults aged 55–70.
sources.intervention: 15 mg or 30 mg zinc/day for 6 months.
sources.findings: 30 mg/day lowered B-lymphocyte count at month 3 only; 15 mg/day raised the CD4:CD8 ratio at month 6. Authors concluded total zinc intakes up to 40 mg/day had no significant long-term effects on immune status.
sources.limitations: Participant number not given in abstract; immune markers only.
sources.funding: Listed in PubMed as non-US government supported; details not in abstract.
sources.cited_for: No meaningful immune effect of zinc in healthy older adults.

sources.title: Zinc supplementation decreases incidence of infections in the elderly: effect of zinc on generation of cytokines and oxidative stress.
sources.authors: Prasad AS, Beck FW, Bao B, Fitzgerald JT, Snell DC, Steinberg JD, Cardozo LJ.
sources.population: Healthy adults aged 55–87 from a senior center.
sources.intervention: Zinc gluconate, 45 mg elemental zinc/day, or placebo for 12 months.
sources.findings: Infections, TNF-alpha generation and oxidative stress markers were significantly lower with zinc; plasma zinc was higher. At baseline the older participants had lower plasma zinc than younger adults.
sources.limitations: Small single trial; participants had lower baseline zinc; number of infections not given in abstract.
sources.funding: Listed in PubMed as NIH extramural and non-US government supported.
sources.cited_for: Possible reduction in infections in older adults with lower zinc status.

sources.title: Zinc-Induced Hematologic Toxicities: A Systematic Review of Descriptive Studies.
sources.authors: Dutta A, Chaudhary V, Kumari S, Rohita, Sharma KK, Pal B.
sources.population: People with zinc-induced blood abnormalities, reported 1972–2025.
sources.intervention: Excess zinc from oral supplements, denture adhesive creams or coin ingestion; about 50 mg to over 1,500 mg/day for weeks to years.
sources.findings: Anaemia in nearly all cases, often with neutropenia and leukopenia; serum copper low in all patients; often misdiagnosed as myelodysplastic syndrome. Stopping zinc plus copper supplementation usually reversed blood abnormalities within weeks to months; neurological symptoms improved more slowly and sometimes incompletely.
sources.limitations: Case reports only; cannot estimate how common this is.
sources.funding: Authors declared no competing interests.
sources.cited_for: Copper deficiency and blood problems from excess zinc.

sources.title: Zinc: Fact Sheet for Health Professionals
sources.authors: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements
sources.population: General population; groups at risk of inadequacy.
sources.findings: RDAs (11 mg men, 8 mg women), UL 40 mg/day based on copper status, food-content table, absorption (phytates, supplement forms), common-cold summary (inconsistent trials; earlier review found benefit only above 75 mg/day; 2021 meta-analysis found no prevention after rhinovirus inoculation), toxicity (≥50 mg/day interferes with copper, lowers HDL, reduces immune function), interactions, risk groups, and zinc's role in immune function.
sources.limitations: Summary document; last-updated date not recorded at time of reading.
sources.funding: US federal government (NIH).
sources.cited_for: Food table, RDA, upper limit, absorption, copper risk, interactions, risk groups, cold evidence summary.
